Sharp Capacity Thresholds in Linear Associative Memory:
From Top-1 Retrieval to Tail-Average Learning

Nicholas Barnfield    Juno Kim    Eshaan Nichani Affiliation: Harvard University  University of California, Berkeley  Princeton University    Jason D. Lee    Yue M. Lu ††thanks: Correspondence: yuelu@seas.harvard.edu.
August 19, 2026
Abstract

How many key-value associations can a d×dd\times d linear memory store? The answer depends not only on the d2d^{2} degrees of freedom in the memory matrix, but also on the retrieval criterion. Under isotropic Gaussian embeddings, we prove a sharp threshold for top-1 retrieval, where every signal must beat its largest distractor: the critical value of d2/(n​log⁡n)d^{2}/(n\log n) is 22. Above the threshold, we explicitly construct a linear memory that retrieves all nn associations with high probability; below it, no data-dependent linear memory can do so. The log⁡n\log n factor is therefore the unavoidable extreme-value cost of winner-take-all decoding.

Without the logarithmic factor—that is, when n/d2→α∈(0,∞)n/d^{2}\to\alpha\in(0,\infty)—simultaneous top-1 retrieval is impossible. The matched target can nevertheless remain near the top of the ranking. We capture this weaker retrieval goal with the Tail-Average Margin (TAM), which, for list size kk, compares each signal with the average of its kk strongest competitors; a positive TAM margin certifies that the target belongs to the top-kk candidate list. When k/n→r∈(0,1)k/n\to r\in(0,1), we learn the memory by empirical risk minimization with a smoothed TAM objective and derive an exact high-dimensional characterization through a two-parameter scalar variational problem. The result gives limiting laws for signal and competitor scores, margins, and percentile ranks. Sending the ridge parameter to zero after the high-dimensional limit yields a closed-form critical load αc​(r)\alpha_{c}(r) separating vanishing from positive average loss.

The analysis in this work also develops a coupled leave-one-out method for matrix-valued empirical risk problems in which each sample enters many dependent comparisons, a tool that may be useful beyond associative memory.

1 Introduction

Associative memory refers broadly to the ability of a system to store and retrieve relationships between objects. Given a collection of input-output pairs, one would like the system to recover the correct target when presented with a corresponding cue. This basic mechanism appears in many forms, ranging from the first neural network models for pattern learning (Kohonen, 1972; Amari, 1972; Anderson, 1972; Hopfield, 1982; Hopfield, 1984), to modern key-value retrieval systems (Vaswani et al., 2017; Ramsauer et al., 2021; Gershman et al., 2025). Associative memory has also recently attracted attention as a model of factual recall in large language models (Cabannes et al., 2024a; Cabannes et al., 2024b; Jiang et al., 2024; Nichani et al., 2024) as trained transformer layers have been observed to function as key-value memories (Geva et al., 2021; Meng et al., 2022; Bietti et al., 2023).

A central theoretical question in associative memory is: given nn associations, how large must the memory model be in order to retrieve them under a prescribed criterion? In this paper, we study this question in the simple but already nontrivial setting of linear associative memory. Given pairs of key vectors (embeddings) viv_{i} and associated targets (unembeddings) uiu_{i}, we consider a matrix memory model W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} and define the score matrix S=(sj,i)1≤i,j≤nS=(s_{j,i})_{1\leq i,j\leq n} as

sj,i=uj⊤​W​vi,{(ui,vi)}i=1n⊂ℝd×ℝd,W∈ℝd×d.s_{j,i}=u_{j}^{\top}Wv_{i},\qquad\{(u_{i},v_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d},\qquad W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. (1)

This score matrix encodes the predictions for the target when decoding to a fixed vocabulary of size nn. Rather than requiring the output W​viWv_{i} of the memory model on an input viv_{i} to equal its associated target uiu_{i}, as in classical models of associative memory (Hopfield, 1982), we compare the score of the matched target, si,is_{i,i}, with its competing scores (sj,i)j≠i(s_{j,i})_{j\neq i}. The capacity of a linear associative memory depends sharply on how retrieval is defined. We first study the strongest natural criterion, which requires the matched target to outrank every competitor.

This criterion is known as top-1 retrieval, or exact retrieval (Kohonen, 1972; Cabannes et al., 2024a; Cabannes et al., 2024b; Nichani et al., 2024). Under this criterion, each key must retrieve its matched target with the largest score:

si,i>sj,i,∀j≠i,∀i∈[n].s_{i,i}>s_{j,i},\qquad\forall j\neq i,\quad\forall i\in[n]. (2)

This is the natural criterion for exact winner-take-all decoding. It is also the hard-attention (low-temperature) limit of softmax attention mechanisms in transformer-based architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017).

To derive a sharp high-dimensional characterization of top-1 capacity, we study the isotropic Gaussian model

ui,vi∼i.i.d.𝒩⁡(0,Id/d),i∈[n],u_{i},v_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}/d),\qquad i\in[n], (3)

where all vectors in the two collections are mutually independent. This model isolates the effect of high-dimensional interference without imposing additional structure on the stored associations. As one of the main results of this work, Theorem 1 shows that, under (3), the asymptotic ratio d2/(n​log⁡n)d^{2}/(n\log n) has the sharp critical value 22. Specifically, for every fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0,

d2≥(2+ϵ)​n​log⁡n\displaystyle d^{2}\geq(2+\epsilon)n\log n ⟹top-1 retrieval is achievable with high probability,\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad\text{top-1 retrieval is achievable with high probability}, (4)
d2≤(2−ϵ)​n​log⁡n\displaystyle d^{2}\leq(2-\epsilon)n\log n ⟹top-1 retrieval is impossible with high probability.\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad\text{top-1 retrieval is impossible with high probability}.

Here, achievability means that some (data-dependent) linear memory W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} satisfies (2), whereas impossibility means no linear memory can satisfy (2). The critical value 22 was conjectured in an earlier version of this paper and independently in the concurrent work of Giorlandino et al. (2026).

The logarithmic factor in (4) comes from an extreme value. To see this heuristically, fix a query ii and suppose that its competing scores {sj,i}j≠i\{s_{j,i}\}_{j\neq i} behave as independent centered Gaussians. Under the Gaussian model (3), the matched score has natural scale one, while an individual competing score has standard deviation σ≈n/d\sigma\approx\sqrt{n}/d. The largest of the n−1n-1 competitors is therefore about σ​2​log⁡n≈2​n​log⁡n/d\sigma\sqrt{2\log n}\approx\sqrt{2n\log n}/d. Equating this extreme competitor scale with the order-one matched score gives 2​n​log⁡n/d≈1\sqrt{2n\log n}/d\approx 1, or d2≈2​n​log⁡nd^{2}\approx 2n\log n. Theorem 1 makes this prediction rigorous.

The logarithmic penalty is specific to the requirement that every target beat its largest competitor. Removing this factor brings us to the critical load n/d2→α∈(0,∞)n/d^{2}\to\alpha\in(0,\infty), where a linear memory has only a constant number of parameters per association and top-1 retrieval is impossible. Even so, the matched target need not disappear from the ranking: it may still outrank all but a fraction of its competitors. This residual ranking information is useful when a memory access is an intermediate computation whose output is refined by later layers, heads, or rerankers. We thus ask:

At critical load, how close to the top can a linear memory still place every matched target?

We call this coarser notion of retrieval listwise retrieval. Our second main result introduces a convex certificate for listwise retrieval and gives a sharp high-dimensional theory for learning a memory under this criterion.

For a fixed query ii, order the n−1n-1 competing scores as s(1),i≥s(2),i≥⋯≥s(n−1),is_{(1),i}\geq s_{(2),i}\geq\cdots\geq s_{(n-1),i}, and, for a tail fraction r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1], let k=⌈r⁡(n−1)⌉k=\lceil r(n-1)\rceil. Direct top-kk retrieval asks that si,i>s(k),is_{i,i}>s_{(k),i}, so that at most k−1k-1 competitors outrank the matched target. Except when k=1k=1, this rank constraint is nonconvex. Yet the average of the kk largest competing scores is a convex upper bound on s(k),is_{(k),i} (Rockafellar and Uryasev, 2000; Rockafellar and Uryasev, 2002). This motivates us to propose the Tail-Average Margin (TAM) criterion:

si,i>TAMr⁡((sj,i)j≠i):=1k​∑ℓ=1ks(ℓ),i,∀i∈[n].s_{i,i}>\TAM_{r}((s_{j,i})_{j\neq i})\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}s_{(\ell),i},\qquad\forall i\in[n]. (5)

Because TAMr⁡((sj,i)j≠i)≥s(k),i\TAM_{r}((s_{j,i})_{j\neq i})\geq s_{(k),i}, (5) certifies that the matched target has rank at most kk, and hence belongs to the top-kk candidate list. The tail fraction rr controls the resolution of retrieval. At the finest endpoint, r=1/(n−1)r=1/(n-1), TAM is the largest competing score and the criterion recovers the top-1 condition (2); at the coarsest endpoint, r=1r=1, it is the mean competing score. For fixed r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1), TAM therefore controls the collective strength of the top rr-fraction of competitors rather than a single extreme score.

This fractional-rank perspective is in the same spirit as list decoding in coding theory, where the decoder is allowed to retain a controlled list of plausible messages rather than make a unique decision (Elias, 1957; Guruswami, 2007). It is also aligned with listwise ranking losses in information retrieval, which optimize criteria defined on ranked candidate lists rather than on a single pairwise comparison (Cao et al., 2007). For fixed rr, the certified list contains a fixed fraction of the vocabulary; the guarantee is therefore one of percentile rank rather than a sublinear shortlist.

1.1 Summary of main results

Sharp top-1 capacity.

Our first main result is Theorem 1 in Section 2, which identifies the exact capacity of linear associative memory under top-1 retrieval as d2/(n​log⁡n)=2d^{2}/(n\log n)=2. This critical threshold applies to the entire class of data-dependent linear memories, rather than to a particular construction or learning rule.

The achievability proof begins with a classical benchmark model, called the correlation matrix memory (CMM), which stores the associations as a superposition of outer products (Kohonen, 1972; Elhage et al., 2022). Previous work of Nichani et al. (2024) showed that CMM succeeds when d2≥C​n​(log⁡n)4d^{2}\geq Cn(\log n)^{4} for a sufficiently large constant CC. We sharpen this benchmark by proving the sufficient condition lim infd2/(n​log⁡n)>8\liminf d^{2}/(n\log n)>8 (Proposition 1). We then introduce an adaptive sparse repair, which uses CMM on a large coordinate block to store most associations, then corrects wrong (or small-margin) associations using a small reserve block of size o⁡(d)o(d). This reserve-and-repair principle is related in spirit to multiscale constructions for random perceptrons (Kim and Roche, 1998; Abbe et al., 2022; Ding and Sun, 2025). Our construction succeeds throughout the regime lim infd2/(n​log⁡n)>2\liminf d^{2}/(n\log n)>2 (Proposition 2); see Sections 2.1–2.2 for details. Conversely, a dual certificate rules out every linear memory with high probability when lim supd2/(n​log⁡n)<2\limsup d^{2}/(n\log n)<2 (Theorem 1(ii)). Moreover, Section 2.4 presents Conjecture 1, suggested by a simpler surrogate model: a −3​n​log⁡log⁡n-3n\log\log n second-order correction that better captures finite-size behavior.

Tail-Average Margin.

Our second main result gives an exact high-dimensional theory for a convex learning rule based on the listwise criterion (5). With logistic loss ℓ⁡(t)=log⁡(1+e−t)\ell(t)=\log(1+e^{-t}), ridge parameter λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, we consider the estimator

W^∈arg​minW∈ℝd×d⁡{1n​∑i=1nℓ⁡(si,i​(W)−TAMr,β⁡((sj,i​(W))j≠i))+λ2​d2​‖W‖𝖥2}.\widehat{W}\in\argmin_{W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}}\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\left(s_{i,i}(W)-\TAM_{r,\beta}\bigl((s_{j,i}(W))_{j\neq i}\bigr)\right)+\frac{\lambda}{2d^{2}}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert W\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}\right\}. (6)

Here TAMr,β\TAM_{r,\beta} is an exponentially smoothed version of the TAM functional TAMr\TAM_{r} in (5), with β>0\beta>0 the smoothing parameter. For every fixed score vector xx, TAMr,β⁡(x)→TAMr⁡(x)\TAM_{r,\beta}(x)\to\TAM_{r}(x) as β→∞\beta\to\infty. Its precise definition is given in Section 3.1, specifically in (27), and the corresponding convex learning formulation is developed in Section 3.2; see (30). The main goal of the TAM theory is to understand the asymptotic behavior of this ERM in the regime

n,d→∞,nd2→α∈(0,∞),r∈(0,1)​fixed.n,d\to\infty,\qquad\frac{n}{d^{2}}\to\alpha\in(0,\infty),\qquad r\in(0,1)\ \text{fixed}. (7)

Our main asymptotic conclusions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    Scalar reduction. The high-dimensional ERM admits a scalar variational description involving only two parameters, stated in Theorem 2 in Section 4.3;

  2. 2.

    Score and margin laws. The scalar description gives limiting predictions for the fitting loss, the laws of the true and competing scores, and the induced margin and percentile profiles, developed in Section 4 and Section 5;

  3. 3.

    Ridgeless phase transition. In the ridgeless limit, the scalar theory yields a sharp phase transition at a critical load

    αc​(r)=1(1+κr2)​Φ​(κr)+κr​φ​(κr),κr=φ​(Φ−1​(1−r))r,\alpha_{c}(r)=\frac{1}{(1+\kappa_{r}^{2})\Phi(\kappa_{r})+\kappa_{r}\varphi(\kappa_{r})},\qquad\kappa_{r}=\frac{\varphi(\Phi^{-1}(1-r))}{r}, (8)

    where φ\varphi and Φ\Phi denote the standard normal density and distribution function. When α<αc​(r)\alpha<\alpha_{c}(r), the limiting TAM fitting loss vanishes in the ridgeless limit; when α>αc​(r)\alpha>\alpha_{c}(r), it remains positive. Thus αc​(r)\alpha_{c}(r) is the sharp threshold for asymptotically perfect TAM recovery—vanishing average TAM loss and hence successful TAM retrieval for all but a vanishing fraction of keys.

A coupled leave-one-out method.

Our third contribution is methodological: we develop a new coupled leave-one-out method for matrix-valued empirical-risk problems with shared samples. This method forms the technical core of our TAM theory. Classical leave-one-out analyses of high-dimensional MM-estimators remove one independent loss term, leaving an optimizer that is nearly independent of the held-out feature (El Karoui et al., 2013; Lei et al., 2018). That basic decoupling fails here: a stored pair supplies its own signal score, while its target also appears as a competitor for every other query. Removing one pair therefore perturbs order nn loss terms and their data-dependent tail thresholds.

We develop a coupled leave-one-out expansion that tracks this global response. Its key conclusion is that, after all induced changes are accounted for, the leading perturbation of the optimizer is the inverse leave-one-out Hessian applied to the single rank-one feature uh​vh⊤u_{h}v_{h}^{\top}; the remaining terms are lower order. Iterating this expansion and combining it with new spectral and self-averaging estimates yields the Gaussian competitor law and the scalar description in Theorem 2. This method may be of independent interest for other matrix-valued or listwise ERMs in which each observation participates in many dependent comparisons rather than one separable loss term. Section 4.2 develops the coupled reduction, and the supporting estimates are proved in Appendices C–F.

1.2 Related work

Neural associative memory.

Associative memory dates back to early neural models that store patterns through correlations in the weights (Amari, 1972; Anderson, 1972; Nakano, 1972; Kohonen, 1972; Hopfield, 1982; Hopfield, 1984). The Hopfield network (Hopfield, 1982) is the symmetric case, where the goal is to memorize and retrieve the patterns themselves. We focus instead on associative recall: a key should retrieve its paired target, and the two need not coincide (Amari, 1972). In particular, Kohonen (1972) define correlation matrix memory as a sum of rank-one key-target outer products, the construction analyzed in Section 2.1. Bidirectional associative memory is another paired-pattern model based on outer-product updates (Kosko, 1988).

Modern versions of neural networks with built-in associative memory capabilities include the neural Turing machine (Graves et al., 2014), memory networks (Weston et al., 2015), dense associative memory (Krotov and Hopfield, 2016; Lucibello and Mézard, 2024), MCHN (Ramsauer et al., 2021), MCSDM (Kanerva, 1988; Bricken and Pehlevan, 2021), and universal Hopfield networks (Millidge et al., 2022). Binary variants of matrix memory have also been studied in the literature (Willshaw et al., 1969; Gardner, 1987; Hobson, 2011).

Transformers and factual recall.

Transformer models trained on factual recall tasks have been empirically observed to implement associative memory through their weight matrices. Feedforward as well as attention layers have been shown to behave like key-value memories (Geva et al., 2021; Bietti et al., 2023), and the linear memory perspective has been used to study factual editing, induction head tasks, and latent space retrieval (Meng et al., 2022; Bietti et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2024). On the theory side, Nichani et al. (2024) study a sequence-based factual recall task where one token functions as the key, and show that a one-layer transformer solves the task with capacity scaling linearly with parameter count, up to logarithmic factors. This storage scaling has also been empirically observed in large language models (Allen-Zhu and Li, 2024). Related theoretical analyses include optimization dynamics for a single-layer transformer on a token recall task (Vural et al., 2026), and a measure-theoretic formulation of transformers with implicit associative memory mechanisms (Kawata and Suzuki, 2026).

Storage capacity.

Nichani et al. (2024) study the capacity of linear and MLP associative memories with random spherical embeddings, showing in particular that correlation matrix memory succeeds when d2≫n​(log⁡n)4d^{2}\gg n(\log n)^{4}. Cabannes et al. (2024a) propose the exact retrieval criterion and study correlation matrix memory under a weighted data distribution. From an optimization perspective, Cabannes et al. (2024b) study gradient descent under a multiclass logistic formulation, and Kim et al. (2026) compare the capacity of memory matrices obtained by different optimizers under Gaussian embeddings. Compared with these works, our top-1 result identifies the exact statistical threshold d2=2​n​log⁡nd^{2}=2n\log n for arbitrary linear memories. We also introduce the TAM criterion and, to our knowledge, give the first capacity theory for linear associative memory under a listwise retrieval rule.

We also briefly mention that storage capacity has been studied in detail for the Hopfield network and its variants. The capacity d≍nd\asymp n of Hopfield networks is classical, see e.g., McEliece et al. (1987); Folli et al. (2017) and the works cited within, while modern extensions such as dense associative memory have been shown to achieve exponential capacity (Demircigil et al., 2017; Ramsauer et al., 2021; Lucibello and Mézard, 2024). The scaling in these works differ from our results since we decode to a fixed vocabulary of size nn, while the classical Hopfield formulation decodes to the hypercube.

Concurrent work.

The sharp top-1 threshold was conjectured in an earlier version of this paper and independently in the concurrent work of Giorlandino et al. (2026). The latter studies the capacity of linear associative memory under the top-1 retrieval criterion through a decoupled model. In this simplified formulation, the output embeddings {uj}j≤n\{u_{j}\}_{j\leq n} are resampled across constraints, thus removing the statistical dependence structure among the retrieval inequalities in (2). Based on numerical evidence comparing training and test errors, and score distributions, they conjecture that the original and decoupled problems have the same critical capacity. For the decoupled model, they carry out a Gardner-type statistical physics calculation and predict the critical threshold n​log⁡nd2=12\frac{n\log n}{d^{2}}=\frac{1}{2} for top-1 retrieval, which we rigorously prove in Section 2. They further extend both the decoupling conjecture and the capacity calculation to rank-constrained memories, corresponding to two-layer linear MLPs.

Classification and leave-one-out methods.

The TAM learning problem is also connected to high-dimensional classification through its logistic loss. The classical work of Cover (1965) computed the separability capacity of random patterns, and the perceptron capacity was later studied through statistical physics methods, including margin-constrained variants (Gardner, 1988). In ordinary unregularized logistic regression, the existence of the maximum likelihood estimator is equivalent to nonseparability of the labeled data; equivalently, the failure of existence is a linear separability, or capacity, event. Sur and Candès (2019) established a high-dimensional phase transition for this event under Gaussian covariates. A broader line of work in statistical physics studies optimal errors and phase transitions in high-dimensional generalized linear models via the approximate message passing algorithm (Barbier et al., 2019; Aubin et al., 2020; Mignacco et al., 2020). From a technical point of view, our TAM analysis uses a leave-one-out approach, which has played an important role in precise asymptotics for high-dimensional MM-estimators (El Karoui et al., 2013; El Karoui, 2018; Lei et al., 2018). At a conceptual level, this is also the cavity method from spin glass theory (Mézard et al., 1987).

The present problem differs from standard high-dimensional regression and classification in several ways. The unknown is a matrix rather than a vector; the effective covariates are rank-one tensors uj​vi⊤u_{j}v_{i}^{\top} with strong dependencies; each sample contributes both a signal score and a full column of competitor scores; and the TAM threshold is endogenous, selected by the learned scores themselves. These couplings prevent existing leave-one-out theories from applying as black boxes; the resulting cavity calculation is matrix-valued, listwise, and self-consistent in a way that does not arise in standard high-dimensional regression.

Notation

We write

U=[u1⋯un]∈ℝd×nandV=[v1⋯vn]∈ℝd×nU=[u_{1}\ \cdots\ u_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad V=[v_{1}\ \cdots\ v_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} (9)

for the target and key matrices, respectively. Under the Gaussian model (3), d​U\sqrt{d}\,U and d​V\sqrt{d}\,V are independent standard Gaussian matrices in ℝd×n\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}. vec⁡(⋅)\vecop(\cdot) denotes column-wise vectorization.

We write X​=(d)​YX\overset{(d)}{=}Y when two random variables, vectors, or matrices have the same distribution. For matrices, ⟨A,B⟩\langle A,B\rangle is understood as the matrix inner product.

We use Xn=Oℙ​(Yn)X_{n}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(Y_{n}) and Xn=oℙ​(Yn)X_{n}=o_{\mathbb{P}}(Y_{n}) in their standard meanings: Xn/YnX_{n}/Y_{n} is tight and converges to zero in probability, respectively. These notations record behavior at the displayed scale. In situations where we need tail control, especially uniformly over polynomial-size index sets, we use stochastic domination (Erdős and Yau, 2017). Let {Xα(n)}α∈ℐn\{X_{\alpha}^{(n)}\}_{\alpha\in\mathcal{I}_{n}} be nonnegative random variables, where ℐn\mathcal{I}_{n} may depend on nn and has polynomial cardinality, and let Yn≥0Y_{n}\geq 0 be deterministic. We write

Xα(n)=𝒪≺​(Yn)uniformly in ​α∈ℐnX_{\alpha}^{(n)}=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(Y_{n})\qquad\text{uniformly in }\alpha\in\mathcal{I}_{n} (10)

if, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 and D>0D>0,

ℙ⁡(maxα∈ℐn⁡Xα(n)>nε​Yn)≤n−D\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal{I}_{n}}X_{\alpha}^{(n)}>n^{\varepsilon}Y_{n}\right)\leq n^{-D} (11)

for all sufficiently large nn. When ℐn\mathcal{I}_{n} is a singleton, we suppress the uniformity qualifier. Thus, (10) permits an nεn^{\varepsilon} slack in exchange for n−Dn^{-D} tail control, uniformly over the indicated polynomial-size index set.

2 Top-1 retrieval: the sharp threshold

Throughout this section, we work under the Gaussian model (3) and the top-1 retrieval criterion (2). For a realization (U,V)(U,V) and a matrix W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, define the perfect-retrieval condition

𝖯𝖱(W;U,V)⟺ui⊤Wvi>maxj≠iuj⊤Wvifor every i∈[n].\mathsf{PR}(W;U,V)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u_{i}^{\top}Wv_{i}>\max_{j\neq i}u_{j}^{\top}Wv_{i}\quad\text{for every }i\in[n]. (12)

We study the random feasibility event

𝖯𝖱n≔{(U,V):there exists W∈ℝd×d such that 𝖯𝖱(W;U,V) occurs}.\mathsf{PR}_{n}\coloneqq\left\{(U,V)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\text{there exists }W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\text{ such that }\mathsf{PR}(W;U,V)\text{ occurs}\right\}. (13)

The matrix WW in this definition may depend arbitrarily on the realized data (U,V)(U,V). Accordingly, 𝖯𝖱n\mathsf{PR}_{n} asks whether a random instance is retrievable by any linear memory, without imposing a particular learning rule.

Theorem 1 (Sharp top-1 threshold).

Along any sequence n,d→∞n,d\to\infty:

  1. (i)

    If lim infd2n​log⁡n>2\liminf\frac{d^{2}}{n\log n}>2, then ℙ⁡(𝖯𝖱n)→1\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{PR}_{n})\to 1.

  2. (ii)

    If lim supd2n​log⁡n<2\limsup\frac{d^{2}}{n\log n}<2, then ℙ⁡(𝖯𝖱n)→0\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{PR}_{n})\to 0.

The sharp threshold at d2=2​n​log⁡nd^{2}=2n\log n was conjectured in an earlier version of this paper and independently in the concurrent work of Giorlandino et al. (2026). We establish the achievability and impossibility directions in Section 2.2 and Section 2.3, respectively. Before turning to these proofs, Section 2.1 introduces the correlation matrix memory (CMM), a classical outer-product construction. Its analysis exposes the extreme-value origin of the logarithmic factor and motivates the sparse repair used in the achievability proof. We note that an order-wise Ω⁡(n​log⁡n)\Omega(n\log n) lower bound is also suggested in Nichani et al. (2024, Theorem 7) via an information-theoretic argument, but it does not identify the sharp constant and applies only to finite-bit learners. Finally, Section 2.4 studies finite-size scaling and proposes a second-order conjecture.

2.1 Correlation matrix memory and the logarithmic factor

The simplest linear memory stores each association by its outer product and superposes the results:

W𝖢𝖬𝖬≔U​V⊤=∑k=1nuk​vk⊤.W_{\mathsf{CMM}}\coloneqq UV^{\top}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}u_{k}v_{k}^{\top}. (14)

This is the classical correlation matrix memory (CMM) (Kohonen, 1972) and is the direct analogue of the classical self-organizing network (Amari, 1972) for asymmetric key and target pairs. When the key viv_{i} is presented, the kkth summand contributes uk​⟨vk,vi⟩u_{k}\langle v_{k},v_{i}\rangle: the desired vector uiu_{i} appears with coefficient ‖vi‖2\|v_{i}\|^{2}, while the remaining terms create cross-talk. The rule is transparent and admits a rank-one update whenever an association is added or removed. It also illustrates superposition: the stored vectors need not be mutually orthogonal for retrieval to succeed (Elhage et al., 2022).

To understand the performance of this particular, data-dependent memory, write

αn≔nd2\alpha_{n}\coloneqq\frac{n}{d^{2}}

and denote the CMM scores by sj,i=uj⊤​W𝖢𝖬𝖬​vis_{j,i}=u_{j}^{\top}W_{\mathsf{CMM}}v_{i}. Expanding (14) gives

si,i\displaystyle s_{i,i} =‖ui‖2​‖vi‖2+∑k≠i⟨ui,uk⟩​⟨vk,vi⟩,\displaystyle={\|u_{i}\|^{2}\|v_{i}\|^{2}}+\sum_{k\neq i}\langle u_{i},u_{k}\rangle\langle v_{k},v_{i}\rangle, (15)
sj,i\displaystyle s_{j,i} =⟨uj,ui⟩​‖vi‖2+‖uj‖2​⟨vj,vi⟩+∑k∉{i,j}⟨uj,uk⟩​⟨vk,vi⟩,j≠i.\displaystyle=\langle u_{j},u_{i}\rangle\|v_{i}\|^{2}+\|u_{j}\|^{2}\langle v_{j},v_{i}\rangle+\sum_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\langle u_{j},u_{k}\rangle\langle v_{k},v_{i}\rangle,\qquad j\neq i. (16)

Under the Gaussian model, ∥ui∥2=1+Oℙ(d−1/2)\|u_{i}\|^{2}=1+O_{\mathbb{P}}(d^{-1/2}) and ∥vi∥2=1+Oℙ(d−1/2)\|v_{i}\|^{2}=1+O_{\mathbb{P}}(d^{-1/2}), so the first term in (15) is 1+Oℙ(d−1/2)1+O_{\mathbb{P}}(d^{-1/2}). Conditional on (ui,vi)(u_{i},v_{i}), the summands in the cross-talk term of (15) are independent and centered, each with variance ‖ui‖2​‖vi‖2/d2\|u_{i}\|^{2}\|v_{i}\|^{2}/d^{2}. Their sum therefore has variance approximately n/d2=αnn/d^{2}=\alpha_{n} and is approximately Gaussian by the central limit theorem.

Turning to a competitor score, the same conditional central limit argument applies to the cross-talk sum over k∉{i,j}k\notin\{i,j\} in (16). The remaining k=ik=i and k=jk=j contributions, ⟨uj,ui⟩​‖vi‖2\langle u_{j},u_{i}\rangle\|v_{i}\|^{2} and ‖uj‖2​⟨vj,vi⟩\|u_{j}\|^{2}\langle v_{j},v_{i}\rangle, respectively, are only Oℙ(d−1/2)O_{\mathbb{P}}(d^{-1/2}). At the scale d2≍n​log⁡nd^{2}\asymp n\log n, they and the norm fluctuations above are therefore Oℙ(d−1/2)=oℙ(αn)O_{\mathbb{P}}(d^{-1/2})=o_{\mathbb{P}}(\sqrt{\alpha_{n}}).

Combining these estimates suggests the following leading-order Gaussian picture for the scores associated with a fixed query:

si,i≈1+αn​Zi,sj,i≈αn​Zj,i,j≠i.s_{i,i}\approx 1+\sqrt{\alpha_{n}}\,Z_{i},\qquad s_{j,i}\approx\sqrt{\alpha_{n}}\,Z_{j,i},\quad j\neq i. (17)

Here the variables on the right are heuristically treated as independent standard Gaussians. The exact one-column representation in Lemma 3 provides a finite-(n,d)(n,d) description underlying this picture. For a fixed ordered pair i≠ji\neq j, (17) predicts

si,i−sj,i≈1+2​αn​Gj,i,Gj,i∼𝒩⁡(0,1),s_{i,i}-s_{j,i}\approx 1+\sqrt{2\alpha_{n}}\,G_{j,i},\qquad G_{j,i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),

and hence, by standard Gaussian tail bounds,

ℙ⁡(si,i≤sj,i)≈exp⁡(−14​αn).\mathbb{P}(s_{i,i}\leq s_{j,i})\approx\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{4\alpha_{n}}\right).

Perfect retrieval requires all n⁡(n−1)n(n-1) such margins to be positive. A union bound therefore predicts

ℙ⁡(W𝖢𝖬𝖬 fails perfect retrieval)≲n2​exp⁡(−14​αn)=exp⁡(2​log⁡n−d24​n),\mathbb{P}\big(\text{$W_{\mathsf{CMM}}$ fails perfect retrieval}\big)\lesssim n^{2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{4\alpha_{n}}\right)=\exp\!\left(2\log n-\frac{d^{2}}{4n}\right), (18)

which vanishes whenever lim infd2/(n​log⁡n)>8\liminf d^{2}/(n\log n)>8. This also reveals the origin of the logarithmic factor: cross-talk has size n/d\sqrt{n}/d, but the worst of quadratically many Gaussian-like margins incurs an additional log⁡n\sqrt{\log n} extreme-value factor.

Previously, Nichani et al. (2024, Theorem 1) proved that CMM succeeds with high probability when d2≥C​n​(log⁡n)4d^{2}\geq Cn(\log n)^{4} for a sufficiently large constant CC. The calculation above sharpens this sufficient condition to the n​log⁡nn\log n scale and predicts the leading constant 88. The following proposition makes this improvement rigorous.

Proposition 1 (CMM succeeds above constant 88).

Along any sequence n,d→∞n,d\to\infty,

lim infd2n​log⁡n>8⟹ℙ⁡(𝖯𝖱⁡(W𝖢𝖬𝖬,U,V))→1.\liminf\frac{d^{2}}{n\log n}>8\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathbb{P}\big(\mathsf{PR}(W_{\mathsf{CMM}};U,V)\big)\to 1.
Proof.

See Appendix A.2. ∎

This sufficient constant 88 is nevertheless four times the optimal constant 22 in Theorem 1 (and one can show that this is unimprovable for CMM). Where does this gap come from? The calculation leading to (18) examines one pairwise margin at a time and then protects all n⁡(n−1)n(n-1) margins by a union bound. This does not require the margins to be independent, but it discards their strong dependence. For a fixed query viv_{i}, the signal score si,is_{i,i} is realized only once and is shared by every comparison, whereas, at leading order, the competitor scores {sj,i:j≠i}\{s_{j,i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}j\neq i\} behave as independent Gaussians. The exact distributional representation behind this claim is given in Appendix A.1. The natural query-wise object is therefore

si,i−maxj≠i⁡sj,i≈1+αn​Zi−2​αn​log⁡n.s_{i,i}-\max_{j\neq i}s_{j,i}\approx 1+\sqrt{\alpha_{n}}Z_{i}-\sqrt{2\alpha_{n}\log n}.

Here 2​αn​log⁡n\sqrt{2\alpha_{n}\log n} comes from the standard estimate for the maximum of nn independent Gaussian variables with variance αn\alpha_{n}. The constant 88 arises in the all-pairs argument because it repeatedly pays for fluctuations of the same signal score as though each comparison were a separate bad event; the query-wise picture pays for the maximum of the competitors only once.

If d2/(n​log⁡n)>2d^{2}/(n\log n)>2 by a fixed amount, the display above predicts a positive margin for any typical query. Perfect retrieval, however, requires all nn queries to succeed, and a typical-query calculation cannot rule out a small set with unusually low margins. Thus CMM correctly handles the bulk at constant 22, but by itself does not provide the required all-query guarantee. This naturally suggests a sparse correction: retain the CMM solution for most queries and modify it only to repair the exceptional ones. Section 2.2 makes this idea precise.

2.2 Achievability by adaptive sparse repair

We reserve a vanishing fraction of the coordinates for repair and use the rest to form a base CMM. Independence of the reserved block then allows us to repair only the deficient queries. Specifically, we construct a block-diagonal memory

W⋆≔diag⁡(W0,W1),W^{\star}\coloneqq\diag(W^{0},W^{1}),

Here W0∈ℝd0×d0W^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}\times d_{0}} is the base memory and W1∈ℝd1×d1W^{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{1}} is the repair; the block dimensions d0,d1d_{0},d_{1} are specified below. Split every vector into independent coordinate blocks ui=(ui0,ui1)u_{i}=(u_{i}^{0},u_{i}^{1}) and vi=(vi0,vi1)v_{i}=(v_{i}^{0},v_{i}^{1}) of dimensions

d1=⌊d(logn)−1/8⌋,d0=d−d1.d_{1}=\left\lfloor d(\log n)^{-1/8}\right\rfloor,\qquad d_{0}=d-d_{1}.

The large block stores all associations using the rescaled CMM

W0≔d2d02​∑k=1nuk0​(vk0)⊤,sj,i≔(uj0)⊤​W0​vi0.\displaystyle W^{0}\coloneqq\frac{d^{2}}{d_{0}^{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}u_{k}^{0}(v_{k}^{0})^{\top},\qquad s_{j,i}\coloneqq(u_{j}^{0})^{\top}W^{0}v_{i}^{0}.

Its retrieval margin for query ii is

mi≔si,i−maxj≠i⁡sj,i.m_{i}\coloneqq s_{i,i}-\max_{j\neq i}s_{j,i}.

For a tolerance γ>0\gamma>0 (to be chosen later), call a query deficient when its margin is at most γ\gamma, and collect these queries in

ℬ≔{i:mi≤γ}.\mathcal{B}\coloneqq\{i\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}m_{i}\leq\gamma\}.

For each i∈ℬi\in\mathcal{B}, the coefficient 2​γ−mi2\gamma-m_{i} is the amount by which we aim to raise its margin. We therefore use the reserved block to add the targeted rank-one corrections

W1≔d2d12​∑i∈ℬ(2​γ−mi)​ui1​(vi1)⊤.W^{1}\coloneqq\frac{d^{2}}{d_{1}^{2}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}(2\gamma-m_{i})u_{i}^{1}(v_{i}^{1})^{\top}.

Both ℬ\mathcal{B} and the correction coefficients depend only on the large block and are thus independent of the coordinates used for repair.

Suppose lim infn→∞d2/(n​log⁡n)>2\liminf_{n\to\infty}d^{2}/(n\log n)>2. Choose constants cc and γ∈(0,1/2)\gamma\in(0,1/2) such that

2<c<lim infn→∞d2n​log⁡n,c​(1−2​γ)2>2,2<c<\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{d^{2}}{n\log n},\qquad c(1-2\gamma)^{2}>2,

and apply the construction above with this value of γ\gamma. Then

ℙ⁡(𝖯𝖱⁡(W⋆,U,V))→1.\mathbb{P}\big(\mathsf{PR}(W^{\star};U,V)\big)\to 1.

Consequently, Theorem 1(i) holds.

Remark 1 (Relation to perceptron constructions).

The sparse-repair argument in our proof is related in spirit to multiscale majority constructions for random perceptrons, where successive fresh coordinate blocks are used to improve the constraints with the weakest current margins (Kim and Roche, 1998; Abbe et al., 2022). In the related construction of Ding and Sun (2025), the deficits from a main construction are also filled using a small coordinate block. In contrast, our repair is one-shot: a single independent block targets the vanishing set of CMM-deficient queries through weighted rank-one corrections.

2.3 Impossibility via a dual certificate

We now prove the impossibility direction of Theorem 1. The argument has a useful geometric interpretation. For each ordered comparison i≠ji\neq j, define the matrix

Ai​j≔(ui−uj)​vi⊤.A_{ij}\coloneqq(u_{i}-u_{j})v_{i}^{\top}.

A memory WW retrieves every association if and only if ⟨W,Ai​j⟩>0\langle W,A_{ij}\rangle>0 for every i≠ji\neq j. Thus to show impossibility, it is enough to find nonnegative coefficients λ=(λi​j)\lambda=(\lambda_{ij}), not all zero, such that

∑i≠jλi​j​Ai​j=0.\sum_{i\neq j}\lambda_{ij}A_{ij}=0.

Indeed, taking the Frobenius inner product with such a WW would make the left-hand side both zero and strictly positive, a contradiction. Such a nontrivial nonnegative linear dependence among these comparison matrices is our dual certificate. The same principle underlies classical results on random half-spaces and linear separability (Wendel, 1962; Cover, 1965).

The proof constructs the certificate in two stages. First, we choose positive coefficients for which the above weighted sum is already close to zero; the threshold 22 ensures that there are enough comparisons for this approximate cancellation. Second, we show that small adjustments to these coefficients can produce any sufficiently small matrix perturbation, so that the sum can be made to be exactly zero while keeping all coefficients positive.

Proof of Theorem 1(ii).

Since the threshold clearly must be monotonic in nn, we may assume without loss of generality that

12≤d2n​log⁡n≤c<2.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\leq\frac{d^{2}}{n\log n}\leq c<2.

We will use the index cutoff r:=⌊n​(log⁡n)−2⌋r\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\lfloor n(\log n)^{-2}\rfloor to construct the dual certificate. For an array λ=(λi​j)i>r,j≤r\lambda=(\lambda_{ij})_{i>r,\,j\leq r}, define the linear map

𝒜⁡(λ):=∑i=r+1n∑j=1rλi​j​(ui−uj)​vi⊤.\displaystyle\mathcal{A}(\lambda)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{r}\lambda_{ij}(u_{i}-u_{j})v_{i}^{\top}.

If some W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} retrieves every association, it would follow that for every nonzero array λ≥0\lambda\geq 0,

⟨W,𝒜⁡(λ)⟩𝖥=∑i=r+1n∑j=1rλi​j​(ui−uj)⊤​W​vi>0.\displaystyle\langle W,\mathcal{A}(\lambda)\rangle_{\mathsf{F}}=\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{r}\lambda_{ij}(u_{i}-u_{j})^{\top}Wv_{i}>0.

It therefore suffices to construct an array λ\lambda with strictly positive entries such that 𝒜⁡(λ)=0\mathcal{A}(\lambda)=0. We first construct a positive array for which 𝒜⁡(λ)\mathcal{A}(\lambda) is small.

Lemma 1.

With probability tending to 11, there exists an array λ\lambda such that

mini>r,j≤r⁡λi​j≥1r​log⁡n,‖𝒜⁡(λ)‖𝖥=o⁡(nd​log⁡n).\displaystyle\min_{i>r,j\leq r}\lambda_{ij}\geq\frac{1}{r\log n},\qquad\|\mathcal{A}(\lambda)\|_{\mathsf{F}}=o\left(\frac{n}{d\log n}\right).

We next show the following uniform lower bound.

Lemma 2.

There is a constant c0>0c_{0}>0 such that, with probability tending to 11,

inf‖X‖𝖥=1∑i=r+1n∑j=1r|(ui−uj)⊤​X​vi|≥c0​r​nd.\displaystyle\inf_{\mathinner{\!\left\lVert X\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}=1}\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{r}|(u_{i}-u_{j})^{\top}Xv_{i}|\geq c_{0}\frac{rn}{d}.

Moreover on this event,

c0r​nd{X∈ℝd×d:‖X‖𝖥≤1}⊆{𝒜(δ):|δi​j|≤1}.\displaystyle c_{0}\frac{rn}{d}\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert X\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}\leq 1\}\subseteq\{\mathcal{A}(\delta)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}|\delta_{ij}|\leq 1\}.

since the expectation is positive and continuous on the unit circle a2+s2=1a^{2}+s^{2}=1. Therefore, with probability tending to 11, simultaneously for every x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R},

1r​∑j=1r|d​uj⊤​x−s|≥c0​‖x‖2+s2≥c0​‖x‖.\displaystyle\frac{1}{r}\sum_{j=1}^{r}|\sqrt{d}\,u_{j}^{\top}x-s|\geq c_{0}\sqrt{\mathinner{\!\left\lVert x\right\rVert}^{2}+s^{2}}\geq c_{0}\|x\|.

∑j=1r|(ui−uj)⊤​x|≥c0​rd​‖x‖,∀x∈ℝd.\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{r}|(u_{i}-u_{j})^{\top}x|\geq c_{0}\frac{r}{\sqrt{d}}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert x\right\rVert},\qquad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

A similar argument for the vectors vr+1,…,vnv_{r+1},\ldots,v_{n} also gives with probability tending to 11,

∑i=r+1n|x⊤​vi|≥c0​nd​‖x‖∀x∈ℝd.\displaystyle\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}|x^{\top}v_{i}|\geq c_{0}\frac{n}{\sqrt{d}}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert x\right\rVert}\qquad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

X⊤​X=∑k=1dμk​ek​ek⊤,∑k=1dμk=1.\displaystyle X^{\top}X=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\mu_{k}e_{k}e_{k}^{\top},\qquad\sum_{k=1}^{d}\mu_{k}=1.

For every i>ri>r, by Cauchy–Schwarz,

‖X​vi‖\displaystyle\mathinner{\!\left\lVert Xv_{i}\right\rVert} =(∑k=1dμk​(ek⊤​vi)2)1/2≥∑k=1dμk​|ek⊤​vi|.\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{k=1}^{d}\mu_{k}(e_{k}^{\top}v_{i})^{2}\right)^{1/2}\geq\sum_{k=1}^{d}\mu_{k}|e_{k}^{\top}v_{i}|.

∑i=r+1n∑j=1r|(ui−uj)⊤​X​vi|\displaystyle\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{r}|(u_{i}-u_{j})^{\top}Xv_{i}| ≥c0​rd​∑i=r+1n‖X​vi‖\displaystyle\geq c_{0}\frac{r}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert Xv_{i}\right\rVert}
≥c0​rd​∑k=1dμk​∑i=r+1n|ek⊤​vi|≥c0​r​nd.\displaystyle\geq c_{0}\frac{r}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{k=1}^{d}\mu_{k}\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}|e_{k}^{\top}v_{i}|\geq c_{0}\frac{rn}{d}.

This proves the first claim. For the second claim, define the set

𝒦:={𝒜(δ):|δi​j|≤1}.\displaystyle\mathcal{K}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\{\mathcal{A}(\delta)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}|\delta_{ij}|\leq 1\}.

𝒦\mathcal{K} is convex and compact, and it holds that

supY∈𝒦⟨X,Y⟩𝖥\displaystyle\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{K}}\langle X,Y\rangle_{\mathsf{F}} =sup|δi​j|≤1∑i=r+1n∑j=1rδi​j​(ui−uj)⊤​X​vi\displaystyle=\sup_{|\delta_{ij}|\leq 1}\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{r}\delta_{ij}(u_{i}-u_{j})^{\top}Xv_{i}
=∑i=r+1n∑j=1r|(ui−uj)⊤​X​vi|≥c0​r​nd​‖X‖𝖥.\displaystyle=\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{r}|(u_{i}-u_{j})^{\top}Xv_{i}|\geq c_{0}\frac{rn}{d}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert X\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}.
