⟨X,Z⟩𝖥>supY∈𝒦⟨X,Y⟩𝖥≥‖X‖𝖥​‖Z‖𝖥,\displaystyle\langle X,Z\rangle_{\mathsf{F}}>\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{K}}\langle X,Y\rangle_{\mathsf{F}}\geq\mathinner{\!\left\lVert X\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert Z\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}},

a contradiction. ∎

Now from Lemma 1, with probability tending to 11, there exists an array λ\lambda satisfying

λi​j≥1r​log⁡n,‖𝒜⁡(λ)‖𝖥=o⁡(nd​log⁡n),\displaystyle\lambda_{ij}\geq\frac{1}{r\log n},\qquad\|\mathcal{A}(\lambda)\|_{\mathsf{F}}=o\left(\frac{n}{d\log n}\right),

while Lemma 2 implies that, again with probability tending to 11,

c0​n2​d​log⁡n{X:‖X‖𝖥≤1}⊆{𝒜(δ):|δi​j|≤12​r​log⁡n}.\displaystyle\frac{c_{0}n}{2d\log n}\{X\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert X\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}\leq 1\}\subseteq\left\{\mathcal{A}(\delta)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}|\delta_{ij}|\leq\frac{1}{2r\log n}\right\}.

It follows that there exists an array δ\delta satisfying

|δi​j|\displaystyle|\delta_{ij}| ≤12​r​log⁡n,𝒜⁡(δ)=−𝒜⁡(λ).\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2r\log n},\qquad\mathcal{A}(\delta)=-\mathcal{A}(\lambda).

Then 𝒜⁡(λ+δ)=0\mathcal{A}(\lambda+\delta)=0 by linearity and

λi​j+δi​j≥1r​log⁡n−12​r​log⁡n=12​r​log⁡n>0.\displaystyle\lambda_{ij}+\delta_{ij}\geq\frac{1}{r\log n}-\frac{1}{2r\log n}=\frac{1}{2r\log n}>0.

This completes the proof. ∎

2.4 Finite-size scaling and a second-order conjecture

We conclude this section with a numerical study of the top-1 transition. Our goal is to compare its location at moderate dimension with the leading-order threshold in Theorem 1. In our experiments, we learn the memory matrix using ridge-regularized multiclass softmax cross-entropy,

W^𝖢𝖤≔arg​minW∈ℝd×d{∑i=1n[−si,i+log∑j=1nesj,i]+λ​n2​d2‖W‖𝖥2},λ>0.\widehat{W}_{\mathsf{CE}}\coloneqq\argmin_{W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[-s_{i,i}+\log\sum_{j=1}^{n}e^{s_{j,i}}\right]+\frac{\lambda n}{2d^{2}}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert W\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}\right\},\qquad\lambda>0. (21)

This objective provides a constructive search for a retrieving memory. Indeed, if WW has minimum retrieval margin γ=mini⁡minj≠i⁡(si,i−sj,i)>0\gamma=\min_{i}\min_{j\neq i}(s_{i,i}-s_{j,i})>0, then the unregularized cross-entropy at t​WtW is at most n⁡(n−1)​e−t​γn(n-1)e^{-t\gamma} and hence tends to zero as t→∞t\to\infty. Consequently, as the effective ridge coefficient tends to zero, the minimizer in (21) retrieves whenever a strict retrieving memory exists: one can let t→∞t\to\infty slowly enough that both the cross-entropy and ridge penalty vanish, whereas any nonretrieving matrix incurs cross-entropy at least log⁡2\log 2.

On the feasible side, the norm needed to attain a fixed small loss grows as the best retrieval margin shrinks. We therefore use the observed peak of ‖W^𝖢𝖤‖𝖥/d\|\widehat{W}_{\mathsf{CE}}\|_{\mathsf{F}}/d under weak ridge regularization as an empirical proxy for the transition. For each dimension, we sweep the load c=n​log⁡n/d2c=n\log n/d^{2}, using the effective ridge coefficient λ​n/d2=10−8\lambda n/d^{2}=10^{-8}. The results are shown in Figure 1.

Because cc is the reciprocal of the ratio d2/(n​log⁡n)d^{2}/(n\log n) used in Theorem 1, the critical value is 1/21/2 in the present normalization rather than 22. Panel a shows a pronounced peak at every dimension. Denoting its location by c^​(d)\widehat{c}(d), we find that c^​(d)\widehat{c}(d) lies above 1/21/2 and drifts only slowly toward it as dd increases. Thus while Theorem 1 captures the leading location of the transition, the simulations exhibit a substantial finite-size correction. This motivates the following conjecture for the second-order correction to the threshold.

Conjecture 1 (Second-order correction to the top-1 threshold).

Let dc​(n)d_{\mathrm{c}}(n) be the smallest integer dd for which ℙ⁡(𝖯𝖱n)≥1/2\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{PR}_{n})\geq 1/2. Then

dc2​(n)=n⁡(2​log⁡n−3​log⁡log⁡n+o⁡(log⁡log⁡n)).\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}(n)=n\bigl(2\log n-3\log\log n+o(\log\log n)\bigr). (22)

Conjecture 1 is suggested by a simpler model. In the original problem, the n2n^{2} score directions vec⁡(uj​vi⊤)=vi⊗uj\operatorname{vec}(u_{j}v_{i}^{\top})=v_{i}\otimes u_{j} have a correlated Kronecker structure. Suppose instead that we replace them by n2n^{2} independent isotropic Gaussian vectors in ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}, while leaving the top-1 condition (2) unchanged. The score map then has independent Gaussian rows, which allows us to apply the standard conic kinematic formula (Amelunxen et al., 2014). The resulting statistical-dimension calculation gives (22). We omit this calculation, since it does not apply directly to the original model. Proving the conjecture for linear associative memory is left to future work.

The conjecture also appears to be supported by the simulations. Conjecture 1 predicts the threshold to satisfy

dc2​(n)n−2​log⁡n=−3​log⁡log⁡n+o⁡(log⁡log⁡n).\frac{d_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}(n)}{n}-2\log n=-3\log\log n+o(\log\log n).

Panel b plots the numerical peak locations according to the above formula. The fitted slope −2.97-2.97 gives an excellent fit with the predicted slope −3-3. In particular, (22) predicts the critical load cc to converge to 1/21/2 at a rate of O⁡(log⁡log⁡nlog⁡n)O(\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}), explaining the slow convergence.

3 Listwise retrieval and the Tail-Average Margin

Top-1 retrieval has the finest possible resolution: each query must rank its matched target first. This is natural for final decoding. At an intermediate stage, however, it may be enough to keep the target among the strongest candidates and let later computation refine the choice. This motivates the coarser, listwise notion studied here.

A direct listwise requirement would ask the signal score to beat a high competitor quantile, thereby ensuring that the correct target belongs to a controlled candidate set. This rank condition is natural, but it is non-convex and combinatorial. We therefore use a convex certificate: we ask the signal score to beat the average of the strongest competitors. We call the resulting functional the Tail-Average Margin (TAM). TAM is a listwise retrieval criterion in its own right: it controls the mass of strong distractors rather than only the single largest one, while retaining enough convex structure for optimization and asymptotic analysis.

In this section we define the TAM functional, record its basic properties, and formulate the corresponding learning problem and performance criteria for linear associative memory. In the next section, we derive an asymptotic theory of TAM learning in the quadratic regime d2≍nd^{2}\asymp n, with a fixed tail fraction r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1).

3.1 The Tail-Average Margin functional

Let x=(x1,…,xm)∈ℝmx=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and fix a tail fraction r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1]. Set k≔⌈r​m⌉k\coloneqq\lceil rm\rceil.

Definition 1 (Tail-Average Margin).

The Tail-Average Margin (TAM) at level rr is

TAMr⁡(x)≔1k​∑j=1kx(j),\TAM_{r}(x)\coloneqq\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}x_{(j)}, (23)

where x(1)≥x(2)≥⋯≥x(m)x_{(1)}\geq x_{(2)}\geq\cdots\geq x_{(m)} are the order statistics of xx.

We note two boundary cases: TAM1/m⁡(x)=maxj⁡xj\TAM_{1/m}(x)=\max_{j}x_{j} (take k=1k=1), and TAM1⁡(x)=1m​∑jxj\TAM_{1}(x)=\tfrac{1}{m}\sum_{j}x_{j} (take k=mk=m). For fixed r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1), TAM then interpolates strictly between the maximum and the mean by averaging over the top rr-fraction of entries.

The TAM criterion is a conservative certificate for top-kk list retrieval. Indeed, since

TAMr⁡(x)=1k​∑j=1kx(j)≥x(k),\TAM_{r}(x)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}x_{(j)}\geq x_{(k)}, (24)

the inequality si,i>TAMr⁡((sj,i)j≠i)s_{i,i}>\TAM_{r}((s_{j,i})_{j\neq i}) implies si,i>s(k),is_{i,i}>s_{(k),i} for the ordered competitor scores in column ii. Hence at most k−1k-1 competitors can outrank the signal. In this sense, exact top-1 retrieval implies TAM retrieval, and TAM retrieval implies inclusion of the correct item in the top-kk candidate list.

The TAM functional is essentially a reparametrization of the empirical Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) studied extensively in the quantitative risk literature; see e.g., Rockafellar and Uryasev (2000). A classical observation is that TAM admits a convex variational representation,

TAMr⁡(x)=minμ∈ℝ⁡{μ+1k​∑j=1m(xj−μ)+},\TAM_{r}(x)\;=\;\min_{\mu\in\mathbb{R}}\Bigg\{\mu+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{m}(x_{j}-\mu)_{+}\Bigg\}, (25)

where (x)+=max⁡{x,0}(x)_{+}=\max\left\{x,0\right\} is the hinge function. The minimizer μ⋆=x(k)\mu^{\star}=x_{(k)} of (25) is the empirical (1−r)(1-r)-quantile of xx, also known as the Value-at-Risk. The optimal value of (25) is then the mean of the exceedances of xx above this quantile, which recovers the tail-average interpretation of (23). As an immediate consequence of (25), we see that x↦TAMr⁡(x)x\mapsto\TAM_{r}(x) is convex on ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, as it is the pointwise minimum over μ\mu of functions jointly convex in (x,μ)(x,\mu).

For optimization it is convenient to replace the piecewise-linear hinge (⋅)+(\cdot)_{+} in (25) with a differentiable surrogate. For a smoothing parameter β>0\beta>0, let

ϕβ​(t)≔1β​log⁡(1+eβ​t)\phi_{\beta}(t)\;\coloneqq\;\frac{1}{\beta}\log(1+e^{\beta t}) (26)

denote the softplus function, and define the smoothed TAM

TAMr,β⁡(x)≔minμ∈ℝ⁡{μ+1k​∑j=1mϕβ​(xj−μ)}.\TAM_{r,\beta}(x)\;\coloneqq\;\min_{\mu\in\mathbb{R}}\Bigg\{\mu+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\phi_{\beta}(x_{j}-\mu)\Bigg\}. (27)

Since ϕβ\phi_{\beta} is convex, TAMr,β\TAM_{r,\beta} is convex in xx; moreover ϕβ​(t)→(t)+\phi_{\beta}(t)\to(t)_{+} pointwise as β→∞\beta\to\infty, and hence TAMr,β⁡(x)→TAMr⁡(x)\TAM_{r,\beta}(x)\to\TAM_{r}(x) in the same limit. The exact TAM is recovered in the limiting notation TAMr,∞=TAMr\TAM_{r,\infty}=\TAM_{r}.

Throughout the remainder of the paper we specialize TAM to the linear associative memory setting: the collection x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m} is taken to be the competing scores (sj,i)j≠i(s_{j,i})_{j\neq i} associated with a query viv_{i}, so that m=n−1m=n-1 and TAMr\TAM_{r} quantifies the strength of the top rr-fraction of competitors. The next subsection turns this into a convex learning objective.

3.2 Learning under the TAM criterion

With the TAM functional in hand, we now formulate retrieval and learning for the linear associative memory as a convex optimization problem.

Given stored pairs {(ui,vi)}i=1n⊂ℝd×ℝd\{(u_{i},v_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} and a memory or weight matrix W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, recall that the score matrix is sj,i=uj⊤​W​vis_{j,i}=u_{j}^{\top}Wv_{i}. Fix a tail fraction r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1) and set k=⌈r⁡(n−1)⌉k=\lceil r(n-1)\rceil. The TAM retrieval criterion asks that each signal score exceed the TAM-aggregate of its competitors:

si,i>TAMr⁡((sj,i)j≠i),∀i∈[n].s_{i,i}\;>\;\TAM_{r}((s_{j,i})_{j\neq i}),\qquad\forall\,i\in[n]. (28)

For r=1/(n−1)r=1/(n-1), (28) reduces to the exact top-1 criterion (2) studied in Section 2; for fixed r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1), it imposes an upper-tail margin requirement that controls the mass of strong competitors rather than a single extreme-value outlier.

Rather than demanding strict satisfaction of (28), we minimize a convex surrogate that penalizes violations softly. Let

ℓ⁡(t)≔log⁡(1+e−t)\ell(t)\;\coloneqq\;\log(1+e^{-t}) (29)

denote the logistic loss, and let β>0\beta>0 be the smoothing parameter of TAMr,β\TAM_{r,\beta}. We consider the regularized objective

minW∈ℝd×d⁡{∑i=1nℓ⁡(si,i−TAMr,β⁡((sj,i)j≠i))+λ​n2​d2​‖W‖𝖥2},\min_{W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}}\Bigg\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\bigl(s_{i,i}-\TAM_{r,\beta}((s_{j,i})_{j\neq i})\bigr)+\frac{\lambda n}{2d^{2}}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert W\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}\Bigg\}, (30)

where λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 is a ridge penalty. Since each score sj,is_{j,i} is linear in WW and TAMr,β\TAM_{r,\beta} is convex, the margin si,i−TAMr,β⁡((sj,i)j≠i)s_{i,i}-\TAM_{r,\beta}((s_{j,i})_{j\neq i}) is concave in WW; composing with the decreasing convex ℓ\ell yields a convex function of WW, so (30) is a convex program (strongly convex whenever λ>0\lambda>0).

The variational representation (27) of TAMr,β\TAM_{r,\beta} suggests lifting (30) to a joint optimization over WW and the auxiliary quantile variables μ=(μ1,…,μn)∈ℝn\mu=(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Substituting (27) into (30) yields

minW,μ⁡{∑i=1nℓ⁡(si,i−μi−1k​∑j≠iϕβ​(sj,i−μi))+λ​n2​d2​‖W‖𝖥2},\min_{W,\mu}\Bigg\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\biggl(s_{i,i}-\mu_{i}-\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\neq i}\phi_{\beta}(s_{j,i}-\mu_{i})\biggr)+\frac{\lambda n}{2d^{2}}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert W\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}\Bigg\}, (31)

Minimizing (31) over μ\mu at fixed WW recovers (30). This is the workhorse formulation for the leave-one-out analysis of Section 4.

It is useful to compare (30) with the ridge-regularized multiclass softmax cross-entropy (21), the canonical convex surrogate for the top-1 criterion (2) introduced in Section 2.4. Denote the log-sum-exp aggregate of the competitor scores by LSE((sj,i)j≠i)≔log∑j≠iesj,i\mathrm{LSE}((s_{j,i})_{j\neq i})\coloneqq\log\sum_{j\neq i}e^{s_{j,i}}. A short calculation rewrites each summand in (21) as

−si,i+log∑j=1nesj,i=ℓ(si,i−LSE((sj,i)j≠i)),-\,s_{i,i}+\log\sum_{j=1}^{n}e^{s_{j,i}}\;=\;\ell\Bigl(s_{i,i}-\mathrm{LSE}\bigl((s_{j,i})_{j\neq i}\bigr)\Bigr), (32)

with the same logistic loss ℓ\ell used in (30). In this form, (21) has precisely the same structure as the TAM objective (30): a logistic loss applied to the margin between the signal score si,is_{i,i} and a convex aggregate of the competitor scores (sj,i)j≠i(s_{j,i})_{j\neq i}. They differ only in the choice of aggregate. The log-sum-exp is a smoothed maximum, with LSE⁡((sj,i)j≠i)=maxj≠i⁡sj,i+O⁡(log⁡n)\mathrm{LSE}((s_{j,i})_{j\neq i})=\max_{j\neq i}s_{j,i}+O(\log n), and therefore inherits the 2​log⁡n\sqrt{2\log n} extreme-value statistics of the top-1 criterion. Replacing it with the tail average TAMr,β\TAM_{r,\beta}, which remains on the scale of a typical competitor at fixed rr, enables retrieval at the quadratic model-size scale d2≍nd^{2}\asymp n instead of d2≍n​log⁡nd^{2}\asymp n\log n.

3.3 Performance metrics

With the TAM learning problem in place, we consider three asymptotic quantities that together characterize retrieval performance: the empirical average fitting loss, the per-sample TAM margin, and the distribution of signal percentiles. Throughout this subsection, (W^,μ^)(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu}) denotes the unique minimizer of (31), with corresponding scores s^j,i=uj⊤​W^​vi\widehat{s}_{j,i}=u_{j}^{\top}\widehat{W}v_{i}.

Empirical average fitting loss.

Let

Ln​(W,μ)≔1n​∑i=1nℓ⁡(si,i−μi−1k​∑j≠iϕβ​(sj,i−μi))L_{n}(W,\mu)\;\coloneqq\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\left(s_{i,i}-\mu_{i}-\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\neq i}\phi_{\beta}(s_{j,i}-\mu_{i})\right) (33)

denote the normalized data-fitting part of (31), and write L^n≔Ln​(W^,μ^)\widehat{L}_{n}\coloneqq L_{n}(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu}) for its value at the optimizer. We will say that the TAM problem is asymptotically fit at load α\alpha if L^n→0\widehat{L}_{n}\to 0 in probability as n,d→∞n,d\to\infty with n/d2→αn/d^{2}\to\alpha and λ→0\lambda\to 0. Since ℓ\ell is nonnegative and vanishes only in the large-margin limit, asymptotic fit is equivalent to the TAM retrieval criterion (28) holding with a positive margin for all but a vanishing fraction of keys.

TAM margin distribution.

A finer summary than L^n\widehat{L}_{n} is the empirical distribution of the per-sample TAM margins

m^i≔s^i,i−μ^i−1k​∑j≠iϕβ​(s^j,i−μ^i),i∈[n],\widehat{m}_{i}\;\coloneqq\;\widehat{s}_{i,i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i}-\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\neq i}\phi_{\beta}(\widehat{s}_{j,i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i}),\qquad i\in[n],

which are precisely the arguments of the logistic loss appearing in L^n\widehat{L}_{n}. A positively-supported limiting distribution for m^i\widehat{m}_{i} indicates asymptotic fit; its shape shows how comfortably the signal beats the tail average.

Signal percentile distribution.

As a complementary, rank-based summary, we also ask, for each sample, what fraction of competitors have score below the signal. Formally, define the signal percentile

Ωi≔1n−1∑j≠i𝟏{s^j,i≤s^i,i},i∈[n],\Omega_{i}\;\coloneqq\;\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j\neq i}\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{s}_{j,i}\leq\widehat{s}_{i,i}\},\qquad i\in[n],

so that Ωi\Omega_{i} close to 11 signals that the iith signal dominates nearly all of its competitors and Ωi=0\Omega_{i}=0 that every competitor beats it. The random probability measure

νn≔1n​∑i=1nδΩi\nu_{n}\;\coloneqq\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{\Omega_{i}} (34)

on [0,1][0,1] is our object of study: when does νn\nu_{n} converge in probability (say, in Wasserstein-11) to a deterministic limit?

CMM benchmark: from top-1 to percentiles.

Section 2.1 used a Gaussian approximation to the scores of the non-optimized CMM W𝖢𝖬𝖬W_{\mathsf{CMM}} to explain its top-1 behavior. Here we return to the same picture, now in the proportional regime n/d2→α∈(0,∞)n/d^{2}\to\alpha\in(0,\infty), to predict the full distribution of signal percentiles. In particular, (17) suggests, for a fixed query,

si,i≈1+α​Zi,sj,i≈α​Zj,i,j≠i,s_{i,i}\approx 1+\sqrt{\alpha}\,Z_{i},\qquad s_{j,i}\approx\sqrt{\alpha}\,Z_{j,i},\quad j\neq i,

where ZiZ_{i} and (Zj,i)j≠i(Z_{j,i})_{j\neq i} are treated as independent standard Gaussians. As discussed in Section 2.1, Lemma 3 gives the exact one-column representation underlying this approximation: the competitor vector is a random radius times g/‖g‖g/\|g\|, and n​g/‖g‖\sqrt{n}\,g/\|g\| is approximately Gaussian coordinatewise, while the radius concentrates at α\sqrt{\alpha}.

Conditioning on ZiZ_{i} and applying a law-of-large-numbers heuristic to the competitors gives

Ωi≈1n−1∑j≠i{Zj,i≤Zi+α−1/2}≈Φ(Zi+α−1/2).\Omega_{i}\approx\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j\neq i}\mathbf{1}\!\left\{Z_{j,i}\leq Z_{i}+\alpha^{-1/2}\right\}\approx\Phi\!\left(Z_{i}+\alpha^{-1/2}\right).

Consequently, the predicted CDF of the CMM percentile is

Fα(ω)≔Φ(Φ−1(ω)−α−1/2),ω∈(0,1),F_{\alpha}(\omega)\;\coloneqq\;\Phi\!\left(\Phi^{-1}(\omega)-\alpha^{-1/2}\right),\qquad\omega\in(0,1), (35)

with density fα​(ω)=exp⁡(Φ−1​(ω)/α−1/(2​α))f_{\alpha}(\omega)=\exp(\Phi^{-1}(\omega)/\sqrt{\alpha}-1/(2\alpha)). The parameter α−1/2\alpha^{-1/2} plays the role of a signal-to-noise ratio: the law concentrates at 11 as α→0\alpha\to 0 and tends to Unif⁡(0,1)\mathrm{Unif}(0,1) as α→∞\alpha\to\infty.

The next section develops a leave-one-out theory for these three observables under the TAM optimizer in the quadratic regime n/d2→αn/d^{2}\to\alpha with fixed r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1).

4 Asymptotic theory of TAM

We now study the TAM optimizer in the quadratic regime n,d→∞n,d\to\infty with n/d2→αn/d^{2}\to\alpha and k/n→r∈(0,1)k/n\to r\in(0,1). Throughout this section the smoothing parameter β<∞\beta<\infty and ridge parameter λ>0\lambda>0 are fixed. The goal is to predict the empirical laws of the true scores si,i​(W^)s_{i,i}(\widehat{W}) and competitor scores sj,i​(W^)s_{j,i}(\widehat{W}), and hence the limiting TAM loss, margin distribution, and signal-percentile profile introduced in Section 3.3.

The main technique is a leave-one-out (LOO) analysis. We compare the TAM optimizer with the optimizer obtained after removing a held-out pair (uh,vh)(u_{h},v_{h}), and use this comparison to separate the fresh randomness of the held-out sample from the remaining problem. The first three inputs below are LOO stability estimates, proved in Appendix C. The remaining three are spectral and self-averaging estimates: the spectral estimate is proved in Appendix E, while the two self-averaging estimates are proved in Appendix D. Together, the six estimates yield the two-parameter scalar variational description stated in Theorem 2.

The section is organized as follows. We first compute the gradient and Hessian of the smoothed TAM loss. We then formulate the LOO rank-one reduction, state the scalar variational prediction, and finally derive the finite-dimensional equations that lead to this prediction. The ridgeless limit λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0 and the associated phase transition are deferred to Section 5.

4.1 Gradient and Hessian of the TAM loss

Throughout this section the threshold variables are unregularized, and we work with the joint TAM objective of (31), written with the reparameterized ridge:

Ψ⁡(W,μ)=∑i=1nℓ⁡(si,i​(W)−μi−1k​∑j≠iϕβ​(sj,i​(W)−μi))+λ​n2​d2​‖W‖𝖥2,\Psi(W,\mu)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\Big(s_{i,i}(W)-\mu_{i}-\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\neq i}\phi_{\beta}\!\bigl(s_{j,i}(W)-\mu_{i}\bigr)\Big)+\frac{\lambda n}{2d^{2}}\,\mathinner{\!\left\lVert W\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}, (36)

where s⁡(W)=U⊤​W​V∈ℝn×ns(W)=U^{\top}WV\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, with entries sj,i​(W)=uj⊤​W​vis_{j,i}(W)=u_{j}^{\top}Wv_{i}, and U=[u1⋯un]U=[u_{1}\;\cdots\;u_{n}], V=[v1⋯vn]V=[v_{1}\;\cdots\;v_{n}] are the data matrices from the Gaussian model (3). We use lowercase sj,is_{j,i} for finite-dimensional scores, reserving uppercase SS for scalar limiting random variables. When the underlying matrix is clear from context, we write sj,is_{j,i} instead of sj,i​(W)s_{j,i}(W); in particular, at the full optimizer this means sj,i=sj,i​(W^)s_{j,i}=s_{j,i}(\widehat{W}). Since Ψ\Psi depends on WW only through s⁡(W)s(W), the chain rule reduces the computation of ∇WΨ\nabla_{W}\Psi to an n×nn\times n matrix of score derivatives,

∇WΨ=U​G​V⊤+λ​nd2​W,Gj,i:=∂Ψ∂sj,i.\nabla_{W}\Psi\;=\;U\,G\,V^{\top}\;+\;\frac{\lambda n}{d^{2}}\,W,\qquad G_{j,i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial s_{j,i}}. (37)

The remainder of this subsection evaluates the entries of GG and rewrites ∇WΨ\nabla_{W}\Psi in a form convenient for the leave-one-out analysis in Section 4.2.

The ii-th summand of Ψ\Psi equals ℓ⁡(mi)\ell(m_{i}), where the TAM aggregate and margin associated with sample ii are

ci:=μi+1k∑j≠iϕβ(sj,i−μi),mi:=si,i−ci.c_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mu_{i}+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\neq i}\phi_{\beta}\!\big(s_{j,i}-\mu_{i}\big),\qquad m_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=s_{i,i}-c_{i}. (38)

The margin mim_{i} is the only part of the ii-th summand that depends on column ii of the score matrix, and the ii-th summand is the only summand that does. Differentiating ℓ⁡(mi)\ell(m_{i}) in sj,is_{j,i} therefore yields

Gj,i=ℓ′​(mi)​∂mi∂sj,i={ℓ′​(mi),j=i,−1k​ℓ′​(mi)​ϕβ′​(sj,i−μi),j≠i.G_{j,i}\;=\;\ell^{\prime}(m_{i})\,\frac{\partial m_{i}}{\partial s_{j,i}}\;=\;\begin{cases}\ell^{\prime}(m_{i}),&j=i,\\[2.0pt] -\tfrac{1}{k}\,\ell^{\prime}(m_{i})\,\phi_{\beta}^{\prime}(s_{j,i}-\mu_{i}),&j\neq i.\end{cases} (39)

Both ℓ′\ell^{\prime} and ϕβ′\phi_{\beta}^{\prime} are conveniently expressed through the sigmoid σ⁡(t):=(1+e−t)−1\sigma(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=(1+e^{-t})^{-1}:

ℓ′​(t)=σ⁡(t)−1=−σ⁡(−t),ϕβ′​(t)=σ⁡(β​t).\ell^{\prime}(t)\;=\;\sigma(t)-1\;=\;-\,\sigma(-t),\qquad\phi_{\beta}^{\prime}(t)\;=\;\sigma(\beta t). (40)

Substituting into (39) gives the two scalar weights

ai:=σ⁡(−mi)=−ℓ′​(mi)∈(0,1),a_{i}\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\sigma(-m_{i})\;=\;-\,\ell^{\prime}(m_{i})\;\in\;(0,1), (41)

and, for j≠ij\neq i,

qj,i:=σ⁡(β⁡(sj,i−μi))=ϕβ′​(sj,i−μi)∈(0,1),j≠i.q_{j,i}\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\sigma\!\big(\beta\,(s_{j,i}-\mu_{i})\big)\;=\;\phi_{\beta}^{\prime}(s_{j,i}-\mu_{i})\;\in\;(0,1),\qquad j\neq i. (42)

In these variables (39) becomes Gj,i=−aiG_{j,i}=-a_{i} for j=ij=i and Gj,i=1k​qj,i​aiG_{j,i}=\tfrac{1}{k}q_{j,i}a_{i} otherwise. Equivalently G=Q​ΛaG=Q\Lambda_{a}, where Λa:=diag⁡(a1,…,an)\Lambda_{a}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\diag(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}) and

Qj,i:={−1,j=i,1k​qj,i,j≠i.Q_{j,i}\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\begin{cases}-1,&j=i,\\[2.0pt] \dfrac{1}{k}\,q_{j,i},&j\neq i.\end{cases} (43)

Substituting G=Q​ΛaG=Q\Lambda_{a} into (37) and performing the analogous calculation for μ\mu — where ∂mi/∂μi=−1+1k​∑j≠iqj,i=−(Q⊤​𝟏n)i\partial m_{i}/\partial\mu_{i}=-1+\tfrac{1}{k}\sum_{j\neq i}q_{j,i}=-(Q^{\top}\mathbf{1}_{n})_{i} — yields

∇WΨ​(W,μ)=U​Q​Λa​V⊤+λ​nd2​W,\nabla_{W}\Psi(W,\mu)=U\,Q\Lambda_{a}\,V^{\top}\;+\;\frac{\lambda n}{d^{2}}\,W, (44)
∇μΨ​(W,μ)=−Λa​Q⊤​𝟏n,\nabla_{\mu}\Psi(W,\mu)=-\Lambda_{a}\,Q^{\top}\mathbf{1}_{n}, (45)

where 𝟏n∈ℝn\mathbf{1}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the all-ones vector. Expanding (44) by rows of QQ separates the diagonal and off-diagonal contributions,

∇WΨ=−∑i=1naiuivi⊤+1k∑i=1nai∑j≠iqj,iujvi⊤+λ​nd2W.\nabla_{W}\Psi\;=\;-\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\,u_{i}v_{i}^{\top}\;+\;\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}q_{j,i}\,u_{j}v_{i}^{\top}\;+\;\frac{\lambda n}{d^{2}}\,W. (46)

For the Taylor expansion in Section 4.2 we will also need the second derivative of the outer loss at the margin, which is governed by a companion diagonal:

bi:=ℓ′′(mi)=ai(1−ai),Λb:=diag(b1,…,bn).b_{i}\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\ell^{\prime\prime}(m_{i})\;=\;a_{i}(1-a_{i}),\qquad\Lambda_{b}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\diag(b_{1},\dots,b_{n}). (47)
Definition 2 (Full Hessian).

Let H:ℝd×d→ℝd×dH\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} denote the Hessian operator of Ψ\Psi in the WW variable, evaluated at a fixed point (W,μ)(W,\mu). Applied to a perturbation Δ\Delta, it is

H⁡[Δ]:=λ​nd2​Δ+U​M​(U⊤​Δ​V)​V⊤.H[\Delta]\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\frac{\lambda n}{d^{2}}\,\Delta\;+\;U\,M\!\bigl(U^{\top}\Delta V\bigr)\,V^{\top}. (48)

Here M:ℝn×n→ℝn×nM\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} acts columnwise,

M(X):,i=MiX:,i,M(X)_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}\;=\;M_{i}X_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}, (49)

where

Mi\displaystyle M_{i} :=biQ:,iQ:,i⊤+aidiag(R~:,i),\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;b_{i}Q_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}Q_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}^{\top}\;+\;a_{i}\diag(\widetilde{R}_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}), (50)
R~j,i\displaystyle\widetilde{R}_{j,i} :={βk​qj,i​(1−qj,i),j≠i,0,j=i.\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\begin{cases}\dfrac{\beta}{k}\,q_{j,i}(1-q_{j,i}),&j\neq i,\\ 0,&j=i.\end{cases}

The operator HH is self-adjoint and strictly positive-definite, with smallest eigenvalue at least λ​n/d2\lambda n/d^{2}. Under vectorization, writing 𝒟:=diag⁡(M1,…,Mn)∈ℝn2×n2\mathcal{D}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\diag(M_{1},\ldots,M_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}\times n^{2}}, the same operator has matrix representation

H=λ​nd2​Id2+(V⊗U)​𝒟​(V⊗U)⊤.H\;=\;\frac{\lambda n}{d^{2}}\,I_{d^{2}}\;+\;(V\otimes U)\,\mathcal{D}\,(V\otimes U)^{\top}. (51)

4.2 Leave-one-out reduction

We relate the joint minimizer (W^,μ^)(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu}) of (31) to a leave-one-out reference point by a first-order expansion. Fix a held-out index h∈[n]h\in[n], and let (W^∖h,μ^∖h)(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h},\widehat{\mu}^{\setminus h}) denote the minimizer of the TAM objective with sample hh removed from both the outer sum and from all inner summations over interferers:

Ψ∖h​(W,μ):=∑i≠hℓ⁡(si,i​(W)−μi−1k​∑j≠ij≠hϕβ​(sj,i​(W)−μi))+λ​n2​d2​‖W‖𝖥2.\Psi^{\setminus h}(W,\mu)\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\sum_{i\neq h}\ell\Big(s_{i,i}(W)-\mu_{i}-\frac{1}{k}\!\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\neq i\\ j\neq h\end{subarray}}\!\!\phi_{\beta}\bigl(s_{j,i}(W)-\mu_{i}\bigr)\Big)+\frac{\lambda n}{2d^{2}}\,\mathinner{\!\left\lVert W\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}. (52)

Write Δ​W:=W^−W^∖h\Delta W\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\widehat{W}-\widehat{W}^{\setminus h}, Δ​μ:=μ^−μ^∖h\Delta\mu\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\widehat{\mu}-\widehat{\mu}^{\setminus h}, and Δ​S:=U⊤​(Δ​W)​V∈ℝn×n\Delta S\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=U^{\top}(\Delta W)V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} for the corresponding perturbations. A hat decoration (e.g., a^i,q^j,i,b^i,m^i\hat{a}_{i},\hat{q}_{j,i},\hat{b}_{i},\hat{m}_{i}) denotes a quantity from Section 4.1 evaluated at (W^,μ^)(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu}); a superscript ∖h\setminus h denotes the same quantity evaluated at (W^∖h,μ^∖h)(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h},\widehat{\mu}^{\setminus h}). We adopt the conventions ah∖h:=0a_{h}^{\setminus h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=0 and qj,h∖h:=qh,i∖h:=0q_{j,h}^{\setminus h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=q_{h,i}^{\setminus h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=0, so that Q∖h,Λa∖hQ^{\setminus h},\Lambda_{a^{\setminus h}} extend naturally to n×nn\times n arrays.

4.2.1 LOO Hessian and rank-one reduction

The LOO Hessian has the same form as the full Hessian in Definition 2, with the hh-th sample removed and all coefficients evaluated at (W^∖h,μ^∖h)(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h},\widehat{\mu}^{\setminus h}). Explicitly, H∖h:ℝd×d→ℝd×dH^{\setminus h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is defined by

H∖h​[Δ]:=λ​nd2​Δ+U​M∖h​(U⊤​Δ​V)​V⊤,H^{\setminus h}[\Delta]\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\frac{\lambda n}{d^{2}}\,\Delta\;+\;U\,M^{\setminus h}\!\bigl(U^{\top}\Delta\,V\bigr)\,V^{\top}, (53)

where M∖h:ℝn×n→ℝn×nM^{\setminus h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} acts columnwise as

M∖h(X):,i=Mi∖hX:,i(i≠h),M∖h(X):,h= 0.M^{\setminus h}(X)_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}\;=\;M_{i}^{\setminus h}\,X_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}\quad(i\neq h),\qquad M^{\setminus h}(X)_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},h}\;=\;0. (54)

In the above display, Mi∖h∈ℝn×nM_{i}^{\setminus h}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is a symmetric matrix with a rank-one-plus-diagonal form

Mi∖h\displaystyle M_{i}^{\setminus h} :=bi∖hQ:,i∖h(Q:,i∖h)⊤+ai∖hdiag(R~:,i∖h)\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;b_{i}^{\setminus h}\,Q_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}^{\setminus h}(Q_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}^{\setminus h})^{\top}\;+\;a_{i}^{\setminus h}\,\diag\bigl(\widetilde{R}_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}^{\setminus h}\bigr) (55)
R~j,i∖h\displaystyle\widetilde{R}_{j,i}^{\setminus h} :={βk​qj,i∖h​(1−qj,i∖h)j≠i,j≠h0,otherwise.\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\begin{cases}\frac{\beta}{k}\,q_{j,i}^{\setminus h}\bigl(1-q_{j,i}^{\setminus h}\bigr)\,&j\neq i,\ j\neq h\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\\ \end{cases}.

Here bi∖hb_{i}^{\setminus h} is the quantity in (47) evaluated at (W^∖h,μ^∖h)(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h},\widehat{\mu}^{\setminus h}). The operator H∖hH^{\setminus h} is self-adjoint and strictly positive-definite on ℝd×d\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}: its smallest eigenvalue is at least λ​n/d2=Θ⁡(1)\lambda n/d^{2}=\Theta(1) in the regime d2≍nd^{2}\asymp n, so that ‖(H∖h)−1‖op=𝒪≺​(1)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert(H^{\setminus h})^{-1}\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(1).

Rank-one reduction.

The leave-one-out perturbation is governed, to first order, by the held-out feature pair (uh,vh)(u_{h},v_{h}).

Proposition 3 (LOO rank-one reduction).

Under the LOO stability estimates (A1)–(A3) stated below, with high probability,

W^−W^∖h=σ(−m^h)(H∖h)−1[uhvh⊤]+Rh,∥Rh∥𝖥=𝒪≺(d−1/2).\widehat{W}-\widehat{W}^{\setminus h}\;=\;\sigma(-\hat{m}_{h})\,\bigl(H^{\setminus h}\bigr)^{-1}\!\bigl[u_{h}v_{h}^{\top}\bigr]\;+\;R_{h},\qquad\bigl\lVert R_{h}\bigr\rVert_{\mathsf{F}}\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (56)

Here m^h\hat{m}_{h} is the TAM margin at the held-out sample evaluated at the full minimizer (W^,μ^)(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu}):

m^h=sh,h​(W^)−μ^h−1k​∑j≠hϕβ​(sj,h​(W^)−μ^h).\hat{m}_{h}\;=\;s_{h,h}(\widehat{W})\;-\;\hat{\mu}_{h}\;-\;\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\neq h}\phi_{\beta}\!\bigl(s_{j,h}(\widehat{W})-\hat{\mu}_{h}\bigr). (57)

Thus the leading change in the weight matrix is the inverse LOO Hessian applied to σ⁡(−m^h)​uh​vh⊤\sigma(-\hat{m}_{h})\,u_{h}v_{h}^{\top}, with a Frobenius-norm correction of lower order. In Section 4.3, this formula is combined with trace concentration for (H∖h)−1(H^{\setminus h})^{-1} to obtain the susceptibility equation.

4.2.2 Proof of Proposition 3

We derive (56) from the following LOO stability proposition.

Proposition 4 (LOO stability).

Uniformly after removing any fixed finite set of samples,

  1. (A1)

    maxi≠h|(Δμ)i|=𝒪≺(d−3/2)\displaystyle\max_{i\neq h}\,\bigl|(\Delta\mu)_{i}\bigr|\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-3/2});

  2. (A2)

    maxj,i≠h⁡|(Δ​S)j,i|=𝒪≺​(d−1)\displaystyle\max_{j,i\neq h}\,\bigl|(\Delta S)_{j,i}\bigr|\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1});

  3. (A3)

    maxj,i∈[n]⁡|sj,i​(W^)|=𝒪≺​(1)\displaystyle\max_{j,i\in[n]}\,\bigl|s_{j,i}(\widehat{W})\bigr|\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(1).

The proposition is proved in Appendix C. The estimates are in the sense of stochastic domination, absorbing dεd^{\varepsilon} factors. In particular, (A3) applies to the optimizer of each finite-removal problem. These estimates control the Taylor remainder and the coefficient perturbations in the LOO expansion (56).

Step 1: Subtract the stationarity conditions.

The WW-components of the stationarity conditions (44) at the full and LOO optimizers, subtracted, yield

λ​nd2​Δ​W+U⁡(Q^​Λa^−Q∖h​Λa∖h)​V⊤= 0.\frac{\lambda n}{d^{2}}\,\Delta W\;+\;U\,\bigl(\hat{Q}\Lambda_{\hat{a}}-Q^{\setminus h}\Lambda_{a^{\setminus h}}\bigr)\,V^{\top}\;=\;0. (58)
Step 2: Separate the terms involving the held-out sample.

With the extension conventions on a∖ha^{\setminus h} and q∖hq^{\setminus h}, the matrix Q^​Λa^−Q∖h​Λa∖h\hat{Q}\Lambda_{\hat{a}}-Q^{\setminus h}\Lambda_{a^{\setminus h}} decomposes entrywise as

(Q^​Λa^−Q∖h​Λa∖h)j,i={−a^h(j,i)=(h,h),a^h​q^j,h/kj≠h,i=h,a^i​q^h,i/kj=h,i≠h,ℛj,i∖hj,i≠h,\bigl(\hat{Q}\Lambda_{\hat{a}}-Q^{\setminus h}\Lambda_{a^{\setminus h}}\bigr)_{j,i}\;=\;\begin{cases}-\,\hat{a}_{h}&(j,i)=(h,h),\\[2.0pt] \hat{a}_{h}\,\hat{q}_{j,h}/k&j\neq h,\ i=h,\\[2.0pt] \hat{a}_{i}\,\hat{q}_{h,i}/k&j=h,\ i\neq h,\\[2.0pt] \mathcal{R}_{j,i}^{\setminus h}&j,i\neq h,\end{cases} (59)

where the first three cases are the entries involving the held-out sample: the held-out outer term (i=hi=h) and the held-out interferer row (j=hj=h, across interior columns) are present in the full objective but absent in the LOO objective. The remaining entries are collected in ℛ∖h∈ℝn×n\mathcal{R}^{\setminus h}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, supported on {j,i≠h}\{j,i\neq h\}:

ℛj,i∖h:={a^i​q^j,i−ai∖h​qj,i∖hkj≠i,j,i≠h,ai∖h−a^ij=i≠h.\mathcal{R}_{j,i}^{\setminus h}\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\begin{cases}\dfrac{\hat{a}_{i}\,\hat{q}_{j,i}\;-\;a_{i}^{\setminus h}\,q_{j,i}^{\setminus h}}{k}&j\neq i,\ j,i\neq h,\\[8.0pt] a_{i}^{\setminus h}\;-\;\hat{a}_{i}&j=i\neq h.\end{cases} (60)

Separating these entries inside (58),

λ​nd2​Δ​W+U​ℛ∖h​V⊤=a^h​uh​vh⊤−a^h​ηh​vh⊤−uh​ξh⊤,\frac{\lambda n}{d^{2}}\,\Delta W\;+\;U\,\mathcal{R}^{\setminus h}\,V^{\top}\;=\;\hat{a}_{h}\,u_{h}v_{h}^{\top}\;-\;\hat{a}_{h}\,\eta_{h}\,v_{h}^{\top}\;-\;u_{h}\,\xi_{h}^{\top}, (61)

where

ηh:=1k∑j≠hq^j,huj,ξh:=1k∑i≠ha^iq^h,ivi.\eta_{h}\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\neq h}\hat{q}_{j,h}\,u_{j},\qquad\xi_{h}\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\neq h}\hat{a}_{i}\,\hat{q}_{h,i}\,v_{i}. (62)
Step 3: Linearize the common part.

In Appendix B, we carry out a first-order Taylor expansion of ℛ∖h\mathcal{R}^{\setminus h} in the perturbations Δ​S\Delta S and Δ​μ\Delta\mu, with all higher-order terms collected into a residual matrix E^∖h\hat{E}^{\setminus h} supported on {j,i≠h}\{j,i\neq h\}. This yields

ℛ:,i∖h=Mi∖hΔS:,i+E^∖h:,i,i≠h,\mathcal{R}_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}^{\setminus h}\;=\;M_{i}^{\setminus h}\,\Delta S_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}\;+\;\hat{E}^{\setminus h}_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i},\qquad i\neq h, (63)

with Mi∖hM_{i}^{\setminus h} as in (55). Combining (63) with (61) and the definition of H∖hH^{\setminus h} yields

H∖h​[Δ​W]=a^h​uh​vh⊤−a^h​ηh​vh⊤−uh​ξh⊤−U​E^∖h​V⊤.H^{\setminus h}[\Delta W]\;=\;\hat{a}_{h}\,u_{h}v_{h}^{\top}\;-\;\hat{a}_{h}\,\eta_{h}\,v_{h}^{\top}\;-\;u_{h}\,\xi_{h}^{\top}\;-\;U\hat{E}^{\setminus h}V^{\top}. (64)

Moreover, we show in Appendix B that, under (A1)–(A3),

|E^i,i∖h|=𝒪≺(n−1)fori≠h,|E^j,i∖h|=𝒪≺(n−2)forj≠i,j,i≠h.\bigl|\hat{E}^{\setminus h}_{i,i}\bigr|\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(n^{-1})\ \text{for}\ i\neq h,\qquad\bigl|\hat{E}^{\setminus h}_{j,i}\bigr|\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(n^{-2})\ \text{for}\ j\neq i,\ j,i\neq h. (65)
Step 4: Invert and bound the correction.

Applying (H∖h)−1(H^{\setminus h})^{-1} to (64) produces (56) with

Rh=(H∖h)−1​[−a^h​ηh​vh⊤−uh​ξh⊤−U​E^∖h​V⊤].R_{h}\;=\;\bigl(H^{\setminus h}\bigr)^{-1}\!\Bigl[-\hat{a}_{h}\,\eta_{h}\,v_{h}^{\top}\;-\;u_{h}\,\xi_{h}^{\top}\;-\;U\hat{E}^{\setminus h}V^{\top}\Bigr]. (66)

Since ‖(H∖h)−1‖op=𝒪≺​(1)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert(H^{\setminus h})^{-1}\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(1), it suffices to bound each of the three remaining terms in (66) in Frobenius norm at scale 𝒪≺(d−1/2)\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}).

Writing kηh=Uq^:,hk\,\eta_{h}=U\,\hat{q}_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},h} (with the hh-th entry of q^:,h\hat{q}_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},h} understood to be zero), the Marchenko–Pastur bound ‖U‖op=𝒪≺​(d)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert U\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(\sqrt{d}) in the regime d2≍nd^{2}\asymp n, together with the deterministic entrywise bound ‖q^:,h‖2≤n−1\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\hat{q}_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},h}\right\rVert}_{2}\leq\sqrt{n-1}, gives ‖ηh‖2≤‖U‖op‖q^:,h‖2/k=𝒪≺(n​d/n)=𝒪≺(d−1/2)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\eta_{h}\right\rVert}_{2}\leq\mathinner{\!\left\lVert U\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}\,\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\hat{q}_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},h}\right\rVert}_{2}/k=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(\sqrt{nd}/n)=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}); the same argument applies to ξh\xi_{h}. Consequently

‖a^h​ηh​vh⊤‖𝖥=|a^h|‖ηh‖2‖vh‖2=𝒪≺(d−1/2),‖uh​ξh⊤‖𝖥=𝒪≺(d−1/2).\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\hat{a}_{h}\,\eta_{h}\,v_{h}^{\top}\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}\;=\;|\hat{a}_{h}|\,\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\eta_{h}\right\rVert}_{2}\,\mathinner{\!\left\lVert v_{h}\right\rVert}_{2}\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}),\qquad\mathinner{\!\left\lVert u_{h}\,\xi_{h}^{\top}\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (67)

Next, we consider the term U​E^∖h​V⊤U\hat{E}^{\setminus h}V^{\top} in (66). Let E^𝖽\hat{E}^{\mathsf{d}} and E^𝗈\hat{E}^{\mathsf{o}} denote the diagonal and off-diagonal parts of E^∖h\hat{E}^{\setminus h}, respectively. The diagonal part is a diagonal matrix, so ‖E^𝖽‖op=maxi≠h⁡|E^i,i∖h|=𝒪≺​(n−1)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\hat{E}^{\mathsf{d}}\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_{i\neq h}|\hat{E}^{\setminus h}_{i,i}|=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(n^{-1}) by (65). The off-diagonal part is controlled through its Frobenius norm,

‖E^𝗈‖op≤‖E^𝗈‖𝖥=(∑j≠ij,i≠h|E^j,i∖h|2)1/2≤n2⋅𝒪≺​(n−4)=𝒪≺​(n−1),\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\hat{E}^{\mathsf{o}}\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}\;\leq\;\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\hat{E}^{\mathsf{o}}\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}\;=\;\Bigl(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\neq i\\ j,i\neq h\end{subarray}}|\hat{E}^{\setminus h}_{j,i}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2}\;\leq\;\sqrt{n^{2}\cdot\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(n^{-4})}\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(n^{-1}), (68)

again by (65). Combining, ‖E^∖h‖op=𝒪≺​(n−1)=𝒪≺​(d−2)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\hat{E}^{\setminus h}\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(n^{-1})=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-2}). Submultiplicativity with ‖U‖op,‖V‖op=𝒪≺​(d)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert U\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}},\mathinner{\!\left\lVert V\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(\sqrt{d}) yields ‖U​E^∖h​V⊤‖op≤𝒪≺​(d⋅d−2)=𝒪≺​(d−1)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert U\hat{E}^{\setminus h}V^{\top}\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d\cdot d^{-2})=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1}). Since U​E^∖h​V⊤∈ℝd×dU\hat{E}^{\setminus h}V^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} has rank at most dd, ‖⋅‖𝖥≤d​‖⋅‖op\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}\leq\sqrt{d}\,\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}, and

‖U​E^∖h​V⊤‖𝖥≤d‖U​E^∖h​V⊤‖op=𝒪≺(d−1/2).\mathinner{\!\left\lVert U\hat{E}^{\setminus h}V^{\top}\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}\;\leq\;\sqrt{d}\,\mathinner{\!\left\lVert U\hat{E}^{\setminus h}V^{\top}\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (69)

Combining (67) and (69) and applying (H∖h)−1(H^{\setminus h})^{-1} establishes (56). ∎

4.3 Scalar characterization of the TAM optimizer

We now state the asymptotic characterization of the TAM minimizer. In addition to Proposition 4, we use the following spectral and self-averaging proposition. The derivation is given in Section 4.4.

Proposition 5 (Spectral and self-averaging estimates).

We have the following:

  1. (A4)

    (Spectrum bound)

    ‖W^‖op=𝒪≺​(d)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\widehat{W}\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(\sqrt{d}) (70)
  2. (A5)

    (Empirical-mean concentration) Let ψ∈C1​(ℝ)\psi\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}) be pseudo-Lipschitz of order two. Then,

    1n∑i=1nψ(si,i(W^))−𝔼[1n∑i=1nψ(si,i(W^))]=𝒪≺(d−1/2),\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi\bigl(s_{i,i}(\widehat{W})\bigr)-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi\bigl(s_{i,i}(\widehat{W})\bigr)\right]\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}), (71)

    and

    1n⁡(n−1)∑i≠jψ(sj,i(W^))−𝔼[1n⁡(n−1)∑i≠jψ(sj,i(W^))]=𝒪≺(d−1/2).\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}\psi\bigl(s_{j,i}(\widehat{W})\bigr)-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}\psi\bigl(s_{j,i}(\widehat{W})\bigr)\right]\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (72)
  3. (A6)

    (Trace concentration)

    1d2tr(H−1)−𝔼[1d2tr(H−1)]=𝒪≺(d−1/2).\frac{1}{d^{2}}\,\tr\!\left(H^{-1}\right)-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{d^{2}}\,\tr\!\left(H^{-1}\right)\right]\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (73)

The spectral estimate (A4) is proved in Appendix E; the empirical-mean and trace concentration estimates (A5) and (A6) are proved in Appendix D. Here (A4) is a spectral estimate on the optimizer W^\widehat{W}, while (A5) and (A6) are self-averaging estimates at the common scale 𝒪≺(d−1/2)\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}) for empirical means and normalized inverse traces, respectively.

For ν>0\nu>0, define the scalar TAM functional

cr​(ν):=minμ∈ℝ⁡{μ+1r​𝔼Z∼𝒩⁡(0,1)​[ϕβ​(ν​Z−μ)]}.c_{r}(\nu)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\min_{\mu\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\mu+\frac{1}{r}\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\left[\phi_{\beta}(\nu Z-\mu)\right]\right\}. (74)

Let μr​(ν)\mu_{r}(\nu) denote the minimizer in (74). It is characterized by

r=𝔼Z∼𝒩⁡(0,1)​[σ⁡(β⁡(ν​Z−μr​(ν)))].r=\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\left[\sigma\!\bigl(\beta(\nu Z-\mu_{r}(\nu))\bigr)\right]. (75)
Definition 3 (Scalar saddle and reduced potentials).

For ν,χ>0\nu,\chi>0, define the scalar Moreau envelope

Mr​(ν,χ):=𝔼G∼𝒩⁡(0,1)​[mins∈ℝ⁡[(s−ν​G)22​χ+ℓ⁡(s−cr​(ν))]].M_{r}(\nu,\chi)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathbb{E}_{G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\left[\min_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\left[\frac{(s-\nu G)^{2}}{2\chi}+\ell\bigl(s-c_{r}(\nu)\bigr)\right]\right]. (76)

The scalar saddle potential is

𝒫α,r​(ν,χ):=λ2​ν2−ν22​α​χ+Mr​(ν,χ),\mathcal{P}_{\alpha,r}(\nu,\chi)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{\lambda}{2}\nu^{2}-\frac{\nu^{2}}{2\alpha\chi}+M_{r}(\nu,\chi), (77)

and the reduced scalar potential is

𝒱α,r​(ν):=supχ>0𝒫α,r​(ν,χ).\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r}(\nu)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{\chi>0}\mathcal{P}_{\alpha,r}(\nu,\chi). (78)

Proposition 10, stated in Section 4.4, shows that, for each fixed ν>0\nu>0, the maximization over χ\chi is well posed and has a unique maximizer, and that the reduced potential 𝒱α,r\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r} is strongly convex in ν\nu.

For χ>0\chi>0, define

Proxχ⁡(x):=arg​miny∈ℝ⁡{(y−x)22​χ+ℓ⁡(y)}.\Prox_{\chi}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\argmin_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\frac{(y-x)^{2}}{2\chi}+\ell(y)\right\}. (79)

Equivalently, y=Proxχ⁡(x)y=\Prox_{\chi}(x) if and only if

y−χ​σ​(−y)=x.y-\chi\sigma(-y)=x. (80)

Sν,χ:=cr​(ν)+Proxχ⁡(ν​G−cr​(ν)).S_{\nu,\chi}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=c_{r}(\nu)+\Prox_{\chi}\!\bigl(\nu G-c_{r}(\nu)\bigr). (81)

Let ν∗\nu_{\ast} be the minimizer of 𝒱α,r\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r}, and let χ∗\chi_{\ast} be the maximizer of 𝒫α,r​(ν∗,⋅)\mathcal{P}_{\alpha,r}(\nu_{\ast},\cdot). Define μ∗\mu_{\ast} as the minimizer in (74) at ν=ν∗\nu=\nu_{\ast}, and set

c∗:=cr​(ν∗).c_{\ast}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=c_{r}(\nu_{\ast}). (82)

The variational facts used here, including uniqueness and the equivalence with the finite-dimensional equations derived below, are recorded in Proposition 10.

Theorem 2 (Scalar description of the joint TAM minimizer).

Fix (α,r,β,λ)(\alpha,r,\beta,\lambda) with β,λ>0\beta,\lambda>0. Assume that the minimizer ν∗\nu_{\ast} of 𝒱α,r\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r} is positive. In the joint limit n,d→∞n,d\to\infty with n/d2→αn/d^{2}\to\alpha and k/n→rk/n\to r, the following hold in probability:

    (Order-parameter concentration.)

    1d​‖W^‖𝖥⟶ν∗,1d2​tr⁡(H−1)⟶χ∗.\frac{1}{d}\,\|\widehat{W}\|_{\mathsf{F}}\longrightarrow\nu_{\ast},\qquad\frac{1}{d^{2}}\,\tr\!\bigl(H^{-1}\bigr)\longrightarrow\chi_{\ast}. (83)
  2. (ii)

  3. (iii)

Remark 2 (Reading off the retrieval metrics).

Theorem 2 directly answers the three performance questions posed in Section 3.3. Since the TAM aggregate converges to c∗c_{\ast}, the limiting margin is

M∗:=Sν∗,χ∗−c∗,M_{\ast}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=S_{\nu_{\ast},\chi_{\ast}}-c_{\ast}, (84)

and hence the average fitting loss converges to

𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(M∗)].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell(M_{\ast})\right]. (85)

The empirical margin distribution converges to the law of M∗M_{\ast}. Finally, writing Φ\Phi for the standard normal CDF, the signal percentile distribution converges to the law of

Φ⁡(Sν∗,χ∗ν∗),\Phi\!\left(\frac{S_{\nu_{\ast},\chi_{\ast}}}{\nu_{\ast}}\right), (86)

because the competitor scores have limiting law 𝒩⁡(0,ν∗2)\mathcal{N}(0,\nu_{\ast}^{2}).

4.4 Proof of Theorem 2

Define

νd2:=𝔼⁡[‖W^‖𝖥2d2].\nu_{d}^{2}\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\frac{\|\widehat{W}\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}}{d^{2}}\,\right]. (87)

With HH denoting the full Hessian operator from Definition 2, evaluated at (W^,μ^)(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu}), define

χd:=𝔼⁡[1d2​tr⁡(H−1)].\chi_{d}\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{d^{2}}\,\tr\!\left(H^{-1}\right)\right]. (88)

In this section, we prove Theorem 2 by deriving the finite-dimensional equations for νd\nu_{d} and χd\chi_{d}. The proof proceeds in four steps. First, using (A4) and the bilinear coupling estimate in Appendix F, we identify the off-diagonal competitor scores with Gaussians of variance νd2\nu_{d}^{2}. Second, this Gaussian approximation and the trace input (A6) give the proximal characterization of the diagonal score si,i​(W^)s_{i,i}(\widehat{W}). Third, WW-stationarity, together with empirical concentration (A5), yields a finite-dimensional equation for νd\nu_{d}. Fourth, a random matrix calculation for a simplified Hessian gives the companion equation for χd\chi_{d}. Combining the two equations gives an approximate residual system, whose zero-residual limit is the saddle-point condition for the scalar potential in Definition 3.

4.4.1 Gaussian law for competitor scores

We begin with the off-diagonal scores. The statement below gives a finite-dimensional joint Gaussian coupling for any fixed number of competitor scores in a single column, using an iterated leave-one-out reduction and the bilinear coupling estimate of Corollary 1.

Proposition 6 (Joint Gaussian limit for competitor scores).

Fix i∈[n]i\in[n], m≥1m\geq 1, and distinct j1,…,jm∈[n]∖{i}j_{1},\ldots,j_{m}\in[n]\setminus\{i\}. Assume (A1)–(A6). Then, in the joint regime n,d→∞n,d\to\infty with n/d2→αn/d^{2}\to\alpha and k/n→rk/n\to r: on a common probability space, there exist i.i.d. Gaussians Y1,…,Ym∼𝒩⁡(0,νd2)Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{m}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\nu_{d}^{2}) such that

∥(sj1,i(W^),…,sjm,i(W^))−(Y1,…,Ym)∥2=𝒪≺(d−1/2).\bigl\|\bigl(s_{j_{1},i}(\widehat{W}),\ldots,s_{j_{m},i}(\widehat{W})\bigr)-(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{m})\bigr\|_{2}\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (89)
Remark 3 (Connection with the limiting statement).

Proposition 6 is the finite-dimensional form of the off-diagonal Gaussian law in Theorem 2. Empirical-measure consequences, such as weak convergence of 1n−1​∑j≠iδsj,i​(W^)\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j\neq i}\delta_{s_{j,i}(\widehat{W})} to 𝒩⁡(0,νd2)\mathcal{N}(0,\nu_{d}^{2}), follow by combining exchangeability with concentration of the optimizer. The expectation-level replacements used below are obtained from this coupling for the finite list of bounded or C1C^{1} pseudo-Lipschitz observables appearing in the stationarity identities, together with the moment bounds implicit in (A5).

Proof.

Throughout, write Xk:=sjk,i​(W^)X_{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=s_{j_{k},i}(\widehat{W}) for k=1,…,mk=1,\ldots,m. Set W^fresh:=W^∖{i,j1,…,jm}\widehat{W}_{\text{fresh}}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\widehat{W}^{\setminus\{i,j_{1},\ldots,j_{m}\}} and V:=‖W^fresh​vi‖2/dV\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\|\widehat{W}_{\text{fresh}}v_{i}\|^{2}/d.

Step 1: Iterated leave-one-out.

Apply (56) successively after removing the samples i,j1,…,jmi,j_{1},\ldots,j_{m}. The finite-removal version of the LOO stability estimates, together with the spectral and self-averaging estimates (A4)–(A5), gives the same rank-one expansion at each level. The resulting iterated identity expresses

where i0=ii_{0}=i, iℓ=jℓi_{\ell}=j_{\ell} for ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, Iℓ:={i,j1,…,jℓ}I_{\ell}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\{i,j_{1},\ldots,j_{\ell}\}, and each ∥Rℓ∥𝖥=𝒪≺(d−1/2)\|R_{\ell}\|_{\mathsf{F}}=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}) by Section 4.2 applied at the corresponding LOO level.

For each k∈[m]k\in[m], sandwiching (90) with ujk⊤⋅viu_{j_{k}}^{\top}\cdot v_{i} yields

Xk=ujk⊤​W^fresh​vi+ℰk,X_{k}\;=\;u_{j_{k}}^{\top}\widehat{W}_{\text{fresh}}v_{i}\;+\;\mathcal{E}_{k}, (91)

Each rank-one contribution at level ℓ\ell

admits a self-adjoint rewrite that places one of the held-out vectors — uiu_{i} for ℓ=0\ell=0 and viv_{i} for ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 — on the outer test side, independent of the LOO operator (H∖Iℓ)−1(H^{\setminus I_{\ell}})^{-1} (which sees no sample in IℓI_{\ell}). Combined with the operator-norm bound ‖(H∖Iℓ)−1‖op≤d2/(λ​n)=O⁡(1)\|(H^{\setminus I_{\ell}})^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq d^{2}/(\lambda n)=O(1) from the ridge floor and ‖ua​vb⊤‖𝖥=O⁡(1)\|u_{a}v_{b}^{\top}\|_{\mathsf{F}}=O(1), the unmatched-Gaussian inner product gives an 𝒪≺(d−1/2)\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}) bound on each rank-one contribution. |ℰk|=𝒪≺(d−1/2)uniformly in k.|\mathcal{E}_{k}|\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2})\quad\text{uniformly in }k. (93)

Apply Corollary 1 with W=W^freshW=\widehat{W}_{\text{fresh}}, v0=viv_{0}=v_{i}, and ρf=ρop=O(d−1/2)\rho_{f}=\rho_{\mathrm{op}}=O(d^{-1/2}): there exist i.i.d. Y1,…,Ym∼𝒩⁡(0,νd2)Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{m}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\nu_{d}^{2}) with

with Y1,…,YmY_{1},\ldots,Y_{m} i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,νd2)\mathcal{N}(0,\nu_{d}^{2}).

Step 5: Combine.

Triangle inequality applied to (91), (93), and (94) yields (89). ∎

4.4.2 Proximal law for diagonal scores

We next record the finite-dimensional proximal law for the diagonal scores. Set

μd:=μr(νd),cd:=cr(νd),\mu_{d}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mu_{r}(\nu_{d}),\qquad c_{d}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=c_{r}(\nu_{d}), (95)

Proposition 7 (Coupled proximal law for si​is_{ii}).

Assume (A1)–(A6). Fix i∈[n]i\in[n]. On a common probability space, there is a standard Gaussian random variable Gi∼𝒩⁡(0,1)G_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) such that

si,i(W^)=cd+Proxχd(νdGi−cd)+𝒪≺(d−1/2),s_{i,i}(\widehat{W})=c_{d}+\Prox_{\chi_{d}}\!\left(\nu_{d}G_{i}-c_{d}\right)+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}), (96)

where Proxχ\Prox_{\chi} is defined in (79).

Proof.

Apply the LOO rank-one expansion (56) with h=ih=i and contract with ui⊤​(⋅)​viu_{i}^{\top}(\cdot)v_{i}. This gives

si,i(W^)=gi+a^i⟨uivi⊤,(H∖i)−1[uivi⊤]⟩+𝒪≺(d−1/2),s_{i,i}(\widehat{W})=g_{i}+\hat{a}_{i}\bigl\langle u_{i}v_{i}^{\top},\,(H^{\setminus i})^{-1}[u_{i}v_{i}^{\top}]\bigr\rangle+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}), (97)

where

gi:=ui⊤​W^∖i​vi,a^i=σ⁡(−m^i).g_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=u_{i}^{\top}\widehat{W}^{\setminus i}v_{i},\qquad\hat{a}_{i}=\sigma(-\hat{m}_{i}). (98)

The LOO Hessian H∖iH^{\setminus i} is independent of (ui,vi)(u_{i},v_{i}). Lemma 21, (A6), and the finite-removal trace stability therefore give

⟨uivi⊤,(H∖i)−1[uivi⊤]⟩=χd+𝒪≺(d−1/2).\bigl\langle u_{i}v_{i}^{\top},\,(H^{\setminus i})^{-1}[u_{i}v_{i}^{\top}]\bigr\rangle=\chi_{d}+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (99)

Since a^i\hat{a}_{i} is bounded, (97) becomes

si,i(W^)=gi+χdσ(−si,i(W^)+c^i)+𝒪≺(d−1/2),s_{i,i}(\widehat{W})=g_{i}+\chi_{d}\,\sigma\!\bigl(-s_{i,i}(\widehat{W})+\hat{c}_{i}\bigr)+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}), (100)

where

c^i:=μ^i+1k​∑j≠iϕβ​(sj,i​(W^)−μ^i).\hat{c}_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\hat{\mu}_{i}+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\neq i}\phi_{\beta}\!\bigl(s_{j,i}(\widehat{W})-\hat{\mu}_{i}\bigr). (101)

We now replace gig_{i} and c^i\hat{c}_{i} by their finite-dimensional deterministic counterparts. The bilinear coupling estimate, applied to the leave-one-out matrix W^∖i\widehat{W}^{\setminus i} and the fresh pair (ui,vi)(u_{i},v_{i}), gives a coupling

gi=νdGi+𝒪≺(d−1/2),Gi∼𝒩(0,1).g_{i}=\nu_{d}G_{i}+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}),\qquad G_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). (102)

Next, μ\mu-stationarity gives

1n∑j≠iσ(β(sj,i(W^)−μ^i))=r+𝒪≺(d−1/2).\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j\neq i}\sigma\!\bigl(\beta(s_{j,i}(\widehat{W})-\hat{\mu}_{i})\bigr)=r+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (103)

The off-diagonal Gaussian law from Proposition 6, together with the empirical-mean concentration estimate, implies that the left-hand side is

𝔼Z∼𝒩⁡(0,1)[σ(β(νdZ−μ^i))]+𝒪≺(d−1/2).\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\left[\sigma\!\bigl(\beta(\nu_{d}Z-\hat{\mu}_{i})\bigr)\right]+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (104)

For fixed r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1) and fixed β\beta, the bounded-score event keeps μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i} and μd\mu_{d} in a compact set; on this set the derivative in μ\mu of the preceding expectation is bounded away from zero. Hence (75) yields

Applying the same Gaussian approximation to the pseudo-Lipschitz test function ϕβ(⋅−μ)\phi_{\beta}(\cdot-\mu), and using the Lipschitz dependence on μ\mu, gives

Combining (100), (102), and (106), we obtain

si,i(W^)=νdGi+χdσ(−si,i(W^)+cd)+𝒪≺(d−1/2).s_{i,i}(\widehat{W})=\nu_{d}G_{i}+\chi_{d}\,\sigma\!\bigl(-s_{i,i}(\widehat{W})+c_{d}\bigr)+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (107)

Let yi:=si,i​(W^)−cdy_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=s_{i,i}(\widehat{W})-c_{d}. The last display is equivalent to

yi−χdσ(−yi)=νdGi−cd+𝒪≺(d−1/2).y_{i}-\chi_{d}\sigma(-y_{i})=\nu_{d}G_{i}-c_{d}+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (108)

The map y↦y−χd​σ​(−y)y\mapsto y-\chi_{d}\sigma(-y) is strictly increasing with derivative at least one, so its inverse Proxχd\Prox_{\chi_{d}} is 11-Lipschitz. This proves (96). ∎

4.4.3 Finite-dimensional scalar equations and variational consistency

We now derive the two finite-dimensional scalar equations for νd\nu_{d} and χd\chi_{d}, and then identify their zero-residual limit with the saddle-point equations of the scalar variational problem. The variance equation is obtained directly from WW-stationarity. Let GG and ZZ be independent standard Gaussian variables, and define

Sd:=cd+Proxχd⁡(νd​G−cd),\displaystyle S_{d}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=c_{d}+\Prox_{\chi_{d}}\!\left(\nu_{d}G-c_{d}\right), Ad:=σ⁡(−Sd+cd).\displaystyle A_{d}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sigma(-S_{d}+c_{d}). (109)
Proposition 8 (Finite-dimensional variance equation).

Assume (A1)–(A6), and use the coupled diagonal score law of Proposition 7. Then

νd2[λ+1r𝔼[Ad]𝔼[ϕβ′′(νdZ−μd)]]=𝔼[AdSd]+O(d−1/2).\nu_{d}^{2}\left[\lambda+\frac{1}{r}\,\mathbb{E}[A_{d}]\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\phi_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}\!\bigl(\nu_{d}Z-\mu_{d}\bigr)\right]\right]=\mathbb{E}[A_{d}S_{d}]+O(d^{-1/2}). (110)

At the full minimizer, the WW-stationarity condition (44) gives

λ​‖W^‖𝖥2d2=1n​∑i=1nai​(si,i​(W^)−1k​∑j≠iqj,i​sj,i​(W^)).\lambda\,\frac{\|\widehat{W}\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}}{d^{2}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\left(s_{i,i}(\widehat{W})-\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\neq i}q_{j,i}s_{j,i}(\widehat{W})\right). (112)

Taking expectations turns the left-hand side into λ​νd2\lambda\nu_{d}^{2}.

The first empirical average in (112) is a smooth test function of the diagonal score, after replacing cic_{i} by cdc_{d} at the d−1/2d^{-1/2} scale. Proposition 7 and (A5) therefore yield

𝔼[1n∑i=1naisi,i(W^)]=𝔼[AdSd]+O(d−1/2).\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}s_{i,i}(\widehat{W})\right]=\mathbb{E}[A_{d}S_{d}]+O(d^{-1/2}). (113)

Here the distinction between k/nk/n and k/(n−1)k/(n-1) contributes only O⁡(n−1)O(n^{-1}), which is absorbed into O(d−1/2)O(d^{-1/2}). Combining (112)–(115) gives

We next derive the companion equation for the scalar χd\chi_{d} defined in (88). It is the expectation of the normalized inverse trace of the full Hessian, and is often referred to as the susceptibility in the statistical physics literature. Set

5 Ridgeless limit and phase transition

The scalar theory in Section 4.3 gives a limiting variational problem for each fixed ridge parameter λ>0\lambda>0 and fixed smoothing parameter β<∞\beta<\infty. In this section we take the sequential ridgeless limit: first n,d→∞n,d\to\infty with n/d2→αn/d^{2}\to\alpha and k/n→rk/n\to r, and then λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0 while keeping β∈(0,∞)\beta\in(0,\infty) fixed. The limit separates two regimes. Below the critical load αc​(r)\alpha_{c}(r) defined in (133) below, the scalar norm ν\nu escapes to infinity as λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0 and the limiting fitting loss vanishes; we call this the satisfiable, or SAT, phase. Above this critical load the scalar norm remains finite and the limiting fitting loss is positive; we call this the unsatisfiable, or UNSAT, phase. After deriving the transition from the variational principle, we describe the score, margin, and percentile profiles on both sides.

All results in this section concern the scalar saddle problem of Definition 3. They translate into statements about the original TAM minimizer (W^,μ^)(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu}) through the scalar identification in Theorem 2.

5.1 The critical load

Definition 4 (Ridgeless threshold).

Let G∼N⁡(0,1)G\sim N(0,1), and define

κr:=φ​(Φ−1​(1−r))r,\kappa_{r}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{\varphi(\Phi^{-1}(1-r))}{r}, (132)

where Φ\Phi and φ\varphi are the CDF and density of a standard normal random variable. The critical load is

αc​(r)=1𝔼⁡[(κr−G)+2]=1(1+κr2)​Φ​(κr)+κr​φ​(κr).\alpha_{c}(r)=\frac{1}{\mathbb{E}[(\kappa_{r}-G)_{+}^{2}]}=\frac{1}{(1+\kappa_{r}^{2})\Phi(\kappa_{r})+\kappa_{r}\varphi(\kappa_{r})}. (133)

In what follows, we first explain the origin and underlying ideas behind the transition at αc​(r)\alpha_{c}(r). The formal proof is then given in Proposition 11.

We start from the dual form of the reduced potential in (461), writing the ridge parameter explicitly:

𝒱α,r,λ​(ν)\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,\lambda}(\nu) =λ2ν2+sup0≤a⁡(⋅)≤1{𝔼[a(G)(cr(ν)−νG)−I(a(G))]\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda}{2}\nu^{2}+\sup_{0\leq a(\cdot)\leq 1}\Bigg\{\mathbb{E}\!\left[a(G)\bigl(c_{r}(\nu)-\nu G\bigr)-I(a(G))\right] (134)
−να(𝔼[a(G)2])1/2},\displaystyle-\frac{\nu}{\sqrt{\alpha}}\left(\mathbb{E}[a(G)^{2}]\right)^{1/2}\Bigg\},

where G∼N⁡(0,1)G\sim N(0,1) and I⁡(a)=a​log⁡a+(1−a)​log⁡(1−a)I(a)=a\log a+(1-a)\log(1-a). The supremum is over measurable functions a:ℝ→[0,1]a\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]. We write 𝒱α,r,0\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0} for the ridgeless potential obtained by setting λ=0\lambda=0; explicitly,

𝒱α,r,0​(ν)=sup0≤a⁡(⋅)≤1{𝔼⁡[a⁡(G)​(cr​(ν)−ν​G)−I⁡(a⁡(G))]−να​(𝔼⁡[a​(G)2])1/2}.\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}(\nu)=\sup_{0\leq a(\cdot)\leq 1}\Bigg\{\mathbb{E}\!\left[a(G)\bigl(c_{r}(\nu)-\nu G\bigr)-I(a(G))\right]-\frac{\nu}{\sqrt{\alpha}}\left(\mathbb{E}[a(G)^{2}]\right)^{1/2}\Bigg\}. (135)

The phase transition is determined by the large-ν\nu behavior of the ridgeless potential 𝒱α,r,0\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}. The only input from the TAM threshold cr​(ν)c_{r}(\nu) needed for the leading-order calculation is the asymptotic relation

cr​(ν)ν⟶κr.\frac{c_{r}(\nu)}{\nu}\longrightarrow\kappa_{r}. (136)

We defer the verification of (136) to the proof of Proposition 11. Now set mr​(ν):=cr​(ν)/νm_{r}(\nu)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=c_{r}(\nu)/\nu. For fixed a⁡(⋅)a(\cdot), the linear-in-ν\nu part of (134) is

ν⁡[𝔼⁡[a⁡(G)​(mr​(ν)−G)]−1α​‖a‖2],‖a‖2:=(𝔼⁡[a​(G)2])1/2.\nu\left[\mathbb{E}\!\left[a(G)(m_{r}(\nu)-G)\right]-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha}}\|a\|_{2}\right],\qquad\|a\|_{2}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\left(\mathbb{E}[a(G)^{2}]\right)^{1/2}. (137)

The entropy term I⁡(a)I(a) is not multiplied by ν\nu. Thus the large-norm behavior is governed by a simple question: can we choose a nonzero dual profile aa so that the coefficient of the leading linear term in ν\nu is positive?

Letting ν→∞\nu\to\infty in this coefficient and using (136), the relevant expression becomes

𝔼⁡[a⁡(G)​(κr−G)]−1α​‖a‖2.\mathbb{E}[a(G)(\kappa_{r}-G)]-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha}}\|a\|_{2}. (138)

Since a≥0a\geq 0, the negative part of κr−G\kappa_{r}-G can only hurt, so the best profile should live on the event {G<κr}\{G<\kappa_{r}\}. More precisely, by Cauchy–Schwarz, for any 0≤a≤10\leq a\leq 1,

𝔼⁡[a⁡(G)​(κr−G)]≤𝔼⁡[a⁡(G)​(κr−G)+]≤‖a‖2​(𝔼⁡[(κr−G)+2])1/2.\mathbb{E}[a(G)(\kappa_{r}-G)]\leq\mathbb{E}[a(G)(\kappa_{r}-G)_{+}]\leq\|a\|_{2}\,\left(\mathbb{E}[(\kappa_{r}-G)_{+}^{2}]\right)^{1/2}. (139)

The upper bound is sharp despite the pointwise constraint a≤1a\leq 1. Indeed, equality in Cauchy–Schwarz would ask for aa proportional to (κr−G)+(\kappa_{r}-G)_{+}, which is unbounded. We can approximate this direction by the admissible truncations

aM​(G):=min⁡{(κr−G)+M,1},M→∞.a_{M}(G)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\min\left\{\frac{(\kappa_{r}-G)_{+}}{M},1\right\},\qquad M\to\infty. (140)

The ratio 𝔼⁡[aM​(G)​(κr−G)]/‖aM‖2\mathbb{E}[a_{M}(G)(\kappa_{r}-G)]/\|a_{M}\|_{2} converges to (𝔼⁡[(κr−G)+2])1/2\left(\mathbb{E}[(\kappa_{r}-G)_{+}^{2}]\right)^{1/2}. Hence a positive large-ν\nu direction exists exactly when α>αc​(r)\alpha>\alpha_{c}(r), with αc​(r)\alpha_{c}(r) as in (133).

Proposition 11 (Ridgeless scalar phase transition).

Fix r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1) and β∈(0,∞)\beta\in(0,\infty). For each λ>0\lambda>0, let νλ\nu_{\lambda} be the unique minimizer of 𝒱α,r,λ\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,\lambda}.

  1. (i)

    If α<αc​(r)\alpha<\alpha_{c}(r), then

    νλ→∞and𝒱α,r,0​(νλ)→0\nu_{\lambda}\to\infty\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}(\nu_{\lambda})\to 0 (141)

    as λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0.

  2. (ii)

    If α>αc​(r)\alpha>\alpha_{c}(r), then νλ\nu_{\lambda} remains bounded as λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0 and converges to the unique minimizer ν0<∞\nu_{0}<\infty of 𝒱α,r,0\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}. The ridgeless fitting loss 𝒱α,r,0​(ν0)\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}(\nu_{0}) is strictly positive.

Proof.

We first justify (136). Rescaling the definition of crc_{r} by writing μ=ν​t\mu=\nu t gives

cr​(ν)ν=mint∈ℝ⁡{t+1r​𝔼​[ϕβ​(ν​(G−t))ν]}.\frac{c_{r}(\nu)}{\nu}=\min_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{t+\frac{1}{r}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\phi_{\beta}(\nu(G-t))}{\nu}\right]\right\}. (142)

For each fixed yy, the function ν↦ϕβ​(ν​y)/ν\nu\mapsto\phi_{\beta}(\nu y)/\nu is nonincreasing and converges to y+y_{+}. Thus the limiting problem is

mint∈ℝ⁡{t+1r​𝔼​[(G−t)+]}.\min_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{t+\frac{1}{r}\mathbb{E}[(G-t)_{+}]\right\}. (143)

Its minimizer is t=Φ−1​(1−r)t=\Phi^{-1}(1-r) and its value is κr\kappa_{r}, which proves (136). In fact the convergence is monotone decreasing.

SAT case: α<αc​(r)\alpha<\alpha_{c}(r). By (136) and the definition (133), there are δ>0\delta>0 and ν0<∞\nu_{0}<\infty such that, for all ν≥ν0\nu\geq\nu_{0},

(𝔼⁡[(mr​(ν)−G)+2])1/2≤1α−δ.\left(\mathbb{E}[(m_{r}(\nu)-G)_{+}^{2}]\right)^{1/2}\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha}}-\delta. (144)

Therefore, uniformly over 0≤a≤10\leq a\leq 1,

𝔼⁡[a⁡(G)​(mr​(ν)−G)]−1α​‖a‖2≤−δ​‖a‖2.\mathbb{E}[a(G)(m_{r}(\nu)-G)]-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha}}\|a\|_{2}\leq-\delta\|a\|_{2}. (145)

The remaining terms in the dual representation are lower order. More precisely, for any p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) there is Cp<∞C_{p}<\infty such that −I⁡(x)≤Cp​xp-I(x)\leq C_{p}x^{p} for 0≤x≤10\leq x\leq 1, while 𝔼⁡[ap]≤‖a‖2p\mathbb{E}[a^{p}]\leq\|a\|_{2}^{p}. Hence

𝒱α,r,0​(ν)\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}(\nu) ≤sup0≤x≤1{−δνx+Cpxp}⟶0as ν→∞.\displaystyle\leq\sup_{0\leq x\leq 1}\left\{-\delta\nu x+C_{p}x^{p}\right\}\longrightarrow 0\quad\text{as }\nu\to\infty. (146)

Since a=0a=0 is admissible, 𝒱α,r,0​(ν)≥0\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}(\nu)\geq 0, and therefore 𝒱α,r,0​(ν)→0\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}(\nu)\to 0 as ν→∞\nu\to\infty.

To identify the variational value with the scalar fitting loss, fix ν\nu and let χ⁡(ν)\chi(\nu) be the unique maximizer of 𝒫α,r,λ​(ν,⋅)\mathcal{P}_{\alpha,r,\lambda}(\nu,\cdot), whose existence and uniqueness are given by Proposition 10. With the scalar proximal channel Sν,χS_{\nu,\chi} defined in (81), the identity

𝒱α,r,λ​(ν)=λ2​ν2+𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(Sν,χ−cr​(ν))]\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,\lambda}(\nu)=\frac{\lambda}{2}\nu^{2}+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell(S_{\nu,\chi}-c_{r}(\nu))\right] (147)

follows from a short cancellation. Writing A:=σ⁡(−Sν,χ+cr​(ν))A\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sigma(-S_{\nu,\chi}+c_{r}(\nu)), the proximal equation gives Sν,χ−ν​G=χ​AS_{\nu,\chi}-\nu G=\chi A, and hence

Mr​(ν,χ)=χ2​𝔼​[A2]+𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(Sν,χ−cr​(ν))].M_{r}(\nu,\chi)=\frac{\chi}{2}\mathbb{E}[A^{2}]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell(S_{\nu,\chi}-c_{r}(\nu))\right]. (148)

Thus the ridgeless potential is the scalar fitting loss and is strictly positive at every finite ν\nu. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, choose NN so large that 𝒱α,r,0​(N)≤ε\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}(N)\leq\varepsilon, and then choose λ\lambda so small that λ​N2/2≤ε\lambda N^{2}/2\leq\varepsilon. This gives

𝒱α,r,λ​(νλ)≤2​ε.\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,\lambda}(\nu_{\lambda})\leq 2\varepsilon. (149)

Hence the optimal value tends to zero. If νλ\nu_{\lambda} remained bounded along a subsequence, lower semicontinuity would force a finite point with zero ridgeless fitting loss, contradicting strict positivity. Therefore νλ→∞\nu_{\lambda}\to\infty, and the displayed identity implies that the per-sample fitting loss tends to zero.

UNSAT case: α>αc​(r)\alpha>\alpha_{c}(r). By the sharpness of the Cauchy–Schwarz bound, there is a bounded measurable a:ℝ→[0,1]a\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathbb{R}\to[0,1] and a number δ>0\delta>0 such that

𝔼⁡[a⁡(G)​(κr−G)]−1α​‖a‖2≥2​δ.\mathbb{E}[a(G)(\kappa_{r}-G)]-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha}}\|a\|_{2}\geq 2\delta. (150)

Using mr​(ν)→κrm_{r}(\nu)\to\kappa_{r} and bounded convergence, the same aa satisfies, for all sufficiently large ν\nu,

𝔼⁡[a⁡(G)​(mr​(ν)−G)]−1α​‖a‖2≥δ.\mathbb{E}[a(G)(m_{r}(\nu)-G)]-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha}}\|a\|_{2}\geq\delta. (151)

Substituting this fixed test function into (134) gives

𝒱α,r,0​(ν)≥δ​ν−O⁡(1),\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}(\nu)\geq\delta\nu-O(1), (152)

so the ridgeless potential is coercive. The minimizers of 𝒱α,r,λ=𝒱α,r,0+λ​ν2/2\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,\lambda}=\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}+\lambda\nu^{2}/2 therefore remain in a compact set as λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0. Any limit point minimizes 𝒱α,r,0\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0} by the standard variational argument: compare νλ\nu_{\lambda} against an arbitrary fixed ν\nu and let λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0.

We now show that the ridgeless minimizer is unique. For finite β\beta, the TAM threshold crc_{r} is strictly convex. Indeed, with

wν​(Z):=ϕβ′′​(ν​Z−μr​(ν)),w_{\nu}(Z)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\phi_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}\!\bigl(\nu Z-\mu_{r}(\nu)\bigr), (153)

the envelope theorem and the defining equation for μr​(ν)\mu_{r}(\nu) give

cr′′​(ν)=1r​{𝔼⁡[wν​(Z)​Z2]−𝔼​[wν​(Z)​Z]2𝔼​[wν​(Z)]}>0.c_{r}^{\prime\prime}(\nu)=\frac{1}{r}\left\{\mathbb{E}[w_{\nu}(Z)Z^{2}]-\frac{\mathbb{E}[w_{\nu}(Z)Z]^{2}}{\mathbb{E}[w_{\nu}(Z)]}\right\}>0. (154)

For each finite ν\nu, the dual maximizer in (135) has positive expectation. In the primal variables this maximizer is a⁡(G)=σ⁡(−Sν,χ+cr​(ν))a(G)=\sigma(-S_{\nu,\chi}+c_{r}(\nu)), and hence 0<a⁡(G)<10<a(G)<1 almost surely. Therefore 𝒱α,r,0\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0} is strictly convex: if νθ=θ​ν1+(1−θ)​ν2\nu_{\theta}=\theta\nu_{1}+(1-\theta)\nu_{2} with 0<θ<10<\theta<1 and ν1≠ν2\nu_{1}\neq\nu_{2}, evaluating the dual formula at the maximizer for νθ\nu_{\theta} and using the strict convexity of crc_{r} gives

𝒱α,r,0​(νθ)<θ​𝒱α,r,0​(ν1)+(1−θ)​𝒱α,r,0​(ν2).\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}(\nu_{\theta})<\theta\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}(\nu_{1})+(1-\theta)\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r,0}(\nu_{2}). (155)

Thus the ridgeless minimizer is unique; call it ν0\nu_{0}. Hence νλ→ν0\nu_{\lambda}\to\nu_{0}. Since ν0\nu_{0} is finite, the corresponding scalar logistic loss is strictly positive. ∎

Remark 4 (No dependence on the smoothing parameter).

The critical load αc​(r)\alpha_{c}(r) does not depend on the smoothing parameter β∈(0,∞)\beta\in(0,\infty). The parameter β\beta affects the finite-λ\lambda scalar channel and the finite ridgeless minimizer in the UNSAT phase, but it disappears from the large-ν\nu limit (136), where the smoothed logistic tail ϕβ​(ν​y)/ν\phi_{\beta}(\nu y)/\nu converges to y+y_{+}.

5.2 Score, margin, and percentile profiles

We next translate the ridgeless phase transition into predictions for the true scores, the competing scores, the margins, and the percentile rank of the true score among its competitors. The two phases have different scaling behavior. In the SAT phase, Proposition 11 shows that νλ→∞\nu_{\lambda}\to\infty. Thus the true scores and the competitor scores both diverge on the original scale. The meaningful objects are the normalized scores, obtained by dividing by νλ\nu_{\lambda}, and these have a non-degenerate limit. In the UNSAT phase, by contrast, νλ\nu_{\lambda} remains finite, so the ridgeless profiles live on the original scale.

5.2.1 The SAT phase

We begin with the SAT phase, where the limiting normalized profiles are explicit. The single parameter controlling them is the number ρα>κr\rho_{\alpha}>\kappa_{r}, defined as the unique solution of

𝔼⁡[(ρα−G)+2]=1α,G∼N⁡(0,1).\mathbb{E}[(\rho_{\alpha}-G)_{+}^{2}]=\frac{1}{\alpha},\qquad G\sim N(0,1). (156)

The left-hand side is strictly increasing in ρα\rho_{\alpha}, and the boundary value ρα=κr\rho_{\alpha}=\kappa_{r} is exactly (133). Hence ρα\rho_{\alpha} is monotone decreasing in α\alpha and satisfies ρα↓κr\rho_{\alpha}\downarrow\kappa_{r} as α↑αc​(r)\alpha\uparrow\alpha_{c}(r).

Proposition 12 (SAT score, margin, and percentile profiles).

Assume α<αc​(r)\alpha<\alpha_{c}(r), and let ρα>κr\rho_{\alpha}>\kappa_{r} be the unique solution of (156). In the sequential ridgeless limit λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0, the normalized true score satisfies

Sνλ,χλνλ⇒max⁡{G,ρα},G∼N⁡(0,1).\frac{S_{\nu_{\lambda},\chi_{\lambda}}}{\nu_{\lambda}}\Rightarrow\max\{G,\rho_{\alpha}\},\qquad G\sim N(0,1). (157)

Consequently, the normalized TAM margin satisfies

Sνλ,χλ−cr​(νλ)νλ⇒max⁡{G,ρα}−κr,G∼N⁡(0,1).\frac{S_{\nu_{\lambda},\chi_{\lambda}}-c_{r}(\nu_{\lambda})}{\nu_{\lambda}}\Rightarrow\max\{G,\rho_{\alpha}\}-\kappa_{r},\qquad G\sim N(0,1). (158)

Here and below, ⇒\Rightarrow denotes weak convergence of laws as λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0. The associated percentile variable satisfies

Ω⇒Φ⁡(max⁡{G,ρα}).\Omega\Rightarrow\Phi\!\left(\max\{G,\rho_{\alpha}\}\right). (159)

Equivalently, if pα:=Φ⁡(ρα)p_{\alpha}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\Phi(\rho_{\alpha}), then

ℙ⁡(Ω≤ω)={0,ω<pα,ω,pα≤ω≤1.\mathbb{P}(\Omega\leq\omega)=\begin{cases}0,&\omega<p_{\alpha},\\ \omega,&p_{\alpha}\leq\omega\leq 1.\end{cases} (160)
Proof.

By Proposition 11, in the SAT phase νλ→∞\nu_{\lambda}\to\infty and the scalar fitting loss tends to zero. The proof has three steps. First, we rewrite the proximal channel in terms of the normalized score and the correction term created by the loss. Second, we introduce the scalar quantity ρλ\rho_{\lambda} and use the saddle-point equation to show that it is bounded. Third, we identify every subsequential limit of ρλ\rho_{\lambda}; uniqueness of the equation defining ρα\rho_{\alpha} then gives the stated weak convergence.

Set cλ:=cr​(νλ)c_{\lambda}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=c_{r}(\nu_{\lambda}). For each deterministic scalar input g∈ℝg\in\mathbb{R}, define

Sλ(g):=cλ+Proxχλ(νλg−cλ),Xλ(g):=Sλ​(g)νλ.S_{\lambda}(g)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=c_{\lambda}+\Prox_{\chi_{\lambda}}(\nu_{\lambda}g-c_{\lambda}),\qquad X_{\lambda}(g)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{S_{\lambda}(g)}{\nu_{\lambda}}. (161)

Moreover, the zero-loss statement implies that the normalized score does not fall below the TAM threshold. Indeed, with Mλ​(g):=Sλ​(g)−cλM_{\lambda}(g)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=S_{\lambda}(g)-c_{\lambda}, we have pointwise

(−m)+≤ℓ⁡(m).(-m)_{+}\leq\ell(m). (166)

Therefore, since the fitting loss 𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(Mλ)]\mathbb{E}[\ell(M_{\lambda})] tends to zero and νλ→∞\nu_{\lambda}\to\infty,
