5.2.2 The UNSAT phase

Assume α>αc​(r)\alpha>\alpha_{c}(r). In this regime the ridgeless limit does not escape to infinite norm. By Proposition 11, the minimizers νλ\nu_{\lambda} converge to the unique finite minimizer ν0\nu_{0} of the ridgeless reduced potential. The next proposition records the corresponding finite-scale profiles. We omit the proof, since the statement is obtained by specializing the scalar channel from Section 4.3 at the ridgeless minimizer.

Proposition 13 (UNSAT score, margin, and percentile profiles).

Let χ0\chi_{0} be the maximizer in the scalar saddle problem corresponding to ν0\nu_{0}, and define

c0:=cr​(ν0).c_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=c_{r}(\nu_{0}). (178)

Then the limiting true score is the finite-scale scalar random variable

S0:=Sν0,χ0=c0+Proxχ0⁡(ν0​G−c0),G∼N⁡(0,1).S_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=S_{\nu_{0},\chi_{0}}=c_{0}+\Prox_{\chi_{0}}\!\bigl(\nu_{0}G-c_{0}\bigr),\qquad G\sim N(0,1). (179)

The competing scores remain on the same finite scale, with limiting Gaussian scale ν0\nu_{0}. The limiting TAM margin and fitting loss are

M0:=S0−c0,L0:=𝔼[ℓ(M0)]>0.M_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=S_{0}-c_{0},\qquad L_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell(M_{0})\right]>0. (180)

Finally, the limiting percentile rank of the true score is

Ω0:=Φ⁡(S0ν0).\Omega_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\Phi\!\left(\frac{S_{0}}{\nu_{0}}\right). (181)
Remark 5.

Unlike the phase boundary and the SAT normalized profiles, these UNSAT quantities generally retain a dependence on the fixed value of β\beta through the scalar functions cr​(ν)c_{r}(\nu) and Sν,χS_{\nu,\chi}.

5.3 Numerical validation

We now give finite-dimensional numerical checks of the scalar predictions. The most direct prediction is the phase boundary of Proposition 11: as (α,r)(\alpha,r) crosses the curve α=αc​(r)\alpha=\alpha_{c}(r), the optimized fitting loss should separate from zero and the norm scale ν=‖W^‖𝖥/d\nu=\|\widehat{W}\|_{\mathsf{F}}/d should change sharply. Figure 2 tests this prediction in a two-dimensional sweep over the load α=n/d2\alpha=n/d^{2} and the tail scale r=k/(n−1)r=k/(n-1). The empirical transition extracted from the simulations is closely aligned with the theoretical curve (133), both in the loss landscape and in the growth of the norm scale.

The phase diagram gives a global view of the transition. We next look more locally, along a one-dimensional slice in α\alpha (with r=0.15r=0.15), and compare the finite-dimensional optimizer with the scalar predictions on both sides of the transition. This second comparison provides more information: it tests not only the location of the phase boundary, but also the predicted loss, norm scale, margin profile, and percentile distribution.

Figure 3 shows good agreement between the scalar theory and the finite-dimensional simulations. The upper panels compare two scalar observables: the fitting loss and the inverse norm scale 1/ν1/\nu. The loss remains close to zero throughout the SAT phase and becomes positive beyond the predicted critical load. At the same transition, 1/ν1/\nu collapses toward zero on the SAT side, while it remains positive in the UNSAT phase, as predicted by Proposition 11.

The lower panels compare distributional predictions in the SAT phase. The empirical normalized margin distribution follows the limiting law (158), with the visible rounding caused by finite dimension. The percentile panel is particularly informative. The TAM prediction (160) has a hard lower edge at pα=Φ⁡(ρα)p_{\alpha}=\Phi(\rho_{\alpha}), meaning that in the ridgeless SAT limit the true item is never predicted to fall below this percentile among its competitors. The finite-dimensional curve tracks this edge closely. The same panel also shows the correlation-memory heuristic benchmark (35); compared with this non-optimized baseline, the TAM optimizer shifts the signal percentiles sharply toward the upper tail, reflecting the improvement obtained by learning the memory matrix for the listwise objective.

6 Conclusion

The capacity of a linear associative memory depends as much on how it is read as on how many parameters it has. Under isotropic Gaussian embeddings, top-1 retrieval has a sharp threshold: the critical value of d2/(n​log⁡n)d^{2}/(n\log n) is 22. If this ratio stays above 22, our adaptive sparse-repair construction retrieves all nn associations with high probability; if it stays below 22, no data-dependent linear memory can do so. The logarithmic factor is therefore not a weakness of a particular storage rule. It is the price of requiring every query to beat its strongest competitor. The critical value was conjectured in an earlier version of this paper and independently in the concurrent work of Giorlandino et al. (2026).

The picture changes when the correct target need only remain within a fixed fraction of the candidates. TAM captures this regime by comparing the signal with the average of its k=⌈r⁡(n−1)⌉k=\lceil r(n-1)\rceil strongest competitors. For fixed r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1), the list size is k=Θ⁡(n)k=\Theta(n), so this is a percentile-rank guarantee rather than a sublinear shortlist. At any fixed finite smoothing parameter and positive ridge, empirical risk minimization with the smoothed TAM objective has a high-dimensional limit governed by two scalar parameters. These parameters determine the limiting score, margin, and percentile laws. Taking the high-dimensional limit first and then sending the ridge parameter to zero gives the critical load αc​(r)\alpha_{c}(r) for α=n/d2\alpha=n/d^{2}. Below this load, the average fitting loss vanishes and the exact TAM criterion holds for all but a vanishing fraction of keys; above it, the limiting average fitting loss remains positive.

The TAM proof required a leave-one-out argument adapted to the strong dependence among the losses. Removing one association does two things at once: it changes that association’s signal term, and it changes its role as a competitor for every other query. Our coupled leave-one-out expansion tracks both effects and reduces the leading response to an inverse Hessian applied to a single rank-one feature. The accompanying stability, spectral, and self-averaging estimates then lead to the scalar theory. This mechanism is not specific to TAM and may also be useful for other matrix-valued empirical-risk problems in which every sample appears throughout the loss.

Between the two retrieval regimes lies a natural open question: what happens when the list fraction rr tends to zero with nn? This limit should clarify how the quadratic TAM scale crosses over to the extra logarithmic cost of top-1 retrieval. It also remains to prove the second-order correction proposed in Conjecture 1, which appears to capture the slow finite-size drift, and to understand how much of the theory persists beyond isotropic Gaussian embeddings.

Disclosure of AI Assistance

We used AI tools, specifically ChatGPT 5.5 and 5.6, in this work. The problem formulations and central ideas—including the overall approach to top-1 retrieval, the Tail-Average Margin criterion, and the leave-one-out framework for its analysis—originated with the authors. For top-1 retrieval, the authors first established nonmatching achievability and impossibility bounds, based respectively on CMM and a trace comparison using uniform Gaussian anticoncentration, and reported them in an earlier version of this paper. Starting from these arguments, iterative collaboration with AI tools helped sharpen both sides to the exact constant 22. Building on our earlier CMM analysis, the sharp achievability argument augments CMM with an adaptive sparse correction that repairs the exceptional low-margin queries. This construction, formalized in Proposition 2, drew inspiration from multiscale majority and deficit-repair constructions for random perceptrons (Kim and Roche, 1998; Abbe et al., 2022; Ding and Sun, 2025); AI tools assisted in refining the argument. For the converse, the dual-certificate approach was motivated by classical separation and perceptron methods (Wendel, 1962; Cover, 1965), and AI tools assisted substantially in completing the technical arguments. We view this as an encouraging example of how human–AI collaboration can contribute to mathematical research.

The TAM formulation and leave-one-out analysis, including the rank-one reduction in Proposition 3 and the resulting scalar characterization, were developed by the authors and reported in an earlier version of this paper. AI tools assisted in completing and checking several supporting technical arguments, particularly the leave-one-out stability estimates in Proposition 4 and the spectral and self-averaging concentration estimates in Proposition 5. AI tools also assisted with numerical experiments and with editing and polishing the manuscript. The authors carefully verified all results and take full responsibility for the content of this paper.

Appendix A Correlation matrix memory: score law and retrieval

This appendix gives the CMM score-law and retrieval calculations used in Section 2.1. Section A.1 derives the exact one-query law underlying (17), and Section A.2 proves Proposition 1 using a conditional moment-generating function.

Under the Gaussian model (3), let U=[u1⋯un]U=[u_{1}\;\cdots\;u_{n}] and V=[v1⋯vn]V=[v_{1}\;\cdots\;v_{n}] in ℝd×n\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}; their columns are mutually independent 𝒩⁡(0,Id/d)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}/d) vectors. For the correlation matrix memory W𝖢𝖬𝖬=U​V⊤W_{\mathsf{CMM}}=UV^{\top} from (14), throughout this appendix we write

S≔U⊤​W𝖢𝖬𝖬​V=U⊤​U​V⊤​V∈ℝn×n,Sj,i=sj,i=uj⊤​W𝖢𝖬𝖬​vi.S\coloneqq U^{\top}W_{\mathsf{CMM}}V=U^{\top}UV^{\top}V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},\qquad S_{j,i}=s_{j,i}=u_{j}^{\top}W_{\mathsf{CMM}}v_{i}.

Thus column ii contains all decoder scores for query viv_{i}: si,is_{i,i} is its signal score, while (sj,i)j≠i(s_{j,i})_{j\neq i} are its competitor scores.

Moreover, χ⁡(k)\chi(k) denotes the chi distribution with kk degrees of freedom.

Remark 6 (Gaussian consequence of the one-column law).

Suppose that n,d→∞n,d\to\infty with n/d2→α∈(0,∞)n/d^{2}\to\alpha\in(0,\infty). Then, for every fixed mm,

(θ,ξ1,…,ξm)⟹(1+α​G0,α​G1,…,α​Gm),(\theta,\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{m})\Longrightarrow\bigl(1+\sqrt{\alpha}\,G_{0},\sqrt{\alpha}\,G_{1},\ldots,\sqrt{\alpha}\,G_{m}\bigr),

where G0,…,GmG_{0},\ldots,G_{m} are independent standard Gaussians. To see this, apply Lemma 3: each ρℓ\rho_{\ell}, ℓ∈[5]\ell\in[5], and ‖g‖/n\|g\|/\sqrt{n} converge in probability to 11, whereas σ→α\sigma\to\sqrt{\alpha}.

The same representation yields a more general standardized formulation. Set αn≔n/d2\alpha_{n}\coloneqq n/d^{2}. If d/n→0d/n\to 0, then, for every fixed mm,

(θ−1αn,ξ1αn,…,ξmαn)⟹(G0,G1,…,Gm),\left(\frac{\theta-1}{\sqrt{\alpha_{n}}},\frac{\xi_{1}}{\sqrt{\alpha_{n}}},\ldots,\frac{\xi_{m}}{\sqrt{\alpha_{n}}}\right)\Longrightarrow(G_{0},G_{1},\ldots,G_{m}),

where G0,G1,…,GmG_{0},G_{1},\ldots,G_{m} are independent standard Gaussians, and the convergence is joint in ℝm+1\mathbb{R}^{m+1}.

Thus, for a fixed query, the signal score and any fixed number of competitor scores have precisely the leading-order Gaussian form suggested by (17), including their asymptotic independence. This finite-dimensional consequence does not by itself control the maximum over all n−1n-1 competitors; the uniform tail estimate needed for perfect retrieval is proved in Appendix A.2.

A.2 CMM top-1 retrieval above constant 8

Proof of Proposition 1.

For an ordered pair i≠ji\neq j, write

Dj,i≔si,i−sj,i,xj,i≔ui−uj.D_{j,i}\coloneqq s_{i,i}-s_{j,i},\qquad x_{j,i}\coloneqq u_{i}-u_{j}.

The CMM succeeds precisely when Dj,i>0D_{j,i}>0 for every ordered pair. We bound the lower tail of one such margin directly.

Exact conditional moment-generating function.

Fix i≠ji\neq j and condition on (ui,uj,vi)(u_{i},u_{j},v_{i}). With x=xj,ix=x_{j,i} and y=viy=v_{i}, expanding W𝖢𝖬𝖬=∑k=1nuk​vk⊤W_{\mathsf{CMM}}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}u_{k}v_{k}^{\top} gives

Dj,i=aj,i+bj,i​⟨vj,y⟩+∑k∉{i,j}⟨x,uk⟩​⟨vk,y⟩,D_{j,i}=a_{j,i}+b_{j,i}\langle v_{j},y\rangle+\sum_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\langle x,u_{k}\rangle\langle v_{k},y\rangle, (195)

where

aj,i≔⟨x,ui⟩​‖y‖2,bj,i≔⟨x,uj⟩.a_{j,i}\coloneqq\langle x,u_{i}\rangle\|y\|^{2},\qquad b_{j,i}\coloneqq\langle x,u_{j}\rangle.

The terms after aj,ia_{j,i} in (195) are conditionally independent and centered. Moreover, ⟨vj,y⟩∼𝒩⁡(0,‖y‖2/d)\langle v_{j},y\rangle\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\|y\|^{2}/d), while for k∉{i,j}k\notin\{i,j\} the two factors ⟨x,uk⟩\langle x,u_{k}\rangle and ⟨vk,y⟩\langle v_{k},y\rangle are independent centered Gaussians with variances ‖x‖2/d\|x\|^{2}/d and ‖y‖2/d\|y\|^{2}/d. Thus, if Rj,i≔Dj,i−aj,iR_{j,i}\coloneqq D_{j,i}-a_{j,i}, then

𝔼[eλ​Rj,i∣ui,uj,vi]=exp(λ2​bj,i2​‖y‖22​d)(1−λ2​‖x‖2​‖y‖2d2)−(n−2)/2\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\lambda R_{j,i}}\mid u_{i},u_{j},v_{i}\right]=\exp\left(\frac{\lambda^{2}b_{j,i}^{2}\|y\|^{2}}{2d}\right)\left(1-\frac{\lambda^{2}\|x\|^{2}\|y\|^{2}}{d^{2}}\right)^{-(n-2)/2} (196)

whenever λ2​‖x‖2​‖y‖2<d2\lambda^{2}\|x\|^{2}\|y\|^{2}<d^{2}. This identity uses 𝔼et​G​H=(1−t2σG2σH2)−1/2\mathbb{E}e^{tGH}=(1-t^{2}\sigma_{G}^{2}\sigma_{H}^{2})^{-1/2} for independent centered Gaussians G,HG,H.

Uniform concentration.

The condition lim infd2/(n​log⁡n)>8\liminf d^{2}/(n\log n)>8 implies d/log⁡n→∞d/\log n\to\infty. Standard chi-square and Gaussian tail bounds, followed by a union bound, therefore give a deterministic sequence εn→0\varepsilon_{n}\to 0 such that, with probability 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1),

maxi≤n⁡(|‖ui‖2−1|∨|‖vi‖2−1|)≤εn,maxi≠j⁡|⟨ui,uj⟩|≤εn.\begin{split}&\max_{i\leq n}\left(\bigl|\|u_{i}\|^{2}-1\bigr|\vee\bigl|\|v_{i}\|^{2}-1\bigr|\right)\leq\varepsilon_{n},\\ &\hskip 99.58464pt\max_{i\neq j}|\langle u_{i},u_{j}\rangle|\leq\varepsilon_{n}.\end{split} (197)

Call this event ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n}, and let ℋj,i\mathcal{H}_{j,i} denote the corresponding restrictions involving only (ui,uj,vi)(u_{i},u_{j},v_{i}). On ℋj,i\mathcal{H}_{j,i}, uniformly over i≠ji\neq j,

aj,i=1+o⁡(1),bj,i=−1+o⁡(1),‖xj,i‖2​‖vi‖2=2+o⁡(1).a_{j,i}=1+o(1),\qquad b_{j,i}=-1+o(1),\qquad\|x_{j,i}\|^{2}\|v_{i}\|^{2}=2+o(1). (198)

It remains to apply Chernoff’s bound to (196). We do so along an arbitrary subsequence. Passing to a further subsequence, either d/n→0d/n\to 0, or d/nd/n is bounded below by a positive constant.

Suppose first that d/n→0d/n\to 0, and set αn=n/d2\alpha_{n}=n/d^{2}. Conditional on (ui,uj,vi)∈ℋj,i(u_{i},u_{j},v_{i})\in\mathcal{H}_{j,i}, choose λ=aj,i/(2​αn)\lambda=a_{j,i}/(2\alpha_{n}). Then λ/d=O⁡(d/n)=o⁡(1)\lambda/d=O(d/n)=o(1), and −log⁡(1−t)=t+O⁡(t2)-\log(1-t)=t+O(t^{2}) in (196) yields, uniformly over i≠ji\neq j,

log𝔼[e−λ​Rj,i∣ui,uj,vi]=(1+o(1))λ2αn.\log\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-\lambda R_{j,i}}\mid u_{i},u_{j},v_{i}\right]=(1+o(1))\lambda^{2}\alpha_{n}.

Here the Gaussian term in (196) is negligible because 1/d=o⁡(αn)1/d=o(\alpha_{n}). Since Rj,iR_{j,i} is symmetric, Chernoff’s bound and (198) give

sup(ui,uj,vi)∈ℋj,iℙ⁡(Dj,i≤0∣ui,uj,vi)≤exp⁡(−1−o⁡(1)4​αn).\sup_{(u_{i},u_{j},v_{i})\in\mathcal{H}_{j,i}}\mathbb{P}\left(D_{j,i}\leq 0\mid u_{i},u_{j},v_{i}\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{1-o(1)}{4\alpha_{n}}\right). (199)

Choose η>0\eta>0 so that d2/(n​log⁡n)≥8+ηd^{2}/(n\log n)\geq 8+\eta eventually. The exponent on the right-hand side of (199) is then at least (2+cη)​log⁡n(2+c_{\eta})\log n for some cη>0c_{\eta}>0 and all sufficiently large nn.

Suppose instead that d/n≥c0>0d/n\geq c_{0}>0. Taking λ=κ​d\lambda=\kappa d in (196), with κ>0\kappa>0 sufficiently small depending only on c0c_{0}, gives

sup(ui,uj,vi)∈ℋj,iℙ⁡(Dj,i≤0∣ui,uj,vi)≤e−c1​d\sup_{(u_{i},u_{j},v_{i})\in\mathcal{H}_{j,i}}\mathbb{P}\left(D_{j,i}\leq 0\mid u_{i},u_{j},v_{i}\right)\leq e^{-c_{1}d} (200)

for some c1>0c_{1}>0. Indeed, the Chernoff exponent contributes −κ​d​(1+o⁡(1))-\kappa d(1+o(1)), whereas the logarithm of the moment-generating function is O⁡(κ2​(d+n))=O⁡(κ2​d)O(\kappa^{2}(d+n))=O(\kappa^{2}d). Since d/log⁡n→∞d/\log n\to\infty, the right-hand side of (200) is o⁡(n−2)o(n^{-2}).

Finally, a union bound over the n⁡(n−1)n(n-1) ordered pairs gives

ℙ⁡(𝖯𝖱​(W𝖢𝖬𝖬,U,V)c)≤ℙ⁡(ℋnc)+∑i≠jℙ⁡(Dj,i≤0,ℋj,i)=o⁡(1)\begin{split}\mathbb{P}\bigl(\mathsf{PR}(W_{\mathsf{CMM}};U,V)^{c}\bigr)&\leq\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{H}_{n}^{c})+\sum_{i\neq j}\mathbb{P}\bigl(D_{j,i}\leq 0,\mathcal{H}_{j,i}\bigr)\\ &=o(1)\end{split}

along either type of further subsequence. Every subsequence admits such a further subsequence, so the same convergence holds along the original sequence. ∎

Appendix B Taylor expansion of the interior remainder

This appendix carries out the first-order Taylor expansion of the interior remainder ℛ∖h\mathcal{R}^{\setminus h} defined in (60) of Section 4.2, derives the explicit form of the residual E^\hat{E} appearing in the main identity (64), and establishes the entry-size bounds (65) used there. All notation is as in Section 4.2: (W^,μ^)(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu}) and (W^∖h,μ^∖h)(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h},\widehat{\mu}^{\setminus h}) are the full and leave-one-out minimizers, Δ​S:=U⊤​(W^−W^∖h)​V\Delta S\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=U^{\top}(\widehat{W}-\widehat{W}^{\setminus h})V, (Δ​μ)i:=μ^i−μi∖h(\Delta\mu)_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\hat{\mu}_{i}-\mu_{i}^{\setminus h}; a hat denotes a quantity evaluated at (W^,μ^)(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu}) and a superscript ∖h\setminus h one evaluated at (W^∖h,μ^∖h)(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h},\widehat{\mu}^{\setminus h}). The analysis is conditional on the LOO postulates (A1)–(A3).

We record three Taylor identities around the LOO point. Throughout, for a scalar quantity X⁡(W,μ)X(W,\mu) we write Δ​X:=X⁡(W^,μ^)−X⁡(W^∖h,μ^∖h)\Delta X\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=X(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu})-X(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h},\widehat{\mu}^{\setminus h}).

q^j,i−qj,i∖h=k​R~j,i∖h​(Δ​Sj,i−(Δ​μ)i)+ρj,i(q),ρj,i(q)=𝒪≺​(β2​|Δ​Sj,i−(Δ​μ)i|2)=𝒪≺​(β2/d2),\begin{split}\hat{q}_{j,i}-q_{j,i}^{\setminus h}&\;=\;k\,\widetilde{R}_{j,i}^{\setminus h}\,\bigl(\Delta S_{j,i}-(\Delta\mu)_{i}\bigr)\;+\;\rho_{j,i}^{(q)},\\ \rho_{j,i}^{(q)}&\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}\bigl(\beta^{2}\,|\Delta S_{j,i}-(\Delta\mu)_{i}|^{2}\bigr)\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(\beta^{2}/d^{2}),\end{split} (201)

uniformly in (j,i)(j,i).

Appendix C Leave-one-out stability

We use the notation and standing assumptions of Section 4 and Section 4.2: n/d2→α∈(0,∞)n/d^{2}\to\alpha\in(0,\infty), r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1), and β,λ>0\beta,\lambda>0 are fixed. We prove the three stability inputs (A1)–(A3).

The proof has two main steps. First, after profiling out the threshold variables, we construct a one-step Newton candidate for the full optimizer from the leave-one-out optimizer. Freshness of the held-out pair controls the candidate on all surviving scores, while a residual estimate and strong convexity show that the candidate is O≺​(d−1)O_{\prec}(d^{-1})-close to the true optimizer. Second, the exact threshold equation reduces the sharper threshold estimate to a weighted average of these score perturbations. A second use of freshness gains an additional factor d−1/2d^{-1/2} in this average, yielding (A1). The remaining score-stability and boundedness conclusions then follow directly from the same finite-deletion comparison.

C.1 Leave-one-out expansion and Newton comparison

For J⊂[n]J\subset[n] with |J|>k|J|>k, define

𝒯J​(z):=minμ∈ℝ⁡{μ+1k​∑j∈Jϕβ​(zj−μ)}.\mathcal{T}_{J}(z)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\min_{\mu\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\mu+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\in J}\phi_{\beta}(z_{j}-\mu)\right\}.

Its unique minimizer μJ​(z)\mu_{J}(z) satisfies

∑j∈Jqj=k,qj=σ⁡(β⁡(zj−μJ​(z))),pj=qjk,\sum_{j\in J}q_{j}=k,\qquad q_{j}=\sigma\!\left(\beta(z_{j}-\mu_{J}(z))\right),\qquad p_{j}=\frac{q_{j}}{k}, (210)

so 0<pj≤k−10<p_{j}\leq k^{-1}, ∑jpj=1\sum_{j}p_{j}=1, and ∥p∥2≤k−1/2\|p\|_{2}\leq k^{-1/2}.

The next lemma collects the two inputs used throughout the appendix: the first group of estimates is deterministic profiled-tail calculus, while the last group supplies the Gaussian bulk curvature and delocalization needed for uniform leave-one-out bounds.

Lemma 4 (Profiled-tail identities and bulk geometry).

The map 𝒯J\mathcal{T}_{J} is smooth, convex, and translation equivariant with ∇𝒯J=p\nabla\mathcal{T}_{J}=p. Put wj=(β/k)​qj​(1−qj)w_{j}=(\beta/k)q_{j}(1-q_{j}), D=diag⁡(wj)D=\diag(w_{j}), and s=∑jwjs=\sum_{j}w_{j}. Then

∂μJ∂zℓ=wℓs,∇2𝒯J​(z)=BJ​(z):=D−(D​𝟏)​(D​𝟏)⊤𝟏⊤​D​𝟏,\frac{\partial\mu_{J}}{\partial z_{\ell}}=\frac{w_{\ell}}{s},\qquad\nabla^{2}\mathcal{T}_{J}(z)=B_{J}(z)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=D-\frac{(D\mathbf{1})(D\mathbf{1})^{\top}}{\mathbf{1}^{\top}D\mathbf{1}}, (211)

with

0⪯BJ​(z)⪯D⪯β4​k​I.0\preceq B_{J}(z)\preceq D\preceq\frac{\beta}{4k}I. (212)

Consequently, for H=‖h‖∞H=\|h\|_{\infty},

|𝒯J​(z+h)−𝒯J​(z)−p⊤​h|\displaystyle\left|\mathcal{T}_{J}(z+h)-\mathcal{T}_{J}(z)-p^{\top}h\right| ≤β8​k​‖h‖22,\displaystyle\leq\frac{\beta}{8k}\|h\|_{2}^{2}, (213)
‖p⁡(z+h)−p⁡(z)‖2\displaystyle\|p(z+h)-p(z)\|_{2} ≤β4​k​‖h‖2,\displaystyle\leq\frac{\beta}{4k}\|h\|_{2}, (214)
maxj⁡|pj​(z+h)−pj​(z)−(BJ​(z)​h)j|\displaystyle\max_{j}\left|p_{j}(z+h)-p_{j}(z)-(B_{J}(z)h)_{j}\right| ≤Cβk​H2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{C_{\beta}}{k}H^{2}. (215)

Moreover, uniformly under fixed finite deletions, if zj=uj⊤​xz_{j}=u_{j}^{\top}x, ρ=‖x‖/d≤C​d\rho=\|x\|/\sqrt{d}\leq C\sqrt{d}, and ∑j∈Jσ⁡(β⁡(zj−μ))=k+O⁡(1)\sum_{j\in J}\sigma(\beta(z_{j}-\mu))=k+O(1), then

|μ|≤C⁡(1+ρ),∑j∈Jqj​(1−qj)≥c​n1+ρ,‖(qj​(1−qj))j∈J∑ℓqℓ​(1−qℓ)‖22≤C​1+ρn.|\mu|\leq C(1+\rho),\qquad\sum_{j\in J}q_{j}(1-q_{j})\geq c\frac{n}{1+\rho},\qquad\left\|\frac{(q_{j}(1-q_{j}))_{j\in J}}{\sum_{\ell}q_{\ell}(1-q_{\ell})}\right\|_{2}^{2}\leq C\frac{1+\rho}{n}. (216)

If one competitor is inserted, the old tail weights decrease and their change r=pold−pnewr=p^{\rm old}-p^{\rm new} obeys

r≥0,‖r‖2≤Ck​1+ρn.r\geq 0,\qquad\|r\|_{2}\leq\frac{C}{k}\sqrt{\frac{1+\rho}{n}}. (217)
Proof.

The envelope theorem gives ∂zj𝒯J=qj/k\partial_{z_{j}}\mathcal{T}_{J}=q_{j}/k. Differentiating (210) in direction hh gives μ˙=∑jwj​hj/∑jwj\dot{\mu}=\sum_{j}w_{j}h_{j}/\sum_{j}w_{j} and p˙j=wj​(hj−μ˙)\dot{p}_{j}=w_{j}(h_{j}-\dot{\mu}), which proves (211)–(212); integration gives (213) and (214). Along z+t​hz+th, |w˙j|≤2​β​H​wj|\dot{w}_{j}|\leq 2\beta Hw_{j} and the normalized weights have derivative at most 4​β​H4\beta H times themselves, so a second differentiation gives (215).

For the bulk estimates, the quantile equation forces a fixed fraction of uj⊤​xu_{j}^{\top}x to lie on each side of μ\mu up to an O⁡(1)O(1) window, while the Gaussian frame bound gives m−1​∑j(uj⊤​x)2≲ρ2m^{-1}\sum_{j}(u_{j}^{\top}x)^{2}\lesssim\rho^{2}; thus |μ|≲1+ρ|\mu|\lesssim 1+\rho. For g⁡(t)=σ⁡(β​t)​(1−σ⁡(β​t))g(t)=\sigma(\beta t)(1-\sigma(\beta t)), uniformly on this range, 𝔼​g​(ρ​Z−μ)≳(1+ρ)−1\mathbb{E}g(\rho Z-\mu)\gtrsim(1+\rho)^{-1}. Bernstein’s inequality on a d−2d^{-2} net in (x/d,μ)(x/\sqrt{d},\mu), followed by the frame bound and a union bound, yields the curvature estimate in (216); ℓ2\ell_{2} delocalization follows from ‖π‖22≤‖π‖∞​‖π‖1\|\pi\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|\pi\|_{\infty}\|\pi\|_{1}. Finally, interpolate the new competitor with weight ϑ∈[0,1]\vartheta\in[0,1]. The threshold increases, so every old weight decreases, and differentiating the old weights gives an ℓ2\ell_{2} derivative bounded by C​k−1​(1+ρ)/nCk^{-1}\sqrt{(1+\rho)/n}; integration proves (217). ∎

Profiling the full and leave-one-out objectives gives

Ψ⁡(W)=∑i=1nℒi​(W)+λ​n2​d2​‖W‖F2,\Psi(W)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}_{i}(W)+\frac{\lambda n}{2d^{2}}\|W\|_{F}^{2}, (218)
Ψ∖h​(W)=∑i≠hℒi∖h​(W)+λ​n2​d2​‖W‖F2.\Psi^{\setminus h}(W)=\sum_{i\neq h}\mathcal{L}_{i}^{\setminus h}(W)+\frac{\lambda n}{2d^{2}}\|W\|_{F}^{2}. (219)

Thus the profiled objectives are γd\gamma_{d}-strongly convex with γd=λ​n/d2→λ​α>0\gamma_{d}=\lambda n/d^{2}\to\lambda\alpha>0. We also use repeatedly

∥pi∥2≤k−1/2,‖∑j∈Jpj,iuj‖≤∥U∥𝗈𝗉k−1/2=O≺(d−1/2).\|p_{i}\|_{2}\leq k^{-1/2},\qquad\left\|\sum_{j\in J}p_{j,i}u_{j}\right\|\leq\|U\|_{\mathsf{op}}k^{-1/2}=O_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (222)

Fix h∈[n]h\in[n] throughout the one-deletion construction. We use the standard Gaussian frame, Khatri–Rao matrix bounds, and fresh-contraction bounds, uniformly over polynomially many fixed finite deletions.

The deterministic upper bound of Lemma 18 applies unchanged after any fixed finite deletion; hence ‖W^∖h‖F+‖W^‖F=O⁡(d)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\widehat{W}^{\setminus h}\right\rVert}_{F}+\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\widehat{W}\right\rVert}_{F}=O(d).

𝒫h(W):=∑i≠h(ℒi(W)−ℒi∖h(W)),Gh(W):=∇𝒫h(W).\mathcal{P}_{h}(W)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{i\neq h}\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{i}(W)-\mathcal{L}_{i}^{\setminus h}(W)\bigr),\qquad G_{h}(W)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\nabla\mathcal{P}_{h}(W). (223)

For one fixed i≠hi\neq h, unadorned quantities refer to ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i}, and superscript ∖h\setminus h refers to ℒi∖h\mathcal{L}_{i}^{\setminus h}. Let

δ​ti=ti−ti∖h≥0,Ai=ai−ai∖h≥0,\delta t_{i}=t_{i}-t_{i}^{\setminus h}\geq 0,\qquad A_{i}=a_{i}-a_{i}^{\setminus h}\geq 0,

ri=pi∖h−pi,old≥0,ph,i=qh,ik.r_{i}=p_{i}^{\setminus h}-p_{i,\mathrm{old}}\geq 0,\qquad p_{h,i}=\frac{q_{h,i}}{k}.

A direct subtraction of the two column gradients gives the exact identity

Lemma 5 (Size of the insertion gap).

Let WW satisfy ‖W‖F=O≺​(d)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert W\right\rVert}_{F}=O_{\prec}(d), and set

Then

‖(δ​ti)i≠h‖2=O≺​(d−1),‖(Ai)i≠h‖2=O≺​(d−1).\mathinner{\!\left\lVert(\delta t_{i})_{i\neq h}\right\rVert}_{2}=O_{\prec}(d^{-1}),\qquad\mathinner{\!\left\lVert(A_{i})_{i\neq h}\right\rVert}_{2}=O_{\prec}(d^{-1}). (226)

Since k≍n≍d2k\asymp n\asymp d^{2}, this proves the first estimate in (226); the second follows from 0≤Ai≤δ​ti/40\leq A_{i}\leq\delta t_{i}/4. ∎

Lemma 6 (Insertion-gradient bound).

At W^∖h\widehat{W}^{\setminus h},

‖Gh​(W^∖h)‖F=O≺(d−1/2).\mathinner{\!\left\lVert G_{h}(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h})\right\rVert}_{F}=O_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (227)

uniformly in hh. Indeed, the conditional trace scale is at most d−1​‖W^∖h‖F2​‖V‖𝗈𝗉2=O≺​(n)d^{-1}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\widehat{W}^{\setminus h}\right\rVert}_{F}^{2}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert V\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{op}}^{2}=O_{\prec}(n). Hence Lemma 5 applies.

Newton candidate.

We now build one candidate for the full optimizer from the leave-one-out optimizer. The implicit scalar equation absorbs the held-out outer loss, and freshness makes the candidate’s surviving scores small.

Let ℋh:=∇2Ψ∖h​(W^∖h)\mathcal{H}_{h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\nabla^{2}\Psi^{\setminus h}(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h}) and Th:=ℋh−1T_{h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathcal{H}_{h}^{-1}. thloo=𝒯[n]∖{h}​((sj,h​(W^∖h))j≠h),mhloo=sh,h​(W^∖h)−thloo,t_{h}^{\mathrm{loo}}=\mathcal{T}_{[n]\setminus\{h\}}\bigl((s_{j,h}(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h}))_{j\neq h}\bigr),\qquad m_{h}^{\mathrm{loo}}=s_{h,h}(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h})-t_{h}^{\mathrm{loo}},

‖ηhloo‖=O≺(d−1/2),‖Xhloo‖F=O≺(1).\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\eta_{h}^{\mathrm{loo}}\right\rVert}=O_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}),\qquad\mathinner{\!\left\lVert X_{h}^{\mathrm{loo}}\right\rVert}_{F}=O_{\prec}(1). (230)

Set

Bh:=−Th[Gh(W^∖h)],θh:=⟨Xhloo,Th[Xhloo]⟩𝖥,ζh:=⟨Xhloo,Bh⟩𝖥.B_{h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=-T_{h}[G_{h}(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h})],\qquad\theta_{h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\left\langle X_{h}^{\mathrm{loo}},T_{h}[X_{h}^{\mathrm{loo}}]\right\rangle_{\mathsf{F}},\qquad\zeta_{h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\left\langle X_{h}^{\mathrm{loo}},B_{h}\right\rangle_{\mathsf{F}}. (231)

Let ah⋆∈(0,1)a_{h}^{\star}\in(0,1) be the unique solution of

ah⋆=σ⁡(−mhloo−ζh−θh​ah⋆).a_{h}^{\star}=\sigma\left(-m_{h}^{\mathrm{loo}}-\zeta_{h}-\theta_{h}a_{h}^{\star}\right). (232)

Finally, define

W~h:=W^∖h+Bh+ah⋆​Th​[Xhloo].\widetilde{W}_{h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\widehat{W}^{\setminus h}+B_{h}+a_{h}^{\star}T_{h}[X_{h}^{\mathrm{loo}}]. (233)
Theorem 3 (One-deletion Newton comparison).

Uniformly in hh,

maxi,j≠h⁡|uj⊤​(W~h−W^∖h)​vi|\displaystyle\max_{i,j\neq h}|u_{j}^{\top}(\widetilde{W}_{h}-\widehat{W}^{\setminus h})v_{i}| =O≺​(d−1),\displaystyle=O_{\prec}(d^{-1}), (234)
‖∇Ψ​(W~h)‖F\displaystyle\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\nabla\Psi(\widetilde{W}_{h})\right\rVert}_{F} =O≺​(d−1),\displaystyle=O_{\prec}(d^{-1}), (235)
‖W^−W~h‖F\displaystyle\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\widehat{W}-\widetilde{W}_{h}\right\rVert}_{F} =O≺​(d−1).\displaystyle=O_{\prec}(d^{-1}). (236)

The score estimate and stationarity residual yield (A2).

The solution in (232) is unique because the left side is strictly increasing and the right side is decreasing in aa. Also, θh≥0\theta_{h}\geq 0 and θh=O≺​(1)\theta_{h}=O_{\prec}(1). By Lemma 6,

Lemma 7 (Surviving candidate scores).

Uniformly in hh and i,j≠hi,j\neq h,

|uj⊤​(W~h−W^∖h)​vi|=O≺​(d−1).|u_{j}^{\top}(\widetilde{W}_{h}-\widehat{W}^{\setminus h})v_{i}|=O_{\prec}(d^{-1}). (238)
Proof.

Lemma 8 (Held-out row and column increments).

Let Δh=W~h−W^∖h\Delta_{h}=\widetilde{W}_{h}-\widehat{W}^{\setminus h}. Uniformly in hh,

maxi≠h⁡|uh⊤​Δh​vi|\displaystyle\max_{i\neq h}|u_{h}^{\top}\Delta_{h}v_{i}| =O≺(d−1/2),\displaystyle=O_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}), (239)
‖(uj⊤​Δh​vh)j≠h‖2\displaystyle\mathinner{\!\left\lVert(u_{j}^{\top}\Delta_{h}v_{h})_{j\neq h}\right\rVert}_{2} =O≺​(d),\displaystyle=O_{\prec}(\sqrt{d}), (240)

Proof.

By (237), the BhB_{h} contribution is O≺(d−1/2)O_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). For the outer Newton direction, self-adjointness gives

uh⊤​Th​[uh​vh⊤]​vi=⟨Th​[uh​vi⊤],uh​vh⊤⟩𝖥.u_{h}^{\top}T_{h}[u_{h}v_{h}^{\top}]v_{i}=\left\langle T_{h}[u_{h}v_{i}^{\top}],u_{h}v_{h}^{\top}\right\rangle_{\mathsf{F}}.

The remaining estimates use only operator norms:

‖U∖h⊤​Δh​vh‖2≤‖U‖𝗈𝗉​‖Δh‖F​‖vh‖=O≺​(d),\mathinner{\!\left\lVert U_{\setminus h}^{\top}\Delta_{h}v_{h}\right\rVert}_{2}\leq\mathinner{\!\left\lVert U\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{op}}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\Delta_{h}\right\rVert}_{F}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert v_{h}\right\rVert}=O_{\prec}(\sqrt{d}),

which gives (240). Also,

‖(sh,i​(W~h))i≠h‖2≤‖(sh,i​(W^∖h))i≠h‖2+‖V‖𝗈𝗉​‖Δh‖F​‖uh‖.\mathinner{\!\left\lVert(s_{h,i}(\widetilde{W}_{h}))_{i\neq h}\right\rVert}_{2}\leq\mathinner{\!\left\lVert(s_{h,i}(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h}))_{i\neq h}\right\rVert}_{2}+\mathinner{\!\left\lVert V\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{op}}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\Delta_{h}\right\rVert}_{F}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert u_{h}\right\rVert}.

The first term is O≺​(n)O_{\prec}(\sqrt{n}) by the conditional quadratic-form argument used in Lemma 6, while the second is O≺​(d)O_{\prec}(\sqrt{d}); since n≍d2n\asymp d^{2}, (241) follows. ∎

Stationarity residual.

Write

Δh=W~h−W^∖h.\Delta_{h}=\widetilde{W}_{h}-\widehat{W}^{\setminus h}.

Therefore

∇Ψ​(W~h)=R0,h+Rin,h+Rout,h,\nabla\Psi(\widetilde{W}_{h})=R_{0,h}+R_{\mathrm{in},h}+R_{\mathrm{out},h}, (244)

where

R0,h\displaystyle R_{0,h} :=∇Ψ∖h(W^∖h+Δh)−ℋh[Δh],\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\nabla\Psi^{\setminus h}(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h}+\Delta_{h})-\mathcal{H}_{h}[\Delta_{h}], (245)

We bound the three terms separately.

Common leave-one-out remainder.
Lemma 9 (Common residual).

Uniformly in hh,

‖R0,h‖F=O≺​(d−1).\mathinner{\!\left\lVert R_{0,h}\right\rVert}_{F}=O_{\prec}(d^{-1}). (248)
Proof.

By Lemma 7, every surviving score perturbation is ε=O≺​(d−1)\varepsilon=O_{\prec}(d^{-1}). The second-order profiled-tail bounds (213) and (215) therefore produce an n×nn\times n coefficient matrix EE, with row and column hh zero, such that

maxi≠h⁡|Ei​i|=O≺​(d−2),maxi,j≠hi≠j⁡|Ej​i|=O≺​(d−2/k).\max_{i\neq h}|E_{ii}|=O_{\prec}(d^{-2}),\qquad\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\neq h\\ i\neq j\end{subarray}}|E_{ji}|=O_{\prec}(d^{-2}/k).

For its diagonal part, Khatri–Rao synthesis gives ‖U​Ed​V⊤‖F≤O≺​(1)​n​d−2=O≺​(d−1)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert UE_{\mathrm{d}}V^{\top}\right\rVert}_{F}\leq O_{\prec}(1)\sqrt{n}\,d^{-2}=O_{\prec}(d^{-1}). For the off-diagonal part, ‖Eo‖F=O≺​(d−2)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert E_{\mathrm{o}}\right\rVert}_{F}=O_{\prec}(d^{-2}), hence ‖U​Eo​V⊤‖F≤‖U‖𝗈𝗉​‖Eo‖F​‖V‖𝗈𝗉=O≺​(d−1)\mathinner{\!\left\lVert UE_{\mathrm{o}}V^{\top}\right\rVert}_{F}\leq\mathinner{\!\left\lVert U\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{op}}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert E_{\mathrm{o}}\right\rVert}_{F}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert V\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{op}}=O_{\prec}(d^{-1}). The ridge term is exactly linear, proving (248). ∎

Insertion-gradient stability.
Lemma 10 (Insertion-gradient stability along the candidate step).

Uniformly in hh,

‖Rin,h‖F=‖Gh​(W~h)−Gh​(W^∖h)‖F=O≺​(d−1).\mathinner{\!\left\lVert R_{\mathrm{in},h}\right\rVert}_{F}=\mathinner{\!\left\lVert G_{h}(\widetilde{W}_{h})-G_{h}(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h})\right\rVert}_{F}=O_{\prec}(d^{-1}). (249)
Proof.

At both W^∖h\widehat{W}^{\setminus h} and W~h\widetilde{W}_{h}, the deterministic Frobenius bound and Lemma 8 give the hypotheses of Lemma 5. Hence the first three sums in (224) are O≺​(d−1)O_{\prec}(d^{-1}) at each endpoint, by the proof of Lemma 6, and so is their difference.

It remains to compare the structured fourth terms. Write ci​(W)=ai​(W)​ph,i​(W)c_{i}(W)=a_{i}(W)p_{h,i}(W) and ξ⁡(W)=∑i≠hci​(W)​vi\xi(W)=\sum_{i\neq h}c_{i}(W)v_{i}. |ai​(W~h)−ai​(W^∖h)|≤C⁡(ε+δk)=O≺​(d−1),|a_{i}(\widetilde{W}_{h})-a_{i}(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h})|\leq C\left(\varepsilon+\frac{\delta}{k}\right)=O_{\prec}(d^{-1}), (250)

while (211) gives

|ph,i(W~h)−ph,i(W^∖h)|≤Ck(δ+ε)=O≺(d−5/2).|p_{h,i}(\widetilde{W}_{h})-p_{h,i}(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h})|\leq\frac{C}{k}(\delta+\varepsilon)=O_{\prec}(d^{-5/2}). (251)

Combining these bounds with ph,i≤k−1p_{h,i}\leq k^{-1} yields |ci(W~h)−ci(W^∖h)|=O≺(d−5/2)|c_{i}(\widetilde{W}_{h})-c_{i}(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h})|=O_{\prec}(d^{-5/2}). Thus the coefficient difference has ℓ2\ell_{2} norm O≺(d−3/2)O_{\prec}(d^{-3/2}) and

‖uh​(ξ⁡(W~h)−ξ⁡(W^∖h))⊤‖F≤‖uh‖‖V‖𝗈𝗉O≺(d−3/2)=O≺(d−1).\mathinner{\!\left\lVert u_{h}(\xi(\widetilde{W}_{h})-\xi(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h}))^{\top}\right\rVert}_{F}\leq\mathinner{\!\left\lVert u_{h}\right\rVert}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert V\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{op}}O_{\prec}(d^{-3/2})=O_{\prec}(d^{-1}).

Uniformly in distinct h,i∈[n]h,i\in[n],

We now sharpen the threshold perturbation beyond what follows from the pointwise score bound alone. The exact threshold equation below expresses Δ​μi\Delta\mu_{i} through an averaged score perturbation. The denominator is kept uniformly nondegenerate by the bulk curvature estimates, while the Newton decomposition from the preceding subsection makes the numerator smaller by a further factor d−1/2d^{-1/2}.

Let (W^,μ^)(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu}) be the full lifted optimizer and (W^∖h,μ^∖h)(\widehat{W}^{\setminus h},\widehat{\mu}^{\setminus h}) the optimizer after deleting hh. Define

Fix hh and i≠hi\neq h. The labels full and loo denote evaluation at the full and leave-one-out optimizers, respectively. Thus

For every hh and i≠hi\neq h,

Δ​μi=qh,ifull+∑j≠i,hc¯j,i​Δ​sj,i∑j≠i,hc¯j,i.\Delta\mu_{i}=\frac{q_{h,i}^{\mathrm{full}}+\displaystyle\sum_{j\neq i,h}\bar{c}_{j,i}\Delta s_{j,i}}{\displaystyle\sum_{j\neq i,h}\bar{c}_{j,i}}. (258)

Appendix D Spectral and self-averaging estimates

This appendix proves (A5) and (A6). The proof of the spectral estimate (A4) is given in Appendix E. We use the notation of Section 4, in particular the score matrix S⁡(W)=U⊤​W​VS(W)=U^{\top}WV, the joint optimizer (W^,μ^)(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu}), and the coefficients ai,bi,qj,ia_{i},b_{i},q_{j,i} from Section 4.1.

The proofs of (A5) and (A6) use the same sensitivity–concentration scheme. After profiling out the threshold variables μ\mu, we regard the statistic of interest as a function of the Gaussian data (U,V)(U,V). Strong convexity of the profiled objective permits implicit differentiation of the optimizer, and a self-adjoint adjoint solve supplies this optimizer response into a single matrix direction PP. The resulting data-gradient is controlled using the profiled Hessian quadratic form, after which the Gaussian LpL^{p} Poincare inequality gives concentration. For (A6) there is one additional preliminary step: we first replace the lifted Hessian by the simpler rank-one-feature Hessian of (122), and then apply the same adjoint argument used for (A5).

For Ji=[n]∖{i}J_{i}=[n]\setminus\{i\}, write 𝒯i=𝒯Ji\mathcal{T}_{i}=\mathcal{T}_{J_{i}} and μi=μJi\mu_{i}=\mu_{J_{i}} in the notation of the common profiled-tail calculus in Appendix C, Section C.1. The profiled objective is

Φ(W):=∑i=1nℓ(si,i(W)−𝒯i(S−i,i(W)))+γd2‖W‖𝖥2,γd:=λ​nd2.\Phi(W)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\!\left(s_{i,i}(W)-\mathcal{T}_{i}(S_{-i,i}(W))\right)+\frac{\gamma_{d}}{2}\mathinner{\!\left\lVert W\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}^{2},\qquad\gamma_{d}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{\lambda n}{d^{2}}. (270)

Minimizing (270) is equivalent to minimizing the joint objective (31), and its unique minimizer is W^\widehat{W}.

For the score-level bounds used below, set

hj,i:=ϕβ′′(sj,i−μi),Hiμ:=∑j≠ihj,i.h_{j,i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\phi_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}(s_{j,i}-\mu_{i}),\qquad H_{i}^{\mu}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{j\neq i}h_{j,i}. (271)

Let Bi:=BJi​(S−i,i​(W^))B_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=B_{J_{i}}(S_{-i,i}(\widehat{W})). Thus, by (211)–(212),

0⪯Bi⪯1k​diag⁡(h−i,i),∑j≠i|∂qj,i∂sℓ,i|+∑j≠i|∂hj,i∂sℓ,i|≤C.0\preceq B_{i}\preceq\frac{1}{k}\diag(h_{-i,i}),\qquad\sum_{j\neq i}\left|\frac{\partial q_{j,i}}{\partial s_{\ell,i}}\right|+\sum_{j\neq i}\left|\frac{\partial h_{j,i}}{\partial s_{\ell,i}}\right|\leq C. (272)

These are the only threshold derivatives needed below. In particular, we never require a lower bound on HiμH_{i}^{\mu}: differentiation is carried out through the profiled coefficient fields qj,i,hj,iq_{j,i},h_{j,i} rather than through the derivative of μi\mu_{i} in isolation. Let L⁡(S)L(S) denote the unregularized profiled loss and G:=∇SL​(S)G\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\nabla_{S}L(S). As in (46),

Gi,i=−ai,Gj,i=ai​qj,ik(j≠i),‖G‖op≤C.G_{i,i}=-a_{i},\qquad G_{j,i}=\frac{a_{i}q_{j,i}}{k}\quad(j\neq i),\qquad\mathinner{\!\left\lVert G\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}\leq C. (273)

The last bound follows from Schur’s test, since the absolute column sums are at most 22 and the row sums are bounded by 1+(n−1)/k1+(n-1)/k.

For a score perturbation T∈ℝn×nT\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, define

δi(T):=Ti,i−1k∑j≠iqj,iTj,i,𝒬(T):=∑i=1nbiδi(T)2+∑i=1naiT−i,i⊤BiT−i,i.\delta_{i}(T)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=T_{i,i}-\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\neq i}q_{j,i}T_{j,i},\qquad\mathcal{Q}(T)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\delta_{i}(T)^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}T_{-i,i}^{\top}B_{i}T_{-i,i}. (274)

Note that 𝒬⁡(T)\mathcal{Q}(T) is the Hessian quadratic form of LL. In particular,

Let

𝒥:=∇W2​Φ​(W^).\mathcal{J}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\nabla_{W}^{2}\Phi(\widehat{W}). (276)

Then 𝒥\mathcal{J} is self-adjoint and

𝒥⪰γd​I⪰λ​α−​I,‖𝒥−1‖op≤C.\mathcal{J}\succeq\gamma_{d}I\succeq\lambda\alpha_{-}I,\qquad\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\mathcal{J}^{-1}\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{op}}\leq C. (277)

In both proofs of (A5) and (A6) we use the following Gaussian LpL^{p} Poincare inequality which follows from [Pisier, 2006, Theorem 2.2]: if Z∼𝒩⁡(0,IN/d)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{N}/d) and ff is continuously differentiable with the required moments, then, for fixed p≥2p\geq 2,

‖f⁡(Z)−𝔼​f​(Z)‖Lp≤C​pd​‖‖∇f​(Z)‖2‖Lp.\mathinner{\!\left\lVert f(Z)-\mathbb{E}f(Z)\right\rVert}_{L^{p}}\leq C\sqrt{\frac{p}{d}}\,\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\mathinner{\!\left\lVert\nabla f(Z)\right\rVert}_{2}\right\rVert}_{L^{p}}. (278)

D.1 Empirical-mean concentration

We prove a slightly stronger statement. Let ψ∈C1​(ℝ)\psi\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}) be pseudo-Lipschitz of order two and set

Γd:=1n∑i=1nψ(si,i),Γo:=1n⁡(n−1)∑i≠jψ(sj,i).\Gamma_{\mathrm{d}}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi(s_{i,i}),\qquad\Gamma_{\mathrm{o}}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}\psi(s_{j,i}). (279)

Ci,i=biδi(T),Cj,i=−bi​δi​(T)​qj,ik+ai(DiT−i,i)j(j≠i).C_{i,i}=b_{i}\delta_{i}(T),\qquad C_{j,i}=-\frac{b_{i}\delta_{i}(T)q_{j,i}}{k}+a_{i}(D_{i}T_{-i,i})_{j}\quad(j\neq i). (284)

‖P‖𝖥≤C​‖U​B​V⊤‖𝖥,𝒬⁡(T)≤C​‖U​B​V⊤‖𝖥2.\mathinner{\!\left\lVert P\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}\leq C\mathinner{\!\left\lVert UBV^{\top}\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}},\qquad\mathcal{Q}(T)\leq C\mathinner{\!\left\lVert UBV^{\top}\right\rVert}_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}. (288)

D.2 Inverse-trace concentration

We distinguish two Hessians. The operator HH in (A6) is the WW-Hessian of the lifted objective with μ\mu held fixed, evaluated at (W^,μ^)(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu}). The operator 𝒥\mathcal{J} in (276) is instead the Hessian of the profiled objective and governs the response of W^\widehat{W} to the data. Both have the same ridge floor, but only 𝒥\mathcal{J} may be used in implicit differentiation.

Write fj,i:=vec⁡(uj​vi⊤)f_{j,i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\vecop(u_{j}v_{i}^{\top}) and

ξi:=vec⁡([−ui+1k​∑j≠iqj,i​uj]​vi⊤).\xi_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\vecop\left(\left[-u_{i}+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\neq i}q_{j,i}u_{j}\right]v_{i}^{\top}\right). (302)

Then

H=γd​I+∑ibi​ξi​ξi⊤+∑i∑j≠iai​hj,ik​fj,i​fj,i⊤.H=\gamma_{d}I+\sum_{i}b_{i}\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{\top}+\sum_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{a_{i}h_{j,i}}{k}f_{j,i}f_{j,i}^{\top}. (303)

Recall the simplified Hessian H~\widetilde{H} defined in (122), which is also used in Appendix G:

H~=γd​I+∑ibi​fi,i​fi,i⊤+∑i∑j≠iai​hj,ik​fj,i​fj,i⊤,\widetilde{H}=\gamma_{d}I+\sum_{i}b_{i}f_{i,i}f_{i,i}^{\top}+\sum_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{a_{i}h_{j,i}}{k}f_{j,i}f_{j,i}^{\top}, (304)

and set

Θ:=1d2tr(H−1),Θ~:=1d2tr(H~−1).\Theta\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\tr(H^{-1}),\qquad\widetilde{\Theta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\tr(\widetilde{H}^{-1}). (305)

The trace-reduction estimate of Lemma 22 applies verbatim without a cavity index. Here

Appendix E Bounds on the norms of W^\widehat{W}

This appendix establishes two-sided control on ‖W^‖𝖥/d\|\widehat{W}\|_{\mathsf{F}}/d for the joint TAM minimizer of 31 as well as (A4). For the former, the upper bound is deterministic and uniform in the data; the lower bound holds with overwhelming probability (1−d−D1-d^{-D} for every D>0D>0) in the regime n/d2→α∈(0,∞)n/d^{2}\to\alpha\in(0,\infty). Together, they pin

c0−O⁡(d−D)≤νd≤C0,c_{0}-O(d^{-D})\;\leq\;\nu_{d}\;\leq\;C_{0}, (330)

for deterministic constants 0<c0≤C0<∞0<c_{0}\leq C_{0}<\infty depending only on the parameters (α,r,β,λ)(\alpha,r,\beta,\lambda), where νd2=𝔼⁡[‖W^‖𝖥2/d2]\nu_{d}^{2}=\mathbb{E}[\|\widehat{W}\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}/d^{2}] as in (87).

The two Frobenius bounds provide the a priori scale for ‖W^‖𝖥\|\widehat{W}\|_{\mathsf{F}} needed in Section 4.3 and Corollary 1. The corresponding Frobenius concentration estimate is treated there as a consequence of the empirical concentration postulate (A5), applied to the observables in the energy identity. The spectral estimate (A4) is proved at the end of this appendix.

Throughout the appendix, C,cC,c denote positive constants that may depend on (α,r,β,λ)(\alpha,r,\beta,\lambda) but not on dd, and may vary line to line.

E.1 Deterministic Frobenius upper bound

Lemma 18 (Deterministic upper bound).

For any λ>0\lambda>0, β>0\beta>0, r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1), and any data matrices U,V∈ℝd×nU,V\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n},

‖W^‖𝖥2d2≤2λ​[log⁡2+log⁡2r​β]=:C0.\frac{\|\widehat{W}\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}}{d^{2}}\;\leq\;\frac{2}{\lambda}\Big[\,\log 2\;+\;\tfrac{\log 2}{r\beta}\,\Big]\;=\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\;C_{0}. (331)

In particular, νd2≤C0\nu_{d}^{2}\leq C_{0}.

Proof.

Evaluate Ψ\Psi at the test point W=0W=0, μ=0\mu=0. All scores vanish, so

Ψ⁡(0,0)=n⋅ℓ⁡(−1k​(n−1)​ϕβ​(0))=n⋅ℓ⁡(−log⁡2r​β),\Psi(0,0)\;=\;n\cdot\ell\Big(-\tfrac{1}{k}\,(n-1)\,\phi_{\beta}(0)\Big)\;=\;n\cdot\ell\Big(-\tfrac{\log 2}{r\beta}\Big), (332)

using ϕβ​(0)=(log⁡2)/β\phi_{\beta}(0)=(\log 2)/\beta and r=k/(n−1)r=k/(n-1). The function ℓ\ell is convex with |ℓ′|≤1|\ell^{\prime}|\leq 1, so

ℓ⁡(t)≤ℓ⁡(0)+|t|=log⁡2+|t|.\ell(t)\;\leq\;\ell(0)+|t|\;=\;\log 2+|t|. (333)

Applying (333) at t=−(log2)/(rβ)t=-(\log 2)/(r\beta) gives

Ψ⁡(0,0)≤n⁡[log⁡2+log⁡2r​β].\Psi(0,0)\;\leq\;n\Big[\,\log 2+\tfrac{\log 2}{r\beta}\,\Big]. (334)

By optimality of (W^,μ^)(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu}) and nonnegativity of ℓ\ell,

λ​n2​d2​‖W^‖𝖥2≤Ψ⁡(W^,μ^)≤Ψ⁡(0,0).\frac{\lambda n}{2d^{2}}\,\|\widehat{W}\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}\;\leq\;\Psi(\widehat{W},\widehat{\mu})\;\leq\;\Psi(0,0). (335)

Combining (334) and (335) and dividing by λ​n/(2​d2)\lambda n/(2d^{2}) yields (331). The bound on νd2\nu_{d}^{2} follows from νd2=𝔼​‖W^‖𝖥2/d2\nu_{d}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\|\widehat{W}\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}/d^{2}. ∎∎

Lemma 19 (High probability lower bound).

Fix r,α∈(0,1)×(0,∞)r,\alpha\in(0,1)\times(0,\infty) and β,λ>0\beta,\lambda>0, and consider the regime n/d2→αn/d^{2}\to\alpha. There exists a constant c0>0c_{0}>0 such that, for every D>0D>0, there is d0=d0​(D)d_{0}=d_{0}(D) for which

ℙ⁡(‖W^‖𝖥d≥c0)≥ 1−d−D,d≥d0.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\frac{\|\widehat{W}\|_{\mathsf{F}}}{d}\;\geq\;c_{0}\right)\;\geq\;1-d^{-D},\qquad d\geq d_{0}. (336)

In particular, νd2≥c02−O⁡(d−D)\nu_{d}^{2}\geq c_{0}^{2}-O(d^{-D}) for every D>0D>0.

The argument is by objective gap. We exhibit a one-dimensional family Wt=t​W×W_{t}=t\,W^{\times} along the direction

along which Ψ⁡(Wt,μ0​𝟏)\Psi(W_{t},\mu_{0}\mathbf{1}) decreases by Θ⁡(n)=Θ⁡(d2)\Theta(n)=\Theta(d^{2}) at small t>0t>0, and complement this with the convex linearization Ψ⁡(W,μ0​𝟏)≥Ψ⁡(0,μ0​𝟏)+⟨∇WΨ​(0,μ0​𝟏),W⟩\Psi(W,\mu_{0}\mathbf{1})\geq\Psi(0,\mu_{0}\mathbf{1})+\langle\nabla_{W}\Psi(0,\mu_{0}\mathbf{1}),W\rangle, whose linear term is bounded by ‖∇WΨ​(0,μ0​𝟏)‖𝖥​‖W‖𝖥=O⁡(d​‖W‖𝖥)\|\nabla_{W}\Psi(0,\mu_{0}\mathbf{1})\|_{\mathsf{F}}\|W\|_{\mathsf{F}}=O(d\,\|W\|_{\mathsf{F}}). Comparing the two excludes a Frobenius ball of radius η​d\eta d for small η\eta.

Appendix F A coupling lemma for bilinear Gaussian forms

This appendix establishes a coupling estimate for the joint law of bilinear forms uj⊤​W​v0u_{j}^{\top}Wv_{0} that share a common right-side Gaussian vector v0v_{0}. The estimate is the technical input behind the joint Gaussian limit for competitor scores derived in Section 4.3, where it is applied with W=W^∖i,j1,…,jmW=\widehat{W}^{\setminus i,j_{1},\ldots,j_{m}} and v0=viv_{0}=v_{i}.

We first prove the estimate for a deterministic matrix WW, then transfer it to the random case via concentration of ‖W‖𝖥2/d2\|W\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}/d^{2}.

F.1 Deterministic matrix

Lemma 20 (Bilinear Gaussian coupling, deterministic matrix).

Let W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be a deterministic matrix with V0:=‖W‖𝖥2/d2>0V_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\|W\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}/d^{2}>0, and let u1,…,um,v0∈ℝdu_{1},\ldots,u_{m},v_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be independent Gaussian vectors with uk,v0∼𝒩⁡(0,Id/d)u_{k},v_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}/d). Set

Xj:=uj⊤Wv0,j=1,…,m.X_{j}\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;u_{j}^{\top}Wv_{0},\qquad j=1,\ldots,m. (366)

On a common probability space, there exist i.i.d. random variables Y1,…,Ym∼𝒩⁡(0,V0)Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{m}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,V_{0}) such that

‖(X1,…,Xm)−(Y1,…,Ym)‖2=𝒪≺​(‖W⊤​W‖𝖥/(d2​V0)).\bigl\|(X_{1},\ldots,X_{m})-(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{m})\bigr\|_{2}\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}\!\bigl(\|W^{\top}W\|_{\mathsf{F}}/(d^{2}\sqrt{V_{0}})\bigr). (367)
Remark 9 (Interpretation).

The deviation ‖W⊤​W‖𝖥/d2\|W^{\top}W\|_{\mathsf{F}}/d^{2} measures the spread of the eigenvalues of W⊤​W/d2W^{\top}W/d^{2}: when the eigenvalues are concentrated, ‖W⊤​W‖𝖥/d2\|W^{\top}W\|_{\mathsf{F}}/d^{2} is small relative to ‖W‖𝖥2/d2=tr⁡(W⊤​W)/d2\|W\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}/d^{2}=\tr(W^{\top}W)/d^{2}. In the proof below it is exactly the Hanson–Wright scale for the random conditional variance ‖W​v0‖2/d\|Wv_{0}\|^{2}/d.

Proof.

The argument exploits the conditional Gaussian structure of {Xj}\{X_{j}\} given v0v_{0}.

Step 1: Conditional Gaussian.

Set w:=W​v0∈ℝdw\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=Wv_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Conditional on v0v_{0}, ww is deterministic, and Xj=uj⊤​wX_{j}=u_{j}^{\top}w is a Gaussian linear functional of uju_{j}. Since u1,…,um∼𝒩⁡(0,Id/d)u_{1},\ldots,u_{m}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}/d) are independent across jj,

(X1,…,Xm)|v0∼𝒩(0,V⋅Im),V:=‖W​v0‖2d.(X_{1},\ldots,X_{m})\,\big|\,v_{0}\;\sim\;\mathcal{N}\!\bigl(0,\,V\cdot I_{m}\bigr),\qquad V\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\frac{\|Wv_{0}\|^{2}}{d}. (368)
Step 2: Hanson–Wright on the conditional variance.

We have

𝔼⁡[V]=1d​𝔼​[v0⊤​W⊤​W​v0]=1d2​tr⁡(W⊤​W)=‖W‖𝖥2d2=:V0,\mathbb{E}[V]\;=\;\frac{1}{d}\,\mathbb{E}[v_{0}^{\top}W^{\top}Wv_{0}]\;=\;\frac{1}{d^{2}}\,\tr(W^{\top}W)\;=\;\frac{\|W\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}}{d^{2}}\;=\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\;V_{0}, (369)

using 𝔼⁡[v0​v0⊤]=Id/d\mathbb{E}[v_{0}v_{0}^{\top}]=I_{d}/d. The Hanson–Wright inequality applied to the centered quadratic form V−V0=(1/d)​(v0⊤​W⊤​W​v0−‖W‖𝖥2/d)V-V_{0}=(1/d)(v_{0}^{\top}W^{\top}Wv_{0}-\|W\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}/d) in the Gaussian vector v0v_{0} gives

V−V0=𝒪≺​(‖W⊤​W‖𝖥/d2),Var⁡V=2d4​‖W⊤​W‖𝖥2.V-V_{0}\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}\!\bigl(\|W^{\top}W\|_{\mathsf{F}}/d^{2}\bigr),\qquad\var V\;=\;\frac{2}{d^{4}}\,\|W^{\top}W\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}. (370)
Step 3: Coupling.

Define Yj:=Xj⋅V0/VY_{j}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=X_{j}\cdot\sqrt{V_{0}/V} for each jj. Conditional on v0v_{0}, {Yj}\{Y_{j}\} inherit the Gaussianity and independence of {Xj}\{X_{j}\}, with conditional variance V⋅(V0/V)=V0V\cdot(V_{0}/V)=V_{0}. Since the conditional law 𝒩⁡(0,V0⋅Im)\mathcal{N}(0,V_{0}\cdot I_{m}) is independent of v0v_{0}, the unconditional joint law of (Y1,…,Ym)(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{m}) is i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,V0)\mathcal{N}(0,V_{0}) as required.

The deviation factors as

Xj−Yj=Xj​(1−V0/V)=Xj⋅V−V0V.X_{j}-Y_{j}\;=\;X_{j}\bigl(1-\sqrt{V_{0}/V}\bigr)\;=\;X_{j}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{V}-\sqrt{V_{0}}}{\sqrt{V}}. (371)

Two facts: conditional on v0v_{0}, the standardized form Xj/V∼𝒩⁡(0,1)X_{j}/\sqrt{V}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), so |Xj/V|=𝒪≺​(1)|X_{j}/\sqrt{V}|=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(1) uniformly in jj; and |V−V0|≤|V−V0|/V0|\sqrt{V}-\sqrt{V_{0}}|\leq|V-V_{0}|/\sqrt{V_{0}}, by V+V0≥V0\sqrt{V}+\sqrt{V_{0}}\geq\sqrt{V_{0}}. Combined with (370),

|Xj−Yj|=|Xj/V|⋅|V−V0|=𝒪≺​(‖W⊤​W‖𝖥/(d2​V0)),|X_{j}-Y_{j}|\;=\;|X_{j}/\sqrt{V}|\cdot|\sqrt{V}-\sqrt{V_{0}}|\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}\!\bigl(\|W^{\top}W\|_{\mathsf{F}}/(d^{2}\sqrt{V_{0}})\bigr), (372)

uniformly in jj. For fixed mm, we have

‖(X)−(Y)‖22=∑j=1m|Xj−Yj|2=𝒪≺​((‖W⊤​W‖𝖥/(d2​V0))2),\|(X)-(Y)\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}|X_{j}-Y_{j}|^{2}=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}\!\bigl((\|W^{\top}W\|_{\mathsf{F}}/(d^{2}\sqrt{V_{0}}))^{2}\bigr), (373)

which gives (367). ∎

F.2 Random matrix with concentrated Frobenius norm

Corollary 1 (Bilinear Gaussian coupling, random matrix).

Let WW be a random d×dd\times d matrix with ‖W‖𝖥>0\|W\|_{\mathsf{F}}>0, independent of u1,…,um,v0u_{1},\ldots,u_{m},v_{0} which are i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,Id/d)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}/d). Let νd2>0\nu_{d}^{2}>0 be a deterministic constant. Suppose ρf,ρop>0\rho_{f},\rho_{\mathrm{op}}>0 are deterministic rates such that

‖W‖𝖥2d2−νd2=𝒪≺​(ρf),‖W⊤​W‖𝖥d2=𝒪≺​(ρop).\frac{\|W\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}}{d^{2}}-\nu_{d}^{2}\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(\rho_{f}),\qquad\frac{\|W^{\top}W\|_{\mathsf{F}}}{d^{2}}\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(\rho_{\mathrm{op}}). (374)

Set Xj:=uj⊤​W​v0X_{j}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=u_{j}^{\top}Wv_{0} for j=1,…,mj=1,\ldots,m. On a common probability space, there exist i.i.d. random variables Y1,…,Ym∼𝒩⁡(0,νd2)Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{m}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\nu_{d}^{2}) such that

‖(X1,…,Xm)−(Y1,…,Ym)‖2=𝒪≺​((ρop+ρf)/νd).\bigl\|(X_{1},\ldots,X_{m})-(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{m})\bigr\|_{2}\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}\!\bigl((\rho_{\mathrm{op}}+\rho_{f})/\nu_{d}\bigr). (375)
Proof.

The key observation is that, conditional on (W,v0)(W,v_{0}), Xj/V​∼iid​𝒩​(0,1)X_{j}/\sqrt{V}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,1) across jj, where V:=‖W​v0‖2/dV\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\|Wv_{0}\|^{2}/d is the conditional variance.

Define

Yj:=Xjνd2/V,j=1,…,m.Y_{j}\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;X_{j}\,\sqrt{\nu_{d}^{2}/V},\qquad j=1,\ldots,m. (376)

Conditional on (W,v0)(W,v_{0}), {Yj}\{Y_{j}\} inherit the Gaussianity and independence of {Xj}\{X_{j}\} with variance V⋅νd2/V=νd2V\cdot\nu_{d}^{2}/V=\nu_{d}^{2}, so the unconditional joint law of (Y1,…,Ym)(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{m}) is i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,νd2)\mathcal{N}(0,\nu_{d}^{2}) as required. The deviation factors as Xj−Yj=Xj​(1−νd2/V)=Xj​(V−νd2)/VX_{j}-Y_{j}=X_{j}(1-\sqrt{\nu_{d}^{2}/V})=X_{j}\,(\sqrt{V}-\sqrt{\nu_{d}^{2}})/\sqrt{V}, and using |Xj/V|=𝒪≺​(1)|X_{j}/\sqrt{V}|=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(1) together with |V−νd2|≤|V−νd2|/νd2|\sqrt{V}-\sqrt{\nu_{d}^{2}}|\leq|V-\nu_{d}^{2}|/\sqrt{\nu_{d}^{2}},

|Xj−Yj|=|Xj/V|⋅|V−νd2|=𝒪≺​(|V−νd2|/νd2).|X_{j}-Y_{j}|\;=\;|X_{j}/\sqrt{V}|\cdot|\sqrt{V}-\sqrt{\nu_{d}^{2}}|\;=\;\mathcal{O}_{\prec}\!\bigl(|V-\nu_{d}^{2}|/\sqrt{\nu_{d}^{2}}\bigr). (377)

Decompose

V−νd2=(V−V0​(W))+(V0​(W)−νd2),V0​(W):=‖W‖𝖥2/d2.V-\nu_{d}^{2}\;=\;(V-V_{0}(W))\;+\;(V_{0}(W)-\nu_{d}^{2}),\qquad V_{0}(W)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\|W\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{2}/d^{2}. (378)

Hanson–Wright applied to V−V0​(W)V-V_{0}(W) conditional on WW gives

V−V0​(W)=𝒪≺​(‖W⊤​W‖𝖥/d2)=𝒪≺​(ρop),V-V_{0}(W)=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}\!\left(\|W^{\top}W\|_{\mathsf{F}}/d^{2}\right)=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(\rho_{\mathrm{op}}), (379)

using (370). The second piece is 𝒪≺​(ρf)\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(\rho_{f}) by (374). Combining with (377) and summing over jj yields (375). ∎

Appendix G A trace estimate for the inverse Hessian

This appendix records several elementary estimates that will be used in the characterization of the susceptibility parameter χ\chi. The first says that a fresh rank-one Gaussian direction probes the normalized trace of a bounded linear operator on ℝd×d\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. The next two show that the normalized inverse trace is stable under the perturbations needed to simplify the TAM Hessian.

We will use the following moment notation. For a sequence of random variables XdX_{d} and deterministic positive numbers ada_{d}, we write

Xd=Oℒ​(ad)X_{d}=O_{\mathcal{L}}(a_{d}) (380)

if, for every fixed p<∞p<\infty, there is a constant Cp<∞C_{p}<\infty such that ‖Xd‖Lp≤Cp​ad\|X_{d}\|_{L^{p}}\leq C_{p}a_{d} for all sufficiently large dd.

Lemma 21 (Fresh rank-one trace estimate).

Let u,v∈ℝdu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be independent Gaussian vectors with distribution 𝒩⁡(0,Id/d)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}/d). Let T:ℝd×d→ℝd×dT\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be a random symmetric linear operator, independent of (u,v)(u,v), and assume that

‖T‖op=Oℒ​(1).\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_{\mathcal{L}}(1). (381)

Then

⟨uv⊤,T[uv⊤]⟩=tr⁡(T)d2+Oℒ(d−1/2).\biggl\langle uv^{\top},\,T[uv^{\top}]\biggr\rangle=\frac{\tr(T)}{d^{2}}+O_{\mathcal{L}}(d^{-1/2}). (382)

Equivalently, for every fixed p<∞p<\infty,

‖⟨u​v⊤,T⁡[u​v⊤]⟩−tr⁡(T)d2‖Lp≤Cpd.\left\|\biggl\langle uv^{\top},\,T[uv^{\top}]\biggr\rangle-\frac{\tr(T)}{d^{2}}\right\|_{L^{p}}\leq\frac{C_{p}}{\sqrt{d}}. (383)
Proof.

Write u=g/du=g/\sqrt{d} and v=h/dv=h/\sqrt{d}, where g,h∈ℝdg,h\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are independent standard Gaussian vectors. Define

F⁡(g,h,T):=⟨u​v⊤,T⁡[u​v⊤]⟩=1d2​⟨g⊗h,T⁡[g⊗h]⟩.F(g,h,T)\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\;\biggl\langle uv^{\top},\,T[uv^{\top}]\biggr\rangle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\bigl\langle g\otimes h,\,T[g\otimes h]\bigr\rangle. (384)

Since TT is independent of (g,h)(g,h), we have

𝔼⁡[F⁡(g,h,T)∣T]=tr⁡(T)d2.\mathbb{E}\!\left[F(g,h,T)\mid T\right]=\frac{\tr(T)}{d^{2}}. (385)

We first bound the fluctuation in L2L^{2}. By the Gaussian Poincare inequality applied to the variables (g,h)(g,h), with TT kept fixed,

Var⁡(F⁡(g,h,T)∣T)≤𝔼⁡[‖∇gF‖2+‖∇hF‖2∣T].\var\!\left(F(g,h,T)\mid T\right)\leq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\nabla_{g}F\|^{2}+\|\nabla_{h}F\|^{2}\mid T\right]. (386)

For fixed hh, define the compressed operator

Th:=(I⊗h)∗T(I⊗h)on ℝd,T_{h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=(I\otimes h)^{\ast}T(I\otimes h)\qquad\text{on }\mathbb{R}^{d}, (387)

where (I⊗h)​g=g⊗h(I\otimes h)g=g\otimes h. Then

F⁡(g,h,T)=1d2​g⊤​Th​g,∇gF=2d2​Th​g,F(g,h,T)=\frac{1}{d^{2}}g^{\top}T_{h}g,\qquad\nabla_{g}F=\frac{2}{d^{2}}T_{h}g, (388)

using the symmetry of TT. It follows that

𝔼⁡[‖∇gF‖2∣T]=4d4​𝔼​[tr⁡(Th2)∣T].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\nabla_{g}F\|^{2}\mid T\right]=\frac{4}{d^{4}}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tr(T_{h}^{2})\mid T\right]. (389)

Moreover,

‖Th‖op≤‖T‖op​‖h‖2,\|T_{h}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,\|h\|^{2}, (390)

and hence

tr⁡(Th2)≤d​‖Th‖op2≤d​‖T‖op2​‖h‖4.\tr(T_{h}^{2})\leq d\,\|T_{h}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\leq d\,\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\,\|h\|^{4}. (391)

Since 𝔼​‖h‖4=d2+2​d\mathbb{E}\|h\|^{4}=d^{2}+2d, (389) gives

𝔼⁡[‖∇gF‖2∣T]≤C​‖T‖op2d.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\nabla_{g}F\|^{2}\mid T\right]\leq\frac{C\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}}{d}. (392)

The same argument, with the roles of gg and hh interchanged, gives

𝔼⁡[‖∇hF‖2∣T]≤C​‖T‖op2d.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\nabla_{h}F\|^{2}\mid T\right]\leq\frac{C\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}}{d}. (393)

Combining (386), (392), and (393), we obtain

Var⁡(F⁡(g,h,T)∣T)≤C​‖T‖op2d.\var\!\left(F(g,h,T)\mid T\right)\leq\frac{C\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}}{d}. (394)

We now upgrade this L2L^{2} bound to fixed moments. The centered random variable

F⁡(g,h,T)−tr⁡(T)d2F(g,h,T)-\frac{\tr(T)}{d^{2}} (395)

is, for fixed TT, a Gaussian polynomial of degree at most 44 in (g,h)(g,h). By Gaussian hypercontractivity, for every fixed p<∞p<\infty,

‖F⁡(g,h,T)−tr⁡(T)d2‖Lp​(g,h∣T)≤Cp​‖F⁡(g,h,T)−tr⁡(T)d2‖L2​(g,h∣T)≤Cp​‖T‖opd,\left\|F(g,h,T)-\frac{\tr(T)}{d^{2}}\right\|_{L^{p}(g,h\mid T)}\leq C_{p}\left\|F(g,h,T)-\frac{\tr(T)}{d^{2}}\right\|_{L^{2}(g,h\mid T)}\leq\frac{C_{p}\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\sqrt{d}}, (396)

where the last step uses (394). Taking expectation over TT and using ‖T‖op=Oℒ​(1)\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_{\mathcal{L}}(1) yields (383). This proves the lemma. ∎

We next record two deterministic perturbation estimates for the Hessian operators in (53)–(55). We identify ℝd×d\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} with ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}} throughout this discussion. If A,B:ℝd×d→ℝd×dA,B\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} are positive-definite self-adjoint operators, equivalently d2×d2d^{2}\times d^{2} symmetric matrices after vectorization, and E:=A−BE\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=A-B, then the resolvent identity gives the following bound: whenever ‖A−1‖op,‖B−1‖op≤τ−1\|A^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}},\|B^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\tau^{-1},

|1d2​tr⁡(A−1)−1d2​tr⁡(B−1)|≤1τ2​d2​‖E‖∗=1τ2​d2​‖A−B‖∗,\left|\frac{1}{d^{2}}\tr(A^{-1})-\frac{1}{d^{2}}\tr(B^{-1})\right|\leq\frac{1}{\tau^{2}d^{2}}\,\|E\|_{\ast}=\frac{1}{\tau^{2}d^{2}}\,\|A-B\|_{\ast}, (397)

where ∥⋅∥∗\|\cdot\|_{\ast} denotes the nuclear norm on this d2d^{2}-dimensional operator space.

For a fixed cavity index hh, let H∖hH^{\setminus h} be the Hessian in (53). Define the simplified Hessian H~∖h\widetilde{H}^{\setminus h} by replacing the block Mi∖hM_{i}^{\setminus h} in (55), for every i≠hi\neq h, by

M~i∖h:=bi∖heiei⊤+ai∖hdiag(R~:,i∖h),\widetilde{M}_{i}^{\setminus h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=b_{i}^{\setminus h}e_{i}e_{i}^{\top}+a_{i}^{\setminus h}\diag\bigl(\widetilde{R}_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}^{\setminus h}\bigr), (398)

and keeping the hh-th block equal to zero. Equivalently, H~∖h\widetilde{H}^{\setminus h} is obtained from H∖hH^{\setminus h} by replacing bi∖hQ:,i∖h(Q:,i∖h)⊤b_{i}^{\setminus h}Q_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}^{\setminus h}(Q_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}^{\setminus h})^{\top} by bi∖h​ei​ei⊤b_{i}^{\setminus h}e_{i}e_{i}^{\top} in each active block.

Lemma 22 (Trace reduction to the simplified Hessian).

Assume λ​n/d2≥τ>0\lambda n/d^{2}\geq\tau>0 and maxi⁡bi∖h≤B\max_{i}b_{i}^{\setminus h}\leq B. For i≠hi\neq h, write

Q:,i∖h=−ei+ρi∖h,pi∖h:=Uρi∖h.Q_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}^{\setminus h}=-e_{i}+\rho_{i}^{\setminus h},\qquad p_{i}^{\setminus h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=U\rho_{i}^{\setminus h}. (399)

Then

|1d2​tr⁡((H∖h)−1)−1d2​tr⁡((H~∖h)−1)|≤Bτ2​d2​∑i≠h‖vi‖2​(2​‖ui‖​‖pi∖h‖+‖pi∖h‖2).\left|\frac{1}{d^{2}}\tr\!\left((H^{\setminus h})^{-1}\right)-\frac{1}{d^{2}}\tr\!\left((\widetilde{H}^{\setminus h})^{-1}\right)\right|\leq\frac{B}{\tau^{2}d^{2}}\sum_{i\neq h}\|v_{i}\|^{2}\left(2\|u_{i}\|\|p_{i}^{\setminus h}\|+\|p_{i}^{\setminus h}\|^{2}\right). (400)

Consequently, if n/d2=O⁡(1)n/d^{2}=O(1), maxi⁡{‖ui‖,‖vi‖}=O⁡(1)\max_{i}\{\|u_{i}\|,\|v_{i}\|\}=O(1), and maxi≠h⁡‖pi∖h‖≤η\max_{i\neq h}\|p_{i}^{\setminus h}\|\leq\eta, then the normalized inverse trace of H∖hH^{\setminus h} differs from that of the simplified Hessian H~∖h\widetilde{H}^{\setminus h} by O⁡(η)O(\eta).

Proof.

Since

Q:,i∖h(Q:,i∖h)⊤−eiei⊤=−ei(ρi∖h)⊤−ρi∖hei⊤+ρi∖h(ρi∖h)⊤,Q_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}^{\setminus h}(Q_{\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}},i}^{\setminus h})^{\top}-e_{i}e_{i}^{\top}=-e_{i}(\rho_{i}^{\setminus h})^{\top}-\rho_{i}^{\setminus h}e_{i}^{\top}+\rho_{i}^{\setminus h}(\rho_{i}^{\setminus h})^{\top}, (401)

the iith summand in H∖h−H~∖hH^{\setminus h}-\widetilde{H}^{\setminus h} is

Δ↦bi∖h​[−ui​(pi∖h)⊤−pi∖h​ui⊤+pi∖h​(pi∖h)⊤]​Δ​vi​vi⊤.\Delta\mapsto b_{i}^{\setminus h}\left[-u_{i}(p_{i}^{\setminus h})^{\top}-p_{i}^{\setminus h}u_{i}^{\top}+p_{i}^{\setminus h}(p_{i}^{\setminus h})^{\top}\right]\Delta\,v_{i}v_{i}^{\top}. (402)

Each of the three displayed terms is rank one as an operator on ℝd×d\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. For example,

ui​(pi∖h)⊤​Δ​vi​vi⊤=⟨pi∖h​vi⊤,Δ⟩​ui​vi⊤,u_{i}(p_{i}^{\setminus h})^{\top}\Delta\,v_{i}v_{i}^{\top}=\bigl\langle p_{i}^{\setminus h}v_{i}^{\top},\Delta\bigr\rangle\,u_{i}v_{i}^{\top}, (403)

The same bound holds for the transposed cross term, while the pi∖h​(pi∖h)⊤p_{i}^{\setminus h}(p_{i}^{\setminus h})^{\top} term contributes ‖pi∖h‖2​‖vi‖2\|p_{i}^{\setminus h}\|^{2}\|v_{i}\|^{2}. Thus

‖H∖h−H~∖h‖∗≤B​∑i≠h‖vi‖2​(2​‖ui‖​‖pi∖h‖+‖pi∖h‖2).\|H^{\setminus h}-\widetilde{H}^{\setminus h}\|_{\ast}\leq B\sum_{i\neq h}\|v_{i}\|^{2}\left(2\|u_{i}\|\|p_{i}^{\setminus h}\|+\|p_{i}^{\setminus h}\|^{2}\right). (404)

Lemma 23 (Stability at the natural coefficient scale).

Let H~∖h\widetilde{H}^{\setminus h} be the simplified Hessian above. and

maxi≠h⁡|a¯i−ai∖h|≤δa,max⁡∑j≠i,hi≠h⁡R~j,i∖h≤CR,maxj≠i,h⁡|R¯j,i−R~j,i∖h|≤δRk.\max_{i\neq h}|\bar{a}_{i}-a_{i}^{\setminus h}|\leq\delta_{a},\qquad\max_{i\neq h}\sum_{j\neq i,h}\widetilde{R}_{j,i}^{\setminus h}\leq C_{R},\qquad\max_{j\neq i,h}|\bar{R}_{j,i}-\widetilde{R}_{j,i}^{\setminus h}|\leq\frac{\delta_{R}}{k}. |1d2​tr⁡((H¯∖h)−1)−1d2​tr⁡((H~∖h)−1)|\displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{d^{2}}\tr\!\left((\bar{H}^{\setminus h})^{-1}\right)-\frac{1}{d^{2}}\tr\!\left((\widetilde{H}^{\setminus h})^{-1}\right)\right| (407)
≤1τ2​d2​∑i≠h‖vi‖2​∑j≠i,h(δa​R~j,i∖h+B​δRk)​‖uj‖2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\tau^{2}d^{2}}\sum_{i\neq h}\|v_{i}\|^{2}\sum_{j\neq i,h}\left(\delta_{a}\widetilde{R}_{j,i}^{\setminus h}+\frac{B\delta_{R}}{k}\right)\|u_{j}\|^{2}.

O⁡(δa+δR).O(\delta_{a}+\delta_{R}). (408)
Proof.

Δ↦uj​uj⊤​Δ​vi​vi⊤=⟨uj​vi⊤,Δ⟩​uj​vi⊤\Delta\mapsto u_{j}u_{j}^{\top}\Delta\,v_{i}v_{i}^{\top}=\bigl\langle u_{j}v_{i}^{\top},\Delta\bigr\rangle\,u_{j}v_{i}^{\top} (409)

Quadratic forms of the simplified Hessian

We now use the simplified Hessian to extract the scalar equation for χ\chi. In this subsection we suppress the leave-one-out superscript and write

fj​i:=vec(ujvi⊤),rj,i:=βqj,i(1−qj,i),R~j,i=rj,ik.f_{ji}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\vecop(u_{j}v_{i}^{\top}),\qquad r_{j,i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\beta q_{j,i}(1-q_{j,i}),\qquad\widetilde{R}_{j,i}=\frac{r_{j,i}}{k}. (412)

The full simplified Hessian is

H~=λ​nd2​I+∑i=1nbi​fi​i​fi​i⊤+∑i=1n∑j≠iai​rj,ik​fj​i​fj​i⊤.\widetilde{H}=\frac{\lambda n}{d^{2}}I+\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}f_{ii}f_{ii}^{\top}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{a_{i}r_{j,i}}{k}f_{ji}f_{ji}^{\top}. (413)

Here ai,bi,qj,ia_{i},b_{i},q_{j,i} are evaluated at the full minimizer. For the ii-cavity problem, superscript (i)(i) denotes the corresponding quantities after removing sample ii from both tensor legs.

Feature spectral bounds.

We use the following spectral estimates for the feature matrices: uniformly in ii and ℓ\ell,

‖[fℓ​ℓ]ℓ≠i‖op=𝒪≺​(1),‖[fj​ℓ]j≠ℓ,i‖op=𝒪≺​(d).\left\|\bigl[f_{\ell\ell}\bigr]_{\ell\neq i}\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(1),\qquad\left\|\bigl[f_{j\ell}\bigr]_{j\neq\ell,i}\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(\sqrt{d}). (414)
Lemma 24 (LOO coefficient stability).

Assume (A1)–(A3). Then, uniformly in ii,

maxℓ≠i⁡|bℓ−bℓ(i)|=𝒪≺​(d−1),\max_{\ell\neq i}|b_{\ell}-b_{\ell}^{(i)}|=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1}), (415)

and

maxℓ≠i⁡maxj≠ℓ,i​|aℓ​rj,ℓ−aℓ(i)​rj,ℓ(i)|=𝒪≺​(d−1).\max_{\ell\neq i}\max_{j\neq\ell,i}\left|a_{\ell}r_{j,\ell}-a_{\ell}^{(i)}r_{j,\ell}^{(i)}\right|=\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1}). (416)

The functions a=σ⁡(−m)a=\sigma(-m), b=a⁡(1−a)b=a(1-a), and r=β​q​(1−q)r=\beta q(1-q) are uniformly Lipschitz on the bounded-score event supplied by (A3); the corresponding LOO scores are bounded by (A2). Applying the Lipschitz bounds entrywise gives (415)–(416). ∎

Lemma 25 (Diagonal quadratic form).

Assume (A1)–(A6) and the feature spectral bounds (414). Let χd\chi_{d} be as in (88). Then, uniformly in ii,

fi​i⊤H~−1fi​i=χd1+bi​χd+𝒪≺(d−1/2).f_{ii}^{\top}\widetilde{H}^{-1}f_{ii}=\frac{\chi_{d}}{1+b_{i}\chi_{d}}+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (417)

+∑ℓ≠i∑j≠ℓ,iaℓ​rj,ℓ−aℓ(i)​rj,ℓ(i)kfj​ℓfj​ℓ⊤.\displaystyle+\sum_{\ell\neq i}\sum_{j\neq\ell,i}\frac{a_{\ell}r_{j,\ell}-a_{\ell}^{(i)}r_{j,\ell}^{(i)}}{k}f_{j\ell}f_{j\ell}^{\top}.

fi​i⊤H~−1fi​i=fi​i⊤Ai−1fi​i+𝒪≺(d−1/2).f_{ii}^{\top}\widetilde{H}^{-1}f_{ii}=f_{ii}^{\top}A_{i}^{-1}f_{ii}+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (431)

Lemma 26 (Off-diagonal quadratic form).

Under the assumptions of Lemma 25, uniformly for j≠ij\neq i,

fj​i⊤H~−1fj​i=χd+𝒪≺(d−1/2).f_{ji}^{\top}\widetilde{H}^{-1}f_{ji}=\chi_{d}+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}). (434)
Proof.

The proof is the same as that of Lemma 25. One removes all terms involving uju_{j} or viv_{i} to create a cavity independent of fj​if_{ji}. The direct Woodbury correction along fj​if_{ji} has coefficient ai​rj,i/k=O⁡(k−1)a_{i}r_{j,i}/k=O(k^{-1}) and is therefore absorbed into the 𝒪≺(d−1/2)\mathcal{O}_{\prec}(d^{-1/2}) error. The feature-removal and coefficient-removal errors are controlled by the same unmatched-Gaussian and feature-matrix estimates used above. ∎

Remark 10 (Use for χ\chi).

In the leave-one-out analysis, the operator TT will be a Hessian inverse, for example T=(H∖i)−1T=(H^{\setminus i})^{-1}, evaluated on a sigma-field that is independent of a fresh pair (ui,vi)(u_{i},v_{i}). Lemma 21 then gives

⟨uivi⊤,(H∖i)−1[uivi⊤]⟩=1d2tr((H∖i)−1)+Oℒ(d−1/2),\bigl\langle u_{i}v_{i}^{\top},\,(H^{\setminus i})^{-1}[u_{i}v_{i}^{\top}]\bigr\rangle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\tr\!\left((H^{\setminus i})^{-1}\right)+O_{\mathcal{L}}(d^{-1/2}), (435)

provided ‖(H∖i)−1‖op=Oℒ​(1)\|(H^{\setminus i})^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_{\mathcal{L}}(1). Thus the susceptibility can be characterized through the normalized trace of the inverse cavity Hessian. Lemmas 22 and 23 then justify replacing the original Hessian by simpler approximations without changing this normalized trace at leading order.

Appendix H Variational formulation of the scalar equations

This appendix verifies the variational representation used in Section 4.3. Throughout, ZZ and GG denote independent standard normal variables, and ν,χ>0\nu,\chi>0.

H.1 The scalar TAM functional

Recall

cr​(ν)=minμ∈ℝ⁡{μ+1r​𝔼Z​[ϕβ​(ν​Z−μ)]}.c_{r}(\nu)=\min_{\mu\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\mu+\frac{1}{r}\mathbb{E}_{Z}\left[\phi_{\beta}(\nu Z-\mu)\right]\right\}. (436)

The minimizer, denoted μr​(ν)\mu_{r}(\nu), is characterized by

r=𝔼Z​[σ⁡(β⁡(ν​Z−μr​(ν)))].r=\mathbb{E}_{Z}\left[\sigma\!\bigl(\beta(\nu Z-\mu_{r}(\nu))\bigr)\right]. (437)
cr′​(ν)=1r​𝔼Z​[Z​ϕβ′​(ν​Z−μr​(ν))].c_{r}^{\prime}(\nu)=\frac{1}{r}\mathbb{E}_{Z}\left[Z\,\phi_{\beta}^{\prime}\!\bigl(\nu Z-\mu_{r}(\nu)\bigr)\right]. (438)

Stein’s identity gives

cr′​(ν)=νr​𝔼Z​[ϕβ′′​(ν​Z−μr​(ν))].c_{r}^{\prime}(\nu)=\frac{\nu}{r}\mathbb{E}_{Z}\left[\phi_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}\!\bigl(\nu Z-\mu_{r}(\nu)\bigr)\right]. (439)

We will also use that crc_{r} is convex in ν\nu. Indeed, the function

(ν,μ)↦μ+1r​𝔼Z​[ϕβ​(ν​Z−μ)](\nu,\mu)\mapsto\mu+\frac{1}{r}\mathbb{E}_{Z}\left[\phi_{\beta}(\nu Z-\mu)\right] (440)

is jointly convex, and partial minimization over μ\mu preserves convexity.

H.2 Moreau envelope identities

Let S=Sν,χ​(G)S=S_{\nu,\chi}(G) be the minimizer in (76), and set

A:=σ(−S+cr(ν)),B:=A(1−A).A\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sigma\!\bigl(-S+c_{r}(\nu)\bigr),\qquad B\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=A(1-A). (441)

The first-order condition in ss is

S=ν​G+χ​A.S=\nu G+\chi A. (442)

Envelope differentiation in χ\chi gives

∂χMr​(ν,χ)=−12​𝔼​[A2].\partial_{\chi}M_{r}(\nu,\chi)=-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[A^{2}]. (443)

For the derivative in ν\nu, the envelope theorem gives

∂νMr​(ν,χ)=−𝔼⁡[A​G]+𝔼⁡[A]​cr′​(ν).\partial_{\nu}M_{r}(\nu,\chi)=-\mathbb{E}[AG]+\mathbb{E}[A]c_{r}^{\prime}(\nu). (444)

Differentiating (442) with respect to the standard Gaussian coordinate GG yields

d​Ad​G=−ν​B1+χ​B.\frac{dA}{dG}=-\frac{\nu B}{1+\chi B}. (445)

Therefore Stein’s identity gives

𝔼⁡[A​G]=−ν​𝔼​[B1+χ​B].\mathbb{E}[AG]=-\nu\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{B}{1+\chi B}\right]. (446)

Combining (439), (444), and (446),

∂νMr​(ν,χ)=ν​𝔼​[B1+χ​B]+νr​𝔼​[A]​𝔼Z​[ϕβ′′​(ν​Z−μr​(ν))].\partial_{\nu}M_{r}(\nu,\chi)=\nu\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{B}{1+\chi B}\right]+\frac{\nu}{r}\mathbb{E}[A]\,\mathbb{E}_{Z}\left[\phi_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}\!\bigl(\nu Z-\mu_{r}(\nu)\bigr)\right]. (447)

H.3 Saddle-point equations

The saddle potential is

𝒫α,r​(ν,χ)=λ2​ν2−ν22​α​χ+Mr​(ν,χ).\mathcal{P}_{\alpha,r}(\nu,\chi)=\frac{\lambda}{2}\nu^{2}-\frac{\nu^{2}}{2\alpha\chi}+M_{r}(\nu,\chi). (448)

Using (443),

∂χ𝒫α,r​(ν,χ)=ν22​α​χ2−12​𝔼​[A2].\partial_{\chi}\mathcal{P}_{\alpha,r}(\nu,\chi)=\frac{\nu^{2}}{2\alpha\chi^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[A^{2}]. (449)

Hence the χ\chi saddle-point equation is

ν2=α​χ2​𝔼​[A2].\nu^{2}=\alpha\chi^{2}\mathbb{E}[A^{2}]. (450)

Using (447),

∂ν𝒫α,r​(ν,χ)=λ​ν−να​χ+ν​𝔼​[B1+χ​B]+νr​𝔼​[A]​𝔼Z​[ϕβ′′​(ν​Z−μr​(ν))].\partial_{\nu}\mathcal{P}_{\alpha,r}(\nu,\chi)=\lambda\nu-\frac{\nu}{\alpha\chi}+\nu\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{B}{1+\chi B}\right]+\frac{\nu}{r}\mathbb{E}[A]\,\mathbb{E}_{Z}\left[\phi_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}\!\bigl(\nu Z-\mu_{r}(\nu)\bigr)\right]. (451)

Since ν>0\nu>0, the ν\nu saddle-point equation is

1α=λ​χ+χ​𝔼​[B1+χ​B]+χr​𝔼​[A]​𝔼Z​[ϕβ′′​(ν​Z−μr​(ν))].\frac{1}{\alpha}=\lambda\chi+\chi\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{B}{1+\chi B}\right]+\frac{\chi}{r}\mathbb{E}[A]\,\mathbb{E}_{Z}\left[\phi_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}\!\bigl(\nu Z-\mu_{r}(\nu)\bigr)\right]. (452)

This is exactly the χ\chi-equation obtained from the zero-residual limit of (130).

It remains to connect (450) with the variance equation. From (442),

𝔼⁡[A​S]=ν​𝔼​[A​G]+χ​𝔼​[A2].\mathbb{E}[AS]=\nu\mathbb{E}[AG]+\chi\mathbb{E}[A^{2}]. (453)

Using (446) and (450),

𝔼⁡[A​S]=−ν2​𝔼​[B1+χ​B]+ν2α​χ.\mathbb{E}[AS]=-\nu^{2}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{B}{1+\chi B}\right]+\frac{\nu^{2}}{\alpha\chi}. (454)

Substituting (452) into the last display gives

𝔼⁡[A​S]=ν2​[λ+1r​𝔼​[A]​𝔼Z​[ϕβ′′​(ν​Z−μr​(ν))]],\mathbb{E}[AS]=\nu^{2}\left[\lambda+\frac{1}{r}\mathbb{E}[A]\,\mathbb{E}_{Z}\left[\phi_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}\!\bigl(\nu Z-\mu_{r}(\nu)\bigr)\right]\right], (455)

which is the corresponding ν\nu-equation.

H.4 Maximization in χ\chi and convexity in ν\nu

For fixed ν\nu, the inner problem is concave after the change of variables t=1/χt=1/\chi. Indeed,

𝒫α,r​(ν,1/t)=λ2​ν2−ν22​α​t+𝔼​mins∈ℝ​{t2​(s−ν​G)2+ℓ⁡(s−cr​(ν))}.\mathcal{P}_{\alpha,r}(\nu,1/t)=\frac{\lambda}{2}\nu^{2}-\frac{\nu^{2}}{2\alpha}t+\mathbb{E}\min_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\frac{t}{2}(s-\nu G)^{2}+\ell(s-c_{r}(\nu))\right\}. (456)

The last term is the infimum of affine functions of tt, and hence is concave in tt. Thus the inner extremization may equivalently be viewed as a one-dimensional concave maximization in 1/χ1/\chi.

For fixed ν\nu, differentiating A=σ⁡(−S+cr​(ν))A=\sigma(-S+c_{r}(\nu)) with respect to χ\chi gives

∂χA=−A​B1+χ​B.\partial_{\chi}A=-\frac{AB}{1+\chi B}. (457)

Consequently,

dd​χ​(χ2​𝔼​[A2])=2​χ​𝔼​[A21+χ​B]>0.\frac{d}{d\chi}\left(\chi^{2}\mathbb{E}[A^{2}]\right)=2\chi\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{A^{2}}{1+\chi B}\right]>0. (458)

Moreover χ2​𝔼​[A2]→0\chi^{2}\mathbb{E}[A^{2}]\to 0 as χ↓0\chi\downarrow 0, while χ2​𝔼​[A2]→∞\chi^{2}\mathbb{E}[A^{2}]\to\infty as χ→∞\chi\to\infty. By (449), ∂χ𝒫\partial_{\chi}\mathcal{P} changes sign exactly once, from positive to negative. Hence χ↦𝒫α,r​(ν,χ)\chi\mapsto\mathcal{P}_{\alpha,r}(\nu,\chi) has a unique global maximizer.

Finally we prove strong convexity of the reduced potential 𝒱α,r\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r} defined in (78). The logistic loss has the Fenchel representation

ℓ⁡(t)=supa∈[0,1]{−a​t−I⁡(a)},I⁡(a):=a​log⁡a+(1−a)​log⁡(1−a),\ell(t)=\sup_{a\in[0,1]}\left\{-at-I(a)\right\},\qquad I(a)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=a\log a+(1-a)\log(1-a), (459)

with the convention 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0. Applying this pointwise in the Moreau envelope and minimizing over ss gives

Mr​(ν,χ)=supa⁡(⋅)∈[0,1]𝔼⁡[a⁡(G)​(cr​(ν)−ν​G)−I⁡(a⁡(G))−χ2​a​(G)2].M_{r}(\nu,\chi)=\sup_{a(\cdot)\in[0,1]}\mathbb{E}\left[a(G)\bigl(c_{r}(\nu)-\nu G\bigr)-I(a(G))-\frac{\chi}{2}a(G)^{2}\right]. (460)

Taking the supremum over χ>0\chi>0 yields

𝒱α,r​(ν)=λ2​ν2+supa⁡(⋅)∈[0,1]{𝔼⁡[a⁡(G)​(cr​(ν)−ν​G)−I⁡(a⁡(G))]−να​(𝔼⁡[a​(G)2])1/2}.\mathcal{V}_{\alpha,r}(\nu)=\frac{\lambda}{2}\nu^{2}+\sup_{a(\cdot)\in[0,1]}\left\{\mathbb{E}\left[a(G)\bigl(c_{r}(\nu)-\nu G\bigr)-I(a(G))\right]-\frac{\nu}{\sqrt{\alpha}}\left(\mathbb{E}[a(G)^{2}]\right)^{1/2}\right\}. (461)

For each fixed measurable a⁡(⋅)a(\cdot), the expression inside the supremum is a convex function of ν\nu, because crc_{r} is convex and 𝔼⁡[a⁡(G)]≥0\mathbb{E}[a(G)]\geq 0; adding λ​ν2/2\lambda\nu^{2}/2 makes it λ\lambda-strongly convex. The supremum of λ\lambda-strongly convex functions is λ\lambda-strongly convex. This proves the convexity and uniqueness assertions in Proposition 10.

Remark 11 (Meaning of the dual optimizer).

The optimizer a⁡(G)a(G) in (460) is the scalar limit of the sample-wise logistic weights. Indeed, equality in the Fenchel representation (459) is attained at

a=σ⁡(−t).a=\sigma(-t). (462)

Taking t=S−cr​(ν)t=S-c_{r}(\nu), where S=Sν,χ​(G)S=S_{\nu,\chi}(G) is the proximal minimizer, gives

a∗​(G)=σ⁡(−Sν,χ​(G)+cr​(ν)).a_{\ast}(G)=\sigma\!\bigl(-S_{\nu,\chi}(G)+c_{r}(\nu)\bigr). (463)

Equivalently, the proximal first-order condition gives

Sν,χ​(G)=ν​G+χ​a∗​(G).S_{\nu,\chi}(G)=\nu G+\chi a_{\ast}(G). (464)

Thus the dual optimizer is the limiting counterpart of the finite-dimensional coefficients ai=σ⁡(−mi)a_{i}=\sigma(-m_{i}).
